title: Sprintfy
pitch: Agent-native sprint planning where the agent proposes and the human approves. No WebMCP tool ever writes to your plan.
about_excerpt: Agent-native sprint planning where the agent proposes and the human approves. No WebMCP tool ever writes to your plan. Like Comment Story Updates Landing Page Live: https://sprintfy.vercel.app — no account needed to see the whole idea. Open it in the ChatGPT desktop app, in ChatGPT mode : its built-in browser exposes WebMCP on its own, so the tools register with no flag and no extension. Desktop Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing works too, as does Chrome with the ChatGPT extension. One caveat: Codex mode in that same desktop app does not expose WebMCP , so the tools stay dormant there and the page will honestly say so — same app, two modes, two answers. Ask your agent for start_guided_demo , or press "Show me a demo", and you land in a real workspace with a proposal already waiting in the review panel and six tools live. Inspiration Every "agent-ready" app I looked at exposed the same shape of tool: create_task , update_task , delete_task . The model writes straight to the database. That is fine until the model is confidently wrong about your sprint plan, and then you are doing archaeology on a project board, trying to work out what it touched and in what order. Project planning is exactly the wrong domain for blind writes. A plan is an argument about sequencing and effort — it is the thing a lead is paid to have an opinion about. Handing that to an agent as unsupervised INSERTs gets you a plan nobody trusts and everybody re-checks, which is more work than writing it by hand. So I wanted to find out whether WebMCP could carry something other than commands. Can a tool call ask a question and wait for a human's answer? If it can, the agent stops being a thing you supervise and becomes a thing you argue with. What it does Sprintfy is a sprint planner — requirements, sprints, tasks, hour estimates — that exposes its workspace to agents over WebMCP. No agent tool writes to the plan. The loop has three moves: 1. The agent reads the room. get_project_context returns the plan and what the human is currently looking at: active view, selected sprint, status filter, which proposal is open. The agent plans into a context, not a vacuum. 2. The agent proposes a diff. Every write tool authors a change set — an ordered list of operations stored as JSON, rendered in the review panel as a real diff: additions in green, field-level changes as before → after, removals struck through. Nothing has touched the domain tables. An agent can propose a sprint and the twelve tasks inside it as one unit, using local ref ids that resolve to real primary keys only at apply time. 3. The human decides, and the agent hears the answer. apply_pending_changes opens the diff and blocks — the tool call's promise stays open while the person reads it. Approve applies the whole change set in a single Postgres transaction and the tool resolves with what landed. Reject resolves with the reason they typed, delivered back to the agent as the tool result. You do not start from an empty board either. You hand Sprintfy the thing you already have — a backlog note, a PRD as .md , .txt , .pdf or .docx , or a few paragraphs typed in — and it returns a plan sequenced by risk rather than by comfort. A real Turkish brief produced 8 requirements, 4 sprints and 38 tasks in 56 seconds, in Turkish, with the database migration ranked critical and placed first. Sprintfy's own planner is held to the same rule. It does not write the plan either: it authors a change set marked source: "planner" that lands in the same review panel, behind the same gate. How we built it Next.js (App Router) and React on Vercel, Supabase for Postgres, Auth and Realtime, and WebMCP for the agent surface. The architecture is one idea repeated: the write path is a data structure, not a function call. Tools append operations to a change_sets row. A single PL/pgSQL function, apply_change_set , applies them atomically and resolves ref placeholders to real ids as it goes. It is declared security invoker , so row-level security still guards every insert it performs — an agent cannot use it to reach another user's project. On the WebMCP side: Surface detection. The API moved during the spec's life and shipping browsers do not agree yet, so one adapter registers against document.modelContext.registerTool , navigator.modelContext.registerTool , or navigator.modelContext.provideContext , whichever exists, and the header badge reports which one it found. Page-scoped tool sets. Four tools before you sign in, six inside a project. The surface changes as the human navigates. Cancellation is honoured. The AbortSignal passed to apply_pending_changes releases the approval wait, so an agent that walks away does not leave the page stuck on a modal. Tools never throw at the browser. Failures come back as text an agent can recover from, including "these task ids don't exist in this project, call get_project_context again." Planning uses a strict JSON schema derived from the same Zod schema that backs the propose_plan tool — one schema, two authors, so a plan from the model and a plan from an agent are the same shape. Challenges we ran into Tool calls do not wait for React. Two bugs had the same root: an agent could not always see the proposal it had just written, and focus moved the human's view without get_project_context reporting it. A tool call can land before React has committed state, so reading a render closure returns the past. Tools now read from a ref that is written before the state, never from a closure. Both cases became eval scenarios so they cannot come back. Registering the same tool twice. Navigating between pages left the previous page's registration alive and the browser rejected the new one as a duplicate. Fixed with a module-level registry where claiming a name synchronously releases the previous holder. A machine asking a question and getting an HTML redirect. An unauthenticated POST to the planning endpoint was redirected to the sign-in page; Next then read the multipart body as a server action and answered 404. In an app whose premise is that machines are first-class callers, that was the wrong answer to give one. API routes now reply in JSON. The date picker that could not be used. The month grid was absolutely positioned inside a modal that clips its own corners and scrolls its body, so it was sliced off a few pixels below the field. It renders into a portal now, in viewport coordinates, flipping above the field when there is no room below. Knowing where WebMCP actually exists. Support is not a property of an application, it turns out — it is a property of a surface inside it. The ChatGPT desktop app has two modes, and only one of them exposes the API: in ChatGPT mode the built-in browser hands the page document.modelContext with no flag and no extension, while in Codex mode the built-in browser does not, so the same URL in the same application registers six tools or none depending on which mode you are in. I spent a while concluding the tools were broken before realising I had been testing in the wrong half of one app. That is why the page never assumes. It probes each surface, reports which one it found, and — when it finds none — still works and still explains itself, in its own voice, to a person who came in through an ordinary browser. Faking things. An early version showed timed loading stages — "Reading the brief", "Sequencing by risk" — while the model call ran. They were theatre, in a product whose entire argument is that you should not have to take an agent's word for anything. They were replaced with the true elapsed seconds. Accomplishments that we're proud of The blocking approval gate. Turning a WebMCP tool call from a command into a request is the part that is hard to fake, and it means the agent can be genuinely useful — proposing whole plans rather than timid one-row edits — without ever being trusted with the write. The evals. /evals.js runs seven scenarios against the actual ToolDescriptor objects the page registered, on the live site, from the console, with no account. Seven of seven pass in production. They assert the invariants rather than the happy path: a proposal writes zero rows; a rejection arrives as the tool's return value; approval applies a sprint and its tasks in one transaction with refs resolved; hallucinated ids are refused outright rather than half-applied. And the fact that Sprintfy's own planner goes through its own gate. A product arguing for review does not get to exempt its author. What we learned That a tool result is a channel back to the human , not just a status code. Once you treat it that way, "the agent asked and I said no, here's why" becomes a normal part of the protocol rather than something bolted on top. That the reviewable-proposal pattern belongs in the page, not in the model. The site knows what a legitimate change to itself looks like, so the site should render the diff and hold the gate. Any agent — any model, any vendor — inherits that

title: S.O.L.V.E.R.
pitch: Introducing a 3D On-Chain Forensics Platform for Solana, DuckDB-Wasm locally gives sub-millisecond, zero-latency queries over hundreds of on-chain transactions with zero backend overhead.
about_excerpt: Introducing a 3D On-Chain Forensics Platform for Solana, DuckDB-Wasm locally gives sub-millisecond, zero-latency queries over hundreds of on-chain transactions with zero backend overhead. Like Comment Story Updates Banner Inspiration Tracing on-chain transactions during a fast-moving exploit or de-peg is brutal on 2D block explorers with dozens of open tabs. We created S.O.L.V.E.R. (Solana On-Chain Live Visualization & Exploration Engine) to give developers and security analysts a 3D, interactive flight deck that turns complex block history into clear, spatial intelligence. What it does S.O.L.V.E.R. connects directly to Solana mainnet to stream live transaction history for any wallet address into an interactive 3D spatial graph. The application parses raw blockchain data into a client-side DuckDB database, allowing users to run instant SQL queries to filter and analyze transaction flows right in their browser. Crucially, S.O.L.V.E.R. integrates the new W3C WebMCP standard, enabling AI agents to autonomously control the 3D camera, execute data filters, and highlight suspicious wallet activity alongside human analysts. How we built it We built the application using React 18, TypeScript, and Vite, leveraging Three.js and React Three Fiber to render the glowing 3D node graph. To process on-chain data entirely in the browser, we integrated DuckDB-Wasm alongside @solana/web3.js for live RPC communication. We used the @mcp-b/webmcp-types library to register WebMCP tools via document.modelContext, creating a seamless bridge between AI agents and our UI. For production, we crafted a multi-stage Dockerfile that packages a Caddy web server, which is deployed and running live on PaaS. Challenges we ran into Our biggest hurdle was getting DuckDB-Wasm to bundle cleanly inside Vite's production environment, which required handling WebAssembly binaries and Web Worker imports with specific URL directives. We also had to build a robust multi-endpoint RPC fallback system to handle public Solana rate-limits smoothly. Finally, implementing the experimental WebMCP standard meant designing a resilient polyfill fallback so the app works flawlessly on both standard and AI-enabled browsers. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are thrilled to have built a fully functional 3D forensics tool that runs 100% client-side with zero backend server dependencies for data processing. Achieving sub-millisecond SQL query execution over live blockchain data in WebAssembly was a massive win for us. Furthermore, being among the first applications to natively implement W3C WebMCP for AI-driven 3D canvas control showcases how AI agents can operate inside modern web apps. What we learned Building S.O.L.V.E.R. taught us how to effectively combine 3D graphics state with browser-level AI agent protocols. We learned how to manage camera lerping and smooth animations without interfering with user controls, as well as how to harness in-browser WebAssembly to offload heavy data parsing from servers directly to the client. What's next for S.O.L.V.E.R. Moving forward, we plan to implement real-time WebSocket streams so new blocks automatically pop into the 3D graph the second they are mined on-chain. We are also expanding the 3D engine to support multi-wallet cluster analysis, allowing analysts to map complex token-siphoning networks across hundreds of addresses simultaneously. Eventually, we want our AI agents to act as fully autonomous 24/7 sentinels that flag exploit patterns as they happen. Built With duckdb node.js react solana three.js typescript w3c webmcp Try it out demo.twistedlabs.dev Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Researched crypto to determine the project scope and how it will function and then used Gemini and OpenAI to build out the web interface and backend running on a PaaS. title: LINE-CALL
pitch: Human-controlled AI for live-event timing - keep every cue in line.
about_excerpt: Human-controlled AI for live-event timing - keep every cue in line. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Live-event schedules are fragile. A two-second change to one segment can affect speakers, video, lighting, audio, downstream cues, and the final hard-out. I wanted to explore a safer question: what if an AI agent could do the time-consuming reasoning without receiving unlimited control over the production interface? LINECALL started as a human-operated run-of-show application. For the WebMCP Challenge, I extended it into an agent-native control surface where the agent can inspect the schedule, compare possible timing strategies, and prepare a precise change—but a person remains responsible for approving the final action. The guiding idea became: [ \text{Agent explores} \rightarrow \text{Rules verify} \rightarrow \text{Human approves} \rightarrow \text{Agent acts once} ] What it does LINECALL helps an AI agent reason about live production timing through a small set of structured WebMCP tools. The agent can: Read the current run, revision, locks, readiness, and constraints. Compare a local segment move with a downstream ripple. Prepare an exact cue-level preview. Update low-risk cue readiness. Apply a timing plan only after the human approves that exact plan. The main demonstration begins at schedule revision R1. The user asks: The audience Q&A needs to start two seconds later. Find the safest way to absorb that delay without breaking the run, and show me the exact change before anything moves. LINECALL rejects the segment-only option because it breaks chronology. It identifies the safer downstream ripple and prepares a precise 13-cue change set. The live schedule does not change immediately. The operator reviews the proposed result and approves that exact plan. Only then does the fifth WebMCP capability, linecall_apply_approved_retime , become available. The agent applies the approved plan once. LINECALL advances the schedule from R1 to R2, displays a visible receipt, and removes the temporary apply capability. The active tool lifecycle is therefore: [ 4 \rightarrow 5 \rightarrow 4 ] A second test asks the agent to move the Opening sequence. Cue Q014 is human-locked, so LINECALL blocks the change. There is no tool that allows the agent to remove the lock or approve its own request. How we built it LINECALL is built with React 19, Vite 8, modern CSS, the WebMCP Imperative API, and Node’s built-in test runner. The WebMCP layer uses document.modelContext.registerTool to expose five purpose-built tools: linecall_get_run_snapshot linecall_compare_retime_options linecall_preview_segment_retime linecall_set_cue_readiness linecall_apply_approved_retime The tools use strict JSON schemas, explicit revision checks, deterministic plan IDs, and WebMCP trust annotations. The schedule engine is deliberately separate from the language model. It owns: Chronology validation. Minimum spacing rules. Hard-out enforcement. Schedule revisions. Human-owned cue locks. Stale-plan rejection. Exact approval binding. One-time application receipts. The agent helps reason about the available options, but the deterministic engine decides whether the resulting cue changes are valid. The user interface was also designed around two different needs. Operators see a dense, human-friendly cue score with timing, readiness, locks, conflicts, approval state, and receipts. Agents receive a semantic tool interface instead of having to guess what buttons or page elements mean. I added focused agent evaluation cases covering direct inspection, safe retiming, exact-plan application, locked-cue refusal, missing unlock authority, readiness updates, and unrelated questions where no LINECALL tool should be selected. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was designing useful agent authority without making the agent dangerously powerful. It was not enough to reject an unsafe call after it happened. The interface needed to make unavailable authority genuinely unavailable. That is why the apply tool does not appear before approval, appears only for the approved plan, and disappears immediately after use or invalidation. State management was another major challenge. A plan prepared at revision R1 must not be accepted after the schedule has changed. Every timing mutation therefore carries both an exact plan ID and an expected revision. The schedule rules also had to handle more than simple arithmetic. A timing change can create chronology conflicts, spacing violations, hard-out failures, or collisions with human-locked cues. The system needed to explain those conflicts clearly enough for both the agent and the operator. WebMCP browser support is still a new area, so verification required more than checking that JavaScript functions existed. I tested registration, discovery, tool schemas, handler behavior, the visible interface, and the complete approval lifecycle in a real Chromium production build. I also had to make sure the browser evidence process did not modify the project while the project was being fingerprinted for verification. That required separating temporary browser artifacts from the source tree and tightening the build-input checks. Accomplishments that we're proud of The biggest accomplishment is that LINECALL demonstrates a complete collaboration loop rather than a simple tool-call demo: The agent reads the current state. It compares multiple futures. Deterministic rules reject the unsafe option. The agent prepares an exact preview. The human reviews and approves it. The agent applies that exact plan once. The system advances the revision and leaves evidence. A separate locked request is refused. The project has: 30/30 passing tests. A passing production Vite build. A passing Chromium production interaction rehearsal. WebMCP contract and discovery tests. Agent tool-selection and call-order evaluations. A permanent HTTPS deployment. Seven replayed challenge cases with matching expected calls and arguments. An MIT open-source license. A complete illustrated README and narrated demonstration video. We are especially proud that human approval changes the browser-visible capability surface itself. Approval is not just a message or a modal. It changes what the agent is technically able to call. What we learned We learned that semantic tools are much more useful than exposing a general-purpose interface and asking an agent to guess how it works. A tool such as linecall_compare_retime_options gives the agent a meaningful domain operation. It communicates intent, inputs, constraints, and results directly. That is clearer and safer than asking the agent to click through a timetable. We also learned that safety should be represented in the capability model whenever possible. A missing tool is stronger than a tool that is always available but usually refuses. Another important lesson was that language models and deterministic systems are good at different things. The model is useful for interpreting a request and comparing alternatives. The schedule engine is better at enforcing exact rules. Keeping those responsibilities separate makes the whole system easier to test and trust. Finally, we learned that a convincing WebMCP project needs three kinds of proof: The tools are correctly defined. The product works in a real browser. The authority boundaries behave correctly over time. What's next for LINECALL The next step is to connect LINECALL to real production systems and live event workflows rather than the controlled challenge schedule. Planned directions include: Adapters for existing rundown, show-control, and scheduling systems. Team-based approvals with named operators and audit trails. More detailed resource checks across audio, video, lighting, and stage departments. Multi-event support for conferences, theatre, broadcast, live streams, and awards shows. Durable change history with replayable receipts. Additional WebMCP-compatible agent hosts and browser environments. More advanced planning tools while preserving the same human approval boundary. The goal is not to give an agent unrestricted control of live production. The goal is to make the agent genuinely useful while ensuring that people remain in charge of consequential decisions. title: CorrelAct
pitch: CorrelAct is human-governed operational AI that investigates across systems, proposes actions, and executes only what a human explicitly approves.
about_excerpt: CorrelAct is human-governed operational AI that investigates across systems, proposes actions, and executes only what a human explicitly approves. Like Comment Story Updates Login Dashboard Actions Approvals Runs Traces Evals Settings Tasks Billing CRM Investigation Workspace CorrelAct Human-led operational intelligence, built on WebMCP Inspiration Operational problems rarely live inside one system. A customer reports an issue through Support, the account context lives in CRM, and the root cause is buried in Billing. An AI agent can help connect those signals — but giving it permanent write access to operational systems creates a different problem: how do you let it act without giving it standing authority to make consequential changes? CorrelAct started with a simple idea: let the agent investigate broadly, but make its authority to act narrow, explicit, and human-approved. It should gather evidence, correlate information, and recommend an action autonomously. But before it creates a task, changes a customer record, or performs any other consequential write, a human reviews exactly what is about to happen. That became the core architecture of CorrelAct. What it does CorrelAct is a human-led operational intelligence platform that uses WebMCP to let a browser-native AI agent work directly across operational workspaces. The agent can: Read customer evidence from Support. Read account and renewal state from CRM. Read invoice and dispute evidence from Billing. Correlate those signals into one operational diagnosis. Submit a focused Proposed Action for human review. Wait for explicit human approval. Receive only the execution capability that was approved. Perform the approved consequential action through a protected backend. Leave a complete audit trail of the investigation, decision, execution, and outcome. Read → Correlate → Propose → Human Approval → Exact Capability Exposed → Constrained Execution → Audited Outcome The demo scenario Our reference scenario involves ACME , a NorthStar customer whose renewal is blocked. The agent discovers evidence across three operational sources: Support shows an escalated customer case reporting an incorrect invoice and blocked renewal. CRM shows ACME's account and persisted renewal state. Billing shows a disputed invoice with a variance and renewal hold. The agent correlates those signals and submits a Proposed Action. At this point, nothing consequential has happened — the run enters AWAITING_APPROVAL , where a human reviewer can inspect the evidence, recommendation, customer, organization, and the exact execution capability being requested. Only after approval does the run become APPROVED . Even then, approval does not execute the action — it authorizes the agent to perform one previously reviewed capability. Dynamic Agent Authority Most agent systems expose their write tools permanently and rely on the backend to reject inappropriate calls. CorrelAct narrows the capability surface earlier than that. If there is no matching approved work, the consequential WebMCP tools — create_task and update_crm_status — simply are not registered for the agent on the Tasks workspace. After a human approves matching work, the appropriate tool becomes available. After that authority is consumed, the executable run disappears and the available tool set is recalculated. The browser agent never holds permanent standing write authority. Authority appears because a human approved specific work — and disappears the moment that work is done. Two governed write paths, one approval boundary We deliberately implemented two different consequential actions to prove the governance model isn't a special case hardcoded around one integration. create_task creates a real GitHub Issue using the scope that was already reviewed and approved. The execution call cannot rewrite the approved task content, priority, team, customer, or organization. update_crm_status applies one approved CRM renewal-status transition — for example, blocked → escalation_open . The agent does not supply the target state at execution time; that transition is frozen inside the Proposed Action before human review. The execution tool receives only enough information to identify the approved run, organization, and evidence-bound customer. Both capabilities pass through the same governance model: Human Approval → Shared controlled-execution boundary (organization · customer · evidence · approval state · execution type · idempotency · audit) → either create_task → GitHub Issue or update_crm_status → CRM record This mattered to us because we wanted to demonstrate that human-gated agent execution is a reusable architectural pattern, not a one-off built around a single API. Same governed boundary. Different consequential action. WebMCP WebMCP provides the capability surface connecting the browser agent to CorrelAct: Tool Role get_case Read Support evidence get_customer Read CRM account and renewal state get_invoice Read Billing evidence submit_action_point Persist an evidence-grounded Proposed Action create_task Execute an approved GitHub task update_crm_status Execute an approved CRM status transition The three evidence sources intentionally demonstrate different implementation patterns. Support and Billing use deterministic browser-local reference datasets — they make the cross-system WebMCP investigation reproducible without pretending to be production database integrations. CRM is application-backed through FastAPI and PostgreSQL. The consequential actions are application-backed too: create_task and update_crm_status each reach independently protected backend routes. This distinction is intentional: browser-native WebMCP delivers the agent capability experience, while consequential authority stays server-enforced. Security and trust model CorrelAct assumes that browser-side restrictions alone are not sufficient protection for consequential actions — the backend independently re-checks every execution request. Enforced boundaries include: authenticated session and organization access; human approval state and the specific approved execution capability; evidence-bound customer matching; current CRM state for stateful mutations, so a stale approval can't silently overwrite newer data; allow-listed CRM transitions, execution scope, and durable idempotency; full audit persistence. We tested these boundaries through automated tests and live browser-agent abuse scenarios: an approved action tied to one customer cannot be replayed against another customer; a run belonging to one organization cannot be executed against another; a CRM transition whose expected state has gone stale is rejected rather than silently overwritten. Approval itself never performs the external write. Human visibility Human control isn't hidden inside API responses. CorrelAct makes the progressive authority model visible across the product — the reviewer sees the exact execution capability and scope before approval, the Tasks workspace shows whether write authority is locked, available, or consumed, and Runs / Traces preserve the full lifecycle: Agent Read → Agent Proposal → Human Decision → Agent Write → Outcome This makes the governance model both enforceable and inspectable. How we built it WebMCP for browser-native agent capabilities OpenAI-powered agent reasoning for operational investigation FastAPI for the protected application and execution boundary PostgreSQL for runs, evidence, organizations, CRM state, approvals, and execution records GitHub Issues API as a real external write integration JavaScript browser workspaces for Support, CRM, Billing, Investigation, Approvals, Tasks, Runs, and Traces Docker for reproducible deployment Azure Container Apps for the live deployment GitHub Actions for security checks, automated tests, browser testing, evaluation, and deployment The application also includes organization-scoped demo identities so isolation can be tested between NorthStar/ACME and Neptune/GreenMart. Challenges we ran into Separating approval from execution. A deceptively important architectural decision was ensuring that clicking Approve did not perform the action. Approval had to mean "this exact capability and scope may now be executed," not "execute this immediately." Keeping those phases separate made the system significantly easier to reason about and audit. Preventing approved scope from drifting. We didn't want the agent to receive approval for one action and then change its parameters at execution time. For CRM writes, the exact expected and target statuses are frozen before approval. For task creation, task content comes from the approved Proposed Action rather than a new free-form execution payload. Making authority visible. Backend authorization alone wasn't enough for the experience we wanted — we wanted the agent's available tool set itself to reflect current human authorization. That led to Dynamic Agent Authority: controlled execution tools are registered and remove

title: PaperPilot
pitch: A WebMCP research mentor that turns questions on a real scientific paper into source-linked explanations and ideas you can inspect, organize, and undo.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP research mentor that turns questions on a real scientific paper into source-linked explanations and ideas you can inspect, organize, and undo. Like 3 Comment Story Updates PaperPilot A WebMCP research mentor that turns questions on a real scientific paper into source-linked explanations and ideas you can inspect, organize, and undo. Try PaperPilot · Watch the demo · Explore the MIT-licensed code Inspiration Scientific papers assume you know the vocabulary, mathematics, and how to read their figures. A summary can explain the topic without teaching you the sentence that stopped you. Moving that sentence into a separate chat loses its location. Which paragraph supports the answer? What came from the authors, and what is model-supplied background? PaperPilot gives undergraduate-level readers a patient research mentor without losing sight of the paper. What it does The actual PDF stays in the middle, with continuous scrolling, a mentor beside it, and a knowledge graph and evidence trail on the other side. There is no persistent duplicate transcript. Highlight text on the page or mark a region with a description. PaperPilot creates an immutable source anchor, a visible annotation, and a linked reader-authored idea. A whole-paper structural map helps you navigate; separately labeled, unreviewed semantic suggestions provide starting points, not a claim that the application understands every page. The browser agent can explain prerequisites, connect concepts, add a question annotation, and return to the source. Seven mentor sections organize the response from a quick take through mechanisms, evidence, related ideas, and uncertainty. Individual claims distinguish document evidence, interpretation, background, and unverified external citations. Why WebMCP The page knows facts an agent should not invent: the active PDF, selected words, source geometry, issued identifiers, and current graph revision. WebMCP makes that application knowledge and its permitted actions available through structured tools. PaperPilot registers six native capabilities through document.modelContext.registerTool : paperpilot.read_focus , paperpilot.read_graph , paperpilot.focus_source , paperpilot.apply_graph , paperpilot.apply_annotation , and paperpilot.stage_explain . They support bounded reading, literal graph search, source navigation, reversible edits, and explanation staging. The agent changes the same graph and annotations the reader uses. Current public-release evidence records actual native callbacks on Attention Is All You Need and the unrelated GW150914 paper, plus limited-text and invalid-input checks. Registration alone is not our demonstration of agent use. Human–agent collaboration The reader chooses what is confusing. The agent teaches and organizes. The application checks sources, authority, revisions, and duplicate commands before committing an edit with a receipt and reversible history. Stale or foreign-paper requests fail rather than silently changing the context. Agent changes can appear immediately, but reader-side Undo and Redo provide the soft check. Mentor explanations remain local drafts until a separate Save decision. Saving, discarding, Undo/Redo, and PDF export are not WebMCP capabilities. A source link establishes traceability, not scientific correctness. Neither a successful callback nor a digest proves that the model interpreted the paper correctly. How we built it The public application is an anonymous static reader on GitHub Pages: no account, API key, database, or local server is needed. PDF.js renders the document; PaperPilot owns the spatial annotations and source anchors. Canonical records and a reversible reducer govern state. Graphology supplies topology, while Sigma and a complete keyboard-operable DOM outline provide graph views. Moving a node changes presentation, not evidence. Optional browser recovery is tied to the exact PDF bytes by SHA-256. It retains workspace records and saved notes, not the PDF itself or unsaved mentor drafts. The original document is unchanged, and annotated-PDF export is excluded. Codex helped with planning, implementation, tests, bounded parallel reviews, and browser verification. Real failures became regression tests: one navigation bug reported the right page while the viewer settled elsewhere after Undo/Redo. Replaying the repaired interaction checked the visible effect, not just the response. The demo uses edited live capture and disclosed synthetic narration. What I learned This was my first experience with WebMCP and MCPs generally. I learned to design an agent-centric application around explicit capabilities, not an agent's unlimited access. The most valuable lesson was separating intent, source evidence, applied effects, and human judgment—and making those differences visible in the product. Try the flow Open the public app in a WebMCP-capable browser/agent environment. Choose Open the live demo or a supported PDF. Highlight a difficult passage, give it an idea label, and choose Add highlight to the graph above the PDF. Ask the agent to read the selected source and graph, add a grounded concept and question annotation, return to the source, and stage an explanation with background clearly labeled. Inspect the evidence trail, follow a source link, and use Undo/Redo to compare changes. The note can stay unsaved. Honest boundaries This is a single-paper prototype, not universal PDF understanding. Admission is bounded to 25 MiB and 200 pages. Text extraction varies; there is no OCR service. Figure regions currently return locator_only and pixelUseVerified: false : a reader description is not proof that the agent observed pixels. Accessibility shaped keyboard controls, descriptions, status announcements, and the non-canvas outline. The owner manually tested in Microsoft Edge without a screen reader. The project owner has verified access from a second machine for this hackathon entry. Human acceptance of the primary keyboard/screen-reader flow, graph accessibility, and literal 200% zoom remains unverified and is deferred. This is not an accessibility-certified service or general production signoff. Native WebMCP was tested with OpenAI Codex's in-app browser on Windows, not established by the separate Edge report. Without WebMCP, the manual reader remains usable, but native-agent success is not claimed. Existing project, new challenge work PaperPilot already had discovery, project/import, and authenticated-service foundations. The challenge work refocused it into this paper-first public reader: spatial annotations, structural mapping, graph interaction, six native tools, claim-level mentor provenance, reversible commands, and browser recovery. Those older foundations are not presented as new work or as the public deployment's backend. The dated change disclosure and current release evidence preserve that distinction. title: Huginn
pitch: Test the moment, not the grind: a typed WebMCP test port for live browser games.
about_excerpt: Test the moment, not the grind: a typed WebMCP test port for live browser games. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The problem Coding agents are increasingly good at creating browser games, but testing the gameplay they create is still surprisingly blind. A source-code review can suggest what should happen and a screenshot can show pixels, yet neither exposes the authoritative state currently held in browser memory: the board, economy, legal actions, RNG state, campaign progress, or save timeline. That gap is especially painful in games. Important regressions often appear only after a sequence of decisions or behind minutes of progression. Reaching the same late-game moment by keyboard or pointer is slow and difficult to reproduce, while inventing a parallel test simulation risks proving behavior the real game does not have. Why WebMCP This use case depends on the live page. Huginn registers bounded, typed tools directly from the running game through WebMCP. The agent reads the same canonical state the renderer uses and dispatches through the same transition path as the player. The human stays in the loop and watches each committed action render on the real canvas. A backend API would miss the thing being tested: this exact deployed browser build, its in-memory save state, and the visual result currently in front of the designer. DOM automation alone cannot describe a Canvas or WebGL game, and raw coordinate clicking cannot reliably create or replay a semantic game state. What people and agents can do together With Huginn, a designer can direct an experiment in natural language: discover the game's rules, goals, metrics, action vocabulary, and curated setups; enter a real late-game moment without replaying unrelated progression; list only actions that are legal against the current state; run a visible sequence with a fixed seed and bounded steps; branch two plans from the same verified state and compare their outcomes; snapshot and restore the canonical save timeline; capture the rendered frame with an image hash paired to the exact state hash; save meaningful metric expectations as a portable gameplay regression. The submission demonstrates this on three playable games. COIL is a three-level campaign Snake game, STARFALL is physical pinball, and THORNWATCH is tower defense. COIL and STARFALL use native Canvas 2D; THORNWATCH uses PixiJS 8 and WebGL. The same shared tool surface works across both renderer families. The hero demonstration skips directly to COIL's real Level 2 signal gate and branches shielded versus unprotected play from an identical checksum. In THORNWATCH, the agent compares two tower plans through the same deterministic wave, then captures the visible PixiJS result. These are narrow, reproducible test cases—not claims that one seed proves game balance or fun. How it works Huginn is split into four layers: a protocol-independent kernel that owns deterministic execution, legal-action checks, snapshots, checksums, cancellation, and semantic verdicts; a separate WebMCP transport that builds strict JSON Schemas and performs the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool(...) calls; a small protocol-free runtime for reducer-first games; an optional in-page debugger for receipts, captures, and replay controls. Games implement an engine-neutral adapter: initial state, legal actions, reducer, metrics, serialization, restoration, and render callback. Human input and agent tools use the same state authority. The core never imports Canvas, PixiJS, DOM selectors, or a game engine. The shared tools are describe_game , get_game_state , get_metrics , list_legal_actions , apply_action_sequence , snapshot_game , and restore_game . The examples also provide the optional capture_game host capability. Inputs are closed and bounded: no executable code, selectors, arbitrary predicates, URLs, filesystem paths, or network targets. Every game also has a standalone build with identical rules and ordinary controls but no Huginn executable code. The production build traverses and audits those dependency graphs. This keeps Huginn optional instead of turning game development into protocol bureaucracy. What is new Huginn, its kernel, WebMCP transport, debugger, all three game implementations, tests, documentation, and the public site were created during the WebMCP Challenge submission period. A selected set of pre-existing, owner-authorized THORNWATCH art is published under CC BY 4.0 with exact source paths and hashes. All source code is MIT licensed. video_title: Huginn — Test the Moment, Not the Grind | WebMCP Challenge
video_transcript_excerpt: Coding agents can now build entire browser games. Games are a demanding test. State interaction, visuals, timing, and rules all have to work together, but agents still test them surprisingly blind. Source code tells them what should happen. Screenshots show pixels. Neither exposes the live board, legal actions, random seed, campaign progress, or save timeline where gameplay regressions hide. These are three real playable games: campaign snake, physics-based pinball, and tower defense. Each works with keyboard, mouse, or touch. No agent required. Huginn gives a coding agent a type test port into the running game through WebMCP. A person watches the same canvas while the agent reads real state, chooses only legal actions, runs an experiment, and captures reproducible evidence. In Coil, reaching signal gates normally means playing through level one. The agent asks the game to describe itself, then loads a game-owned level two setup. Huginn validates that setup through the real save system and renders it. From seed 12 in the same starting checksum, the first branch advances into the gate and dies. The second arms the shield, advances, and survives. The result is not just a screenshot. It includes type state, decisive events, and checksums. That exact moment can now become a regression test after the next code change. Now the same tool surface drives a different genre and engine. In Thorn Watch, the agent compares two tower placements through the same deterministic wave. The weak plan places towers too far from the road. The gate falls to 12 health with four leaks and no kills. The stronger plan leaves 18 health with three kills and one leak. Both runs started from the same checksum. Huginn's capture tool then returns a visible PNG, its image hash, and the exact game state hash. The agent can reproduce this result without replaying earlier waves or inventing an illegal move. Coil uses native Canvas 2D, Thornwatch uses PixiJS and WebGL. Huginn imports neither renderer. Each game supplies a small adapter for its state, legal actions, save codec metrics, and rendering. Huginn's core stays protocol independent. WebMCP registration and the debuggers sit around it. Huginn does not replace unit tests, visual review, or human judgment. It removes the grind between a coding agent and the gameplay moment that matters. Humans choose what to investigate. Agents reach, branch, compare, and document that moment live, visibly, and reproducibly. Huginn, test the moment, not the grind.

title: BananaLabs - WebMCP DJ
pitch: Everyone can code today. With BananaLabs, anyone can DJ tonight.
about_excerpt: Everyone can code today. With BananaLabs, anyone can DJ tonight. Like 2 Comment Story Updates DJ Interface with an AI prepared set Inspiration DJing is one of the last creative crafts that software never truly automated — because the hard part was never the buttons, it's the judgment. When to tease the next record in, when to slam the drop, how hard to ride the pitch. AI music tools generate songs; DJ software syncs buttons. Nobody had handed an AI agent the booth itself - the decks, the mixer, the FX, and asked it to be good. WebMCP made that question askable. Instead of an agent fumbling through a UI built for hands, we could expose the craft as structured tools and see whether an agent could develop taste: compose a set, perform it live, listen to its own work, and fix what sucked. BananaLabs DJ is our answer. What it does BananaLabs DJ is a web DJ workstation that a person and an agent can play together - same decks, same document, same tools. Upload a handful of tracks and the app measures them in a worker: BPM, musical key, drop points, energy curves, harmony (chroma), vocal regions. From there the agent takes over like a real DJ: It composes — picks track order by solving a mixability path over real join costs, cuts drop-anchored clips (never radio intros), and compiles every transition from a craft grammar: tease-slams that bleed the next record's build in under the current one, tempo and pitch rides, loop rolls, echo throws, backspins - every drop lands exactly on the 1. It performs — live in the browser on two tempo-matched decks, a 3-band EQ/filter mixer, crossfader, delay-throw FX bus and sampler pads, with SoundTouch keylock and a dosed vinyl "pitch scream" on rides. It listens to itself — review_set bounces the set offline and measures every join from the rendered audio: dead air, level jumps, bass stacking, masked first transients, slam punch. If something's rough, it gain-stages the levels and re-measures until clean. It ships — verify gates the document, then the set plays live, exports to WAV, or shares as a .blset. The human can interrupt at any moment - grab a fader, rewrite a join, or just enjoy the set. Live app: https://bananalabs-sable.vercel.app/ · Code (MIT): https://github.com/KushagraAgarwal525/webmcp-dj How we built it The core decision: one document, one pipeline, two performers. Every state change - from a human dragging a crossfader to an agent recompiling a transition - flows through the same SetDoc command pipeline, so human and agent never fork the mix. On top of that: WebMCP tool surface — 66 tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool, in two curated tiers: a compose-first surface (compose, audition, verify, review, play) and a booth-hardware tier (?booth=1) exposing loops, hotcues, EQ, sampler, FX. Per-tool output budgets keep results semantic, never truncated mid-JSON, and every mutation echoes a compile report (where the commit lands, whether it's on the drop): document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "review_set", description: "Bounce the arrangement offline and MEASURE each join from the rendered audio…", inputSchema: { /* index?, fix? */ }, execute: async (input) => { /* render → measure → report/fix */ }, }); Measurement, not narration — a worker analysis pipeline (STFT chroma, EDM-profile key detection, flux beatgrid with downbeats, salience-based drop detection, vocal regions) gives the composer ground truth; the composer never guesses bar math. The agent's ear — an OfflineAudioContext bounce renders the set with full parity to live playback (loop rolls, backspin rewinds, tempo rides included). That one renderer powers both the Download-WAV feature and review_set, so what the agent measures is exactly what the room hears. The loop is documented in the tools — compose with prepare_set, measure the sound with review_set (fix:true to gain-stage), gate with verify_set, then play. The agent never computes bar math and never plays unreviewed when it follows the descriptions. React + TypeScript + Vite on the front, Dexie/IndexedDB + OPFS for persistence, deployed as a static app on Vercel. Challenges we ran into The first agent sets were bad. Instant track-to-track switches read as random , not mixed. We rebuilt the transition grammar around handoffs - the tease_slam, so the crowd hears the next record arriving before the drop slams on the 1. The slam still sounded rough - so we measured it. The drop's first transient was landing mid-sweep and several dB hot. The fix (pre-open the incoming a bar early, a 1/16-bar flick on the 1, and per-entry gain staging) was proven by the agent's own review tool, not by assertion: it caught a +5.9 dB hot slam, staged it, and re-measured clean. Pitch rides went dull before they screamed. Unlocking keylock for a full 16-bar ride made the record creep thin; dosing the unlock to the final 4 bars - stacked with the loop roll and filter rise, made the festival scream. Along the way we found and fixed a keylock restore leak on deck reloads, a set-clock drift during un-laned overlaps, and a clip-clamping bug that silently destroyed drop anchors. Agents don't fail like users fail. Sixty flat tools invite an agent to push faders instead of compose — so we curated tiers. Agents narrate confidently and wrongly — so tools return measured truth, not stories. And our own live-debugging harness needed watchdogs and streaming logs after too many "stuck forever" sessions; vite HMR never swaps long-lived audio modules, so every proof runs on cache-disabled reloads. Accomplishments that we're proud of An agent that genuinely DJs — composes with craft vocabulary, performs live, and is good enough that a friend judged the set by ear and approved it. The agent-ear loop — review_set measures rendered audio and the agent corrects itself without human intervention. Watching it catch and fix a hot slam on its own was the moment the project took shape. Zero prompt magic required — the loop lives in the tool surface. Our most naive test prompt ("compose a dj set using these songs") drove the full compose → measure → fix → verify → play flow. A complete product, not a demo — persistence, undo/redo, WAV export, shareable .blset sets, a proposal banner for agent edits, a full smoke-test suite, and a CDP eval harness that bounces and scorecards every compose. Real DJ details done right — phrase-snapped drops, chroma auditions of actual overlap windows, loop rolls, backspins, echo throws that ring over the next drop. What we learned The tool surface is the prompt. When a naive instruction failed, the fix belonged in the tools - guidance, defaults, and honest echoes - not in cleverer wording. Agents need measurements, not assertions. The single biggest quality jump came from giving the agent an objective ear over its own output. Craft followed from feedback. Design the grammar, not the script. The agent picks what (recipes, order, intent); the engine owns how (bar math, lane compilation, clock). That separation is what made the agent's choices both free and safe. WebMCP's real unlock is shared state. The magic isn't that an agent can click our buttons - it's that two performers can work one instrument. What's next for BananaLabs - WebMCP DJ Calibration corpus — crowd-confirm drop/hook timestamps to keep sharpening the salience detector. Musical pitch rides — semitone-quantized landings keyed by Camelot relation, so rides resolve tonally, not just dramatically. True two-hand collaboration — human and agent performing the same set simultaneously (the shared document already supports it; the UX is next). Deeper measurement — harmonic dissonance scoring from the bounce, energy-arc analysis, and a crowd-simulation score. The pattern as a template — "compose → measure your own output → fix → verify → play" generalizes to video editing, motion design, and any creative app on WebMCP. I'd love to package it as the reference pattern for the agent-native creative web. title: Shared Reference Canvas
pitch: Describing elements in a visual interface to an agent can be really tricky. With this canvas you can easily create shared references that you and the agent can have in common as you work together
about_excerpt:
Describing elements in a visual interface to an agent can be really tricky. With this canvas you can easily create shared references that you and the agent can have in common as you work together
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 I have had a really hard time describing a UI to an agent. It understand teh world in a different way than i do, i usually point to things, mention 'here, there, this thing'. To an agent that is meaningless. I wanted to figure out a way to have a shared language that makes agent collaboration as seamless as possible, and i focused on working in a canvas for an agent. 

 What it does 

 When you select anything on the canvas it creates a short lived keyword that becomes the reference between you and the agent for that specific selection. You can select a group of elements and it creates a shared reference for the group, you can also select different empty regions. This makes describing things to an agent really simple when you are working with it, and you dont have to be sending out screenshots of the Ui for the agent to understand what you are talking about. 

 How we built it 

 I used NextJS, WebMCP, and Codex to build the infinite canvas with different media types. The keywords are meant to be stored locally and all the mcp tools as well so this is a really lightweight implementation that does not require having a stored state, or stored realtime session in a db. There are also dynamic tools when you double click on any element depending on its type, so you can have the agent operate differently depending on media type. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 I would say the biggest challenge was making the tools description and names as relevant as possible for the agent to make sense of them in a way that felt natural to interact with. In the beginning it would find the keywords but not have the necessary context on how the app worked, so its interactions with the user where sometimes confusing. In the beginning i solved this by giving the agent a tool with a really long description that explained the app, the tool was not meant to be used, it was jsut to have the agent read the context of the app. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I am really proud of how natural the interaction with the agent felt at the end. When i began playing around with the canvas and the agent, it felt really simple to just instruct the agent on what i wanted without having to overcomplicate my speech trying to describe an element. 

 What we learned 

 I learned how WebMCP works, this was my first project for the challenge. Having the mcp be registered in the html make sit so that any change in the UI can be immediately referred to by the agent. I also learnt about the Abort Signals for the agent, for destructive actions. 

 What's next for Shared Reference Canvas 

 I would love to see this become some sort of package where maybe its a extension for the browser or an app where any interface we use can also have these shared references as we everyday talk more with agents, and have to spend a painful amount of time describing our world that can sometimes be confusing to describe.

title: GWEN Zero-Credential Agent Authority
pitch: Give AI authority. Never give it your credentials.
about_excerpt: Give AI authority. Never give it your credentials. Like Comment Story Updates 01-GWEN-Devpost-Hero-WebMCP-Connected 02-GWEN-Zero-Credential-Browser-Verification 03-GWEN-One-Time-Email-Verification 04-GWEN-Agent-Requests-Address-Authority 05-GWEN-Human-Authorization-Grant 06-GWEN-Approved-Single-Use-Commit 07-GWEN-Authority-Consumed-Audit-Receipt 08-GWEN-Qwen-Returning-User-Email Inspiration AI agents are becoming capable of doing much more than answering questions. They can interact with websites, update accounts, send messages, schedule appointments, change records, and perform other real actions for people. That created a question I kept coming back to: Why should an AI need my credentials just because I want it to perform one specific action? If I ask an agent to change a delivery address, I may want it to have permission to perform exactly that change. I do not necessarily want to give it my password, a reusable API key, an OAuth token, a broad authenticated browser session, or some other credential that authorizes much more than the task I requested. GWEN started from the idea that human authentication and agent authority should be separate things . The human should authenticate as the human. The AI should receive only the smallest amount of authority necessary for the action the human actually approved. That became the central model behind GWEN: Humans authenticate. Agents receive temporary authority. And the principle behind the project: Give AI authority. Never give it your credentials. WebMCP was a natural fit for this idea because it allows a website to expose structured capabilities directly to an AI agent while the application still controls exactly what those capabilities mean and when they may be used. Instead of treating an AI as another fully logged-in user, GWEN treats the AI as an agent requesting narrowly scoped authority from a human-controlled security boundary. The delivery-address change in the demo is intentionally simple. The important part is not the address. The important part is the authority model behind it. What it does GWEN is a working WebMCP security prototype that separates human authentication from agent authority . A visitor begins by using their own email address to verify control of a browser session through a temporary, one-time sign-in link. The AI never receives that sign-in link, the browser session cookie, the Gmail App Password, or the visitor's credentials. Authentication establishes that there is a verified email-controlled human session. It does not automatically authorize an AI agent to make changes. Once the browser is verified, GWEN exposes structured WebMCP capabilities. The first capability is get_gwen_capabilities . This allows an agent to discover what GWEN supports and understand the authority model without receiving human credentials. The second capability is request_address_change_authority . This allows an agent to request permission for one exact delivery-address change and provide a reason for the request. Nothing changes when the request is made. Instead, GWEN displays the exact proposed value to the human in a visible authorization panel. The human can explicitly choose Authorize GWEN or Deny . Only after the human approves the exact request does GWEN dynamically expose another WebMCP capability: commit_approved_address_change This temporary commit capability does not accept another address. The value approved by the human has already been bound on the server. For example, if the human approves: 42 WebMCP Street the AI cannot substitute: 99 Something Else Street during final execution. There is no replacement-address parameter in the final commit tool. The agent receives authority to execute the exact action the human approved . The resulting GWEN Grant is: bound to the verified human session bound to one specific action bound to the exact approved value short-lived limited to one authorized use consumed after successful execution The current WebMCP grant has a maximum lifetime of 120 seconds. After successful execution, GWEN shows: 1 of 1 consumed and: Authority remaining: NONE The temporary authority disappears. GWEN then creates a persistent, human-bound audit receipt containing the action, previous value, approved new value, grant information, number of uses, remaining authority state, timestamp, and an internal identity hash associated with the verified session. The design principle is: Temporary authority should disappear. Evidence of what happened should remain. GWEN also includes Qwen , a local AI email conversation assistant running through Ollama. Qwen's conversation authority is deliberately separate from WebMCP action authority. A verified visitor can have a normal email conversation with Qwen without giving Qwen the human's Gmail password, magic-link token, or GWEN browser-session credential. The Qwen email capability has a hard 10-minute lifetime. Replies do not extend the original deadline. Per-message capabilities are single-use. Attachments are blocked. Oversized messages are rejected. URLs are not automatically fetched. Automated reply loops are guarded against, and restarting the Qwen worker revokes outstanding Qwen email capabilities. The visible email address remains normal. The short-lived capability is carried through email reply-chain metadata instead of forcing the user to communicate through a strange tokenized email address. GWEN can also maintain compact encrypted continuity for returning verified users without keeping their old authorization alive. That created another important design rule: Memory is not authority. How we built it GWEN's primary security and authority implementation is written in Rust using Axum . I built GWEN as a solo developer and deliberately kept the architecture small enough that I could trace the complete authority path myself. A simple rule emerged while I was building it: Browser shows state. Rust decides state. Redis authorizes state. SQLite records state. Rust and Axum Rust is the main policy and application layer. It handles: email-based browser verification temporary browser sessions server-side authorization WebMCP grant creation human approval exact-value binding one-use execution persistent audit receipt creation Qwen worker supervision application lifecycle and policy enforcement The security-critical authorization decisions are made on the server. Browser JavaScript presents the state and exposes WebMCP tools, but it is not trusted to decide whether an action is actually authorized. WebMCP GWEN registers structured WebMCP tools through the browser's model-context interface using document.modelContext.registerTool() . The initial capabilities are available for agent discovery. The final commit capability only appears after the human has approved the exact requested action. This means the available WebMCP tool surface itself reflects the current authorization state. Before approval, the agent has no commit authority. After approval, the temporary commit capability appears. After successful execution, the capability disappears. The final commit tool intentionally accepts no replacement address because the human-approved value is already bound on the server. Redis GWEN uses a dedicated Redis instance at: 127.0.0.1:6387 Redis stores temporary state including: one-time login capabilities browser sessions WebMCP grants remaining authorized uses temporary Qwen email capabilities worker ownership and lease state The host also has other software using Redis on port 6379 . GWEN deliberately does not use or modify that Redis instance. Redis is a good fit for GWEN because authorization should be temporary, expiring, and capable of being consumed atomically. SQLite SQLite stores information that should persist after temporary authority disappears. That includes: WebMCP audit receipts Qwen client accounting returning-user metadata encrypted compact Qwen continuity This creates a deliberate separation: Temporary authority belongs in Redis. Persistent records belong in SQLite. Human verification GWEN uses temporary one-time email verification. The sign-in link is short-lived and single-use. The resulting browser session also has a hard 10-minute lifetime. GWEN verifies control of the email-based session used by the demonstration. It does not claim to prove a person's legal identity. The correct description is therefore email-controlled session verified , rather than claiming biometric, legal, government, or cryptographic proof of personal identity. Qwen and Ollama Qwen runs locally through Ollama using qwen3-coder:30b . Qwen is the conversation assistant. Qwen is not the source of WebMCP authorization. The Qwen worker receives trusted GWEN project grounding separately from untrusted incoming email content. That means an incoming email cannot redefine GWEN's trusted security architecture simply by containing instructions that claim to change the system's rules. Qwen can also use encrypted compact continuity for returning

title: CharDesk
pitch: A shared visual medium for humans and AI agents. Agents edit structured text through WebMCP while people see and shape the result as a live Unicode canvas.
about_excerpt: A shared visual medium for humans and AI agents. Agents edit structured text through WebMCP while people see and shape the result as a live Unicode canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI agents are fluent in text, but people understand complex ideas faster when they can see structure, position, emphasis, and relationships. Existing collaboration tools usually force one side to compromise: people work through visual interfaces while agents imitate mouse clicks, or agents produce plain text that people must mentally reconstruct. We wanted a medium native to both. CharDesk began with a simple idea: What if the canvas were visual to people, but still made of tokens an agent could read and edit precisely? What CharDesk does CharDesk is a shared visual workspace for humans and AI agents. An agent can create or update a Blackboard through WebMCP. The result immediately appears as a live Unicode canvas that a person can inspect, navigate, and continue discussing with the agent. The same canvas can combine: Unicode and ANSI art Markdown and fenced code Mermaid diagrams Tables, JSON, and YAML Mathematical expressions Scientific plots and Vega-Lite Spatial layouts and character-based slides This makes CharDesk useful for explaining concepts, visualizing research, mapping systems, designing interfaces, presenting stories, and maintaining a shared project workspace. For example, someone can ask: “Explain how a GPU renders one frame.” The agent can turn that request into a structured visual scene containing a pipeline diagram, memory relationships, annotations, and styled interface elements—not just another long answer in chat. Why it is better with WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent would need to guess how to operate the interface or manipulate individual canvas cells. CharDesk instead exposes focused workspace tools for discovering, creating, reading, writing, patching, deleting, and validating Blackboard files. The source remains authoritative; the canvas is a live projection of it. This gives each participant the representation they work with best: Human sees relationships, hierarchy, and visual emphasis ⇅ CharDesk Blackboard ⇅ Agent reads and edits structured, diffable text Agents can also call chardesk_read_materials to learn the visual language from worked examples. The tool teaches not only how to call the API, but how to compose an effective scene. How we built it CharDesk has a protocol-neutral tool layer shared by two thin host adapters: Standard WebMCP for compatible Chrome environments The imperative WebMCP capability supported by ChatGPT Site Tools Both adapters expose the same underlying Blackboard operations, so product behavior does not depend on a particular browser integration. A Blackboard stores source files and layout metadata. Changes are compiled through a shared rendering pipeline into a fixed character grid. This pipeline handles Unicode width, CJK characters, Nerd Font glyphs, ANSI styles, structured diagrams, and multidimensional layouts. The browser keeps the latest valid canvas mounted while an agent edits the source. If an intermediate update is invalid, CharDesk returns diagnostics without replacing the visible scene with a broken or empty state. The same format also works outside the browser through the CharDesk CLI, making projects portable, inspectable, renderable, and friendly to normal version-control workflows. Challenges we faced One unexpected challenge was tool ownership across browser tabs. Opening several CharDesk pages could cause identical tools to be registered multiple times, leaving the agent unable to choose a target. We built an origin-level gateway lease so only one page exposes the tools, with automatic takeover when that page closes. Chrome and ChatGPT also expose different subsets of the evolving WebMCP API. Instead of spreading compatibility checks throughout the product, we isolated those differences behind capability adapters backed by one canonical tool definition. Another challenge was timing: some hosts inject WebMCP after the application has already loaded. CharDesk therefore uses an adaptive registration handshake rather than assuming the API exists at startup. Finally, we learned that exposing tools is not enough. An agent may know how to write a file without knowing how to create a compelling visual explanation. Embedding CharDesk’s materials and examples as a callable tool gave browser agents the missing creative context. What we learned The most important lesson was that agent-native design is not simply automation layered onto an existing UI. A better pattern is to give agents a precise, structured representation while giving people a rich visual projection of the same underlying artifact. WebMCP makes that relationship discoverable directly from the website, without requiring agents to reverse-engineer the interface. CharDesk explores what becomes possible when the web page is no longer just something an agent operates, but a shared medium in which the human and agent can think together. title: Glassbook
pitch: Your money. Your browser. Your agent. The ledger never leaves this tab. The agent comes to it. You see every call. You can rewind every write.
about_excerpt: Your money. Your browser. Your agent. The ledger never leaves this tab. The agent comes to it. You see every call. You can rewind every write. Like Comment Story Updates Dashboard. Spend, income, and net for the month. Transactions. Search, filter, and categorize. Activity log. Every agent call, and undo on writes. Budgets. Monthly limits and how much you spent. Import. CSV, Excel, OFX, or a text PDF. Rules. Save a merchant match and apply it. Inspiration Every budgeting app I have tried wants the statement first. Connect Plaid, upload a CSV, or paste it into a chat so a model can read it. You hand over a year of swipes, then get told you spend too much on dining. I started with a simpler question: can the ledger stay on your machine, and can you still get help? WebMCP is how I tried that. What it does Glassbook is a budgeting app that never leaves the tab. You import a statement, sort your spending, set budgets, and teach it a few rules about merchants you recognize. There is no account and no server. The ledger sits in localStorage . Connect an agent and it gets 18 WebMCP tools pointed at that same ledger. It can categorize a few hundred rows in one call, save a rule when you correct it, find a subscription you forgot about, work out why June cost so much, and set a budget. Every call lands in an activity log. If a write goes wrong, you can undo the last one, or walk back everything the agent touched. Doing this by hand is an hour of clicking category chips. A chat-only agent wants the statement uploaded first. Load the demo and you get about 320 uncategorized rows across four months. Ask the agent to categorize everything and the chips update on screen while it works. Once you connect an agent, tool results do enter its context. The tools send summaries and cleaned merchant names rather than your raw statement, unless you ask for more of them. Every call sits in the log. How I built it There is no MCP server sitting somewhere with a copy of your ledger. The tools run in the page, against the same Zustand store the UI is reading from. The site decides the schema, how little a read hands back, and what undo means. Each tool is defined once and registered on document.modelContext after the store loads, with fallbacks to navigator.modelContext and window.modelContext . Hosts do not agree on where to put it yet. ChatGPT injects it after first paint, and registration retries if it is not there. Then there is one wrapper around every call. It writes the activity row, and on a write it snapshots the whole ledger first, up to fifty deep. undoLast pops one. undoAll walks back a consecutive run of agent writes, including a streak where one call was wrong. Some tools only return text. The ones that make it feel shared also move the screen: highlight_transactions rings a row and scrolls it into view, set_view_filters puts you both on Dining for August, pin_insight leaves a card on the dashboard. Those do not work if the tools live on a server. Import follows the same rule as the ledger. CSV and TSV go through PapaParse, OFX and QFX through a local parser, Excel and text PDFs through AnyDoc WASM in a worker. Nothing is uploaded. await document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "get_overview", description: "Call this first to understand the user's ledger.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: {}, additionalProperties: false }, annotations: { readOnlyHint: true }, execute: async (input) => { const text = await executeRegisteredTool("get_overview", input); return { content: [{ type: "text", text }] }; }, }); Challenges I ran into The first real problem was that I could not get site tools to appear at all. I had ChatGPT desktop from the Microsoft Store, and document.modelContext was simply undefined. The permission settings had no site tools entry in them either. I updated the app, restarted it, tried again, got nowhere, and eventually decided the Windows build did not support WebMCP, wrote that into the README, and pushed it. What actually fixed it was uninstalling the Store version and installing the same app from the ChatGPT website. Different build, same machine. I could not find that documented anywhere. Undo was harder than it looked. Logging what the agent did is easy. I still needed a way to take a write back. The store ended up snapshotting the full ledger on every agent write. That felt heavy until I watched an agent categorize three hundred rows, save a rule, and set a budget in one streak, then rewound all of it with one click. Bank files are not one format: OFX, .xls files that turn out to be HTML tables, European statements where 1.850,00 means one thousand eight hundred and fifty and imports as one euro eighty-five if you are not looking for it. Scanned PDFs still do not work. The fix is OCR, and I am not adding a cloud one. What I'm proud of The demo works end to end. Load 320 rows, connect an agent, categorize the lot, correct a chip, save a rule so the correction sticks, find Scribd at $11.99, ask why June was expensive and watch it ring the Delta and Airbnb rows from the 18th, set a dining budget, then rewind all of it from the activity log. Data minimization is in the tools on purpose. get_spending_summary returns grouped totals instead of three hundred rows. list_transactions sends cleaned merchant names, fifty at a time, and never the raw description. There are no account numbers in the model. What I learned The useful part of WebMCP is that the page owns the contract. The site decides what is readable, how much comes back, and whether it can be undone. Someone who would never paste a bank statement into a chat might still let an agent help. The activity log and the ring around the Delta row mattered more than another read endpoint. If you cannot see the tool call, it is hard to trust it. What's next for Glassbook Rules need to get smarter. Right now it is substring matching on the merchant, and it should handle amounts and date ranges too. The date-order override in the importer works but it is easy to miss, and sooner or later someone will import a European statement and get the days and months flipped. localStorage is also not where a multi-year ledger belongs. IndexedDB at some point. Scanned PDFs stay broken until on-device OCR is good enough.
