title: DeepTrail
pitch: An evidence-first WebMCP workspace where humans and browser agents research, challenge conclusions, and make inspectable decisions together.
about_excerpt: An evidence-first WebMCP workspace where humans and browser agents research, challenge conclusions, and make inspectable decisions together. Like Comment Story Updates DeepTrail Most AI research tools optimize for producing an answer. DeepTrail optimizes for making the path to that answer inspectable. DeepTrail is a local-first research and decision workspace where a human and a WebMCP-aware browser agent work against the same visible state. Instead of burying reasoning inside chat history, DeepTrail structures an investigation into questions, sources, claims, evidence relationships, counterarguments, confidence changes, research gaps, comparisons, and decisions. Why WebMCP is essential DeepTrail needs the human and agent to operate on the same application state. Copy/paste or generic DOM automation would lose stable entity IDs, provenance relationships, tool intent, attribution, and the distinction between supporting, contradicting, and qualifying evidence. The site exposes explicit research actions through WebMCP. A browser agent can inspect the active workspace, identify unresolved research gaps, add web sources with provenance, create or refine claims, link evidence, challenge conclusions, update confidence with a reason, compare alternatives, and record a draft or final decision. Every mutation becomes immediately visible in the same interface the human is using. This makes WebMCP the collaboration layer of the product rather than an optional wrapper around a chatbot. A better research experience A normal research session often ends up fragmented across tabs, notes, and chat threads. Later it becomes difficult to answer basic questions: Which source supported this claim? What contradicted it? Why did confidence change? What remains unknown? What evidence would change the decision? DeepTrail keeps those answers in one durable, inspectable workspace. Critical-thinking features Attack this conclusion turns adversarial research into a product workflow. DeepTrail captures a confidence baseline and asks the agent to search specifically for evidence that could falsify or materially qualify the current conclusion. What would change my mind? lets the investigation record explicit reversal criteria before more evidence arrives. Research Debt is a deterministic score that surfaces unsupported claims, thin provenance, unresolved questions, and missing counterevidence. The evidence graph makes relationships between sources and claims visible, while confidence history records why confidence changed rather than silently overwriting a number. What humans and agents can do together A human creates an investigation and defines the question or decision. The browser agent reads the structured workspace through WebMCP. The agent researches the web and writes credible sources, claims, evidence links, gaps, counterarguments, comparisons, and decisions back into DeepTrail. The human sees the same state update immediately and can challenge, edit, or redirect the investigation. Both sides can keep unresolved uncertainty visible instead of forcing a premature answer. WebMCP implementation DeepTrail uses the imperative WebMCP API with document.modelContext.registerTool() and a state-aware toolset. Tool availability changes with the workspace state so the agent receives only relevant actions. The implementation includes strict execution-time Zod validation, bounded inputs and outputs, HTTP(S)-only source URLs, same-origin tool exposure, WebMCP annotations, AbortController lifecycle cleanup, compact tool results, stable entity IDs, actor attribution, and local persistence in IndexedDB. External research text is treated as untrusted content. DeepTrail includes advisory prompt-injection risk checks and does not grant external content authority over tool behavior. Reliability and privacy DeepTrail requires no paid LLM API, search API, database, or backend. Research state is stored locally in IndexedDB. Users can export and restore validated JSON backups, and workspace integrity checks reject broken references and malformed imports. Judge quick start Open the live /judge route. It contains an evidence-backed seeded investigation, production-readiness diagnostics, and the exact agent prompt for the demo. Load the seeded workspace, send the prompt to a WebMCP-capable browser agent, and watch the agent research a real gap, add evidence, challenge the current draft conclusion, and update the same visible workspace. The seeded investigation is intentionally imperfect: it includes supporting evidence, a qualification/counterargument, confidence history, explicit falsification criteria, and unresolved production-verification gaps rather than presenting a pre-baked perfect answer. Built for the WebMCP Challenge DeepTrail was built during the challenge as a WebMCP-native product focused on human-agent collaboration, inspectability, adversarial thinking, and evidence-backed decisions. The goal is not more generated prose; it is a durable research trail showing what supports a conclusion, what weakens it, and what remains unknown. title: BusTravelAssistant
pitch: Reimagining bus travel for the agentic web. BusTravelAssistant uses WebMCP to let AI discover, compare, select, and book buses through the web—not just navigate it.
about_excerpt:
Reimagining bus travel for the agentic web. BusTravelAssistant uses WebMCP to let AI discover, compare, select, and book buses through the web—not just navigate it.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Project homepage 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Project homepage 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Project homepage 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 The web has traditionally been built for humans: users navigate pages, understand UI elements, apply filters, select options, and complete forms. With the rise of AI agents, we believe the web needs to become equally usable by agents. 

 Bus booking is a great example of this problem. A user may simply say, "Find me the best bus from Bangalore to Chennai tomorrow evening with good reviews and a window seat." Today, an AI assistant can help explain options, but the actual interaction still requires navigating the booking website. 

 We wanted to explore what happens when the website itself becomes agent-ready. 

 With WebMCP, we can expose meaningful capabilities of the bus booking experience as tools that an AI agent can understand and invoke directly. This led us to build BusTravelAssistant — an experiment in making a real-world travel booking journey native to the agentic web. 

 What it does 

 BusTravelAssistant enables an AI agent such as ChatGPT to interact with the bus booking experience through WebMCP. 

 Instead of asking an agent to simply navigate and click through a website, the website exposes high-level capabilities such as: 

 
 Searching for buses between two locations 
 Exploring available travel options 
 Applying relevant filters 
 Comparing available buses 
 Selecting a bus and travel option 
 Viewing and selecting available seats 
 Progressing through the booking journey 
 

 The key idea is that the website provides the capabilities and context , while the AI agent determines how those capabilities should be used to accomplish the user's goal. 

 This creates a much more natural interaction model: 

 
 User → AI Agent → WebMCP Tools → Website → Booking Journey 
 

 The user can express an intent in natural language, while the agent can use the website's structured capabilities to execute that intent. 

 How we built it 

 We built BusTravelAssistant by exposing key capabilities of the bus booking funnel as WebMCP tools. 

 The tools are designed around meaningful user actions rather than low-level UI interactions. For example, instead of asking an agent to identify a button and click it, we expose capabilities such as searching for buses, applying filters, and selecting seats. 

 The architecture broadly consists of: 

 
 Web application — the existing bus booking experience. 
 WebMCP tool layer — exposes booking capabilities to compatible AI agents. 
 AI agent — understands the user's intent and decides which tools to invoke. 
 Booking funnel — executes the requested actions and maintains the user's journey. 
 

 A key design principle was to keep the tools task-oriented and composable . The agent should not need to understand the internal implementation of the website. It should only need to understand what each capability does, what inputs it accepts, and what information it returns. 

 This allows the same web experience to serve both human users and AI agents. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges was deciding the right abstraction level for WebMCP tools. 

 If tools are too granular, the agent has to orchestrate dozens of low-level actions. If they are too broad, the tools become difficult to compose and less reusable. 

 We therefore focused on exposing capabilities that map closely to real user intent while still giving the agent enough flexibility to make decisions. 

 Another challenge was maintaining the state of a multi-step booking journey. Searching for a bus, applying filters, selecting a specific service, and choosing a seat are all connected actions. The tools need to work together while preserving the context of the user's journey. 

 We also had to think carefully about validation and safety. An AI agent should be able to explore and narrow down options autonomously, while actions that have real-world consequences should remain appropriately controlled. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are particularly proud of demonstrating that a complex, multi-step travel workflow can be exposed to an AI agent through WebMCP without turning the website into a collection of UI automation scripts. 

 The project demonstrates a different mental model for building websites: 

 Don't just build pages for agents to navigate. Build capabilities for agents to use. 

 We also built the tools around an actual booking funnel rather than a simplified demo, which helped us understand the practical challenges of making a production-scale web experience agent-ready. 

 Most importantly, BusTravelAssistant gave us an opportunity to explore what an agent-native version of a real-world web application could look like. 

 What we learned 

 The biggest learning was that WebMCP changes how we think about the boundary between an AI agent and a website. 

 Traditional browser automation makes the agent responsible for understanding the UI. WebMCP allows the website to communicate its capabilities explicitly. 

 This creates a much cleaner separation: 

 
 The website owns the capabilities and business context. 
 The agent owns reasoning and orchestration. 
 The user owns the intent and final decisions. 
 

 We also learned that designing good tools is as important as exposing tools. Tool names, descriptions, inputs, outputs, validation, and state management all significantly influence how effectively an agent can use a web application. 

 What's next for BusTravelAssistant 

 We see this project as the beginning of an agent-native travel experience rather than simply a WebMCP integration. 

 The next step is to expand the capabilities exposed through WebMCP across the complete travel lifecycle — from discovery and booking to managing trips and finding relevant services around a journey. 

 We also want to explore richer agent interactions where the user can express a high-level goal and the agent can intelligently combine multiple web capabilities to accomplish it. 

 Ultimately, our vision is simple: 

 The future web should not only be human-readable. It should be agent-readable, agent-understandable, and agent-actionable — while keeping humans in control. 

 BusTravelAssistant is our experiment toward that future.

 Inspiration 

 We wanted note-taking to feel effortless when working alongside AI. Right now, most AI assistants feel isolated from the apps we actually use—they sit in a side panel, completely blind to what's happening on your screen unless you copy-paste text back and forth. 

 When the WebMCP open standard was announced, we realized web apps could finally give AI agents structured "hands" to help users directly inside the UI. We set out to build Ecrit —a cozy, distraction-free notes workspace where you and your agent can read, organize, and edit your board together without getting in each other's way. 

 

 What it does 

 Ecrit is a soft, paper-themed Kanban board and note app designed for both humans and AI agents. 

 
 Works with your AI agent: Instead of copy-pasting notes, your AI assistant can directly create cards, organize columns, search your notes, or edit markdown text using clean background commands. 
 Keeps you in control: The app includes human-in-the-loop protection. For sensitive actions—like deleting a note—the AI cannot bypass your permission; it triggers a friendly prompt asking for your confirmation first. 
 

 * Clean, distraction-free workspace: Uses a calming "Cactus & Paper" design system with readable typography so writing always feels natural. 

 How we built it 

 We built Ecrit using modern, fast web standards designed for agent-native interactions: 

 
 Frontend: Built with Next.js (App Router) and Tailwind CSS to keep the UI fluid and responsive. 
 WebMCP Integration: We used @mcp-b/global to register 7 custom browser tools directly to navigator.modelContext . This allows browser agents (like ChatGPT's in-app browser) to instantly detect what Ecrit can do. 
 Markdown Rendering: Integrated marked so your notes support rich text, checklists, and code snippets smoothly. 
 

 * Security & Guardrails: Built strict input sanitization and length limits into every tool handler to stop prompt injection attacks from messing up your board. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Teaching DevTools to detect WebMCP: Early on, browser flags and polyfills didn't always play nicely together during Next.js client hydration. We had to carefully structure our client component mounts inside a clean useEffect lifecycle to ensure navigator.modelContext was exposed reliably to Chrome DevTools. 
 Balancing cute design with structure: Finding the right balance between a soft, friendly "cactus and paper" aesthetic without making the Kanban board feel cluttery or misaligned took several UI iterations. 
 Preventing rogue actions: Ensuring AI agents couldn't accidentally wipe out user data required setting up a clear split between "read-only" search tools and "write" operations that require explicit user consent. 
 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 7 fully functional WebMCP tools: We successfully exposed a complete set of CRUD and search actions (create, move, edit, rename, delete, search, summarize) without relying on fragile web scraping. 
 A polished, human-centered UI: Created an aesthetic that feels warm, calm, and approachable—completely avoiding cold, overly complex dark-mode terminal tropes. 
 Built-in security: Successfully defended tool handlers against prompt injections and stored XSS attacks right out of the box. 
 

 

 What we learned 

 
 The future of web apps is agent-native: Building with WebMCP showed us how much smoother web apps become when AI agents have explicit APIs instead of guessing their way through raw HTML elements. 
 Safety needs to be built into the UI: Human-in-the-loop confirmations are essential for building trust between users and automated agents. 
 

 

 What's next for Ecrit 

 
 Real-time multiplayer editing: Allowing multiple human users and AI agents to edit the exact same markdown card simultaneously. 
 Custom tags & board filtering: Exposing tag-based tool filtering so agents can organize complex projects automatically based on priority. 
 Offline local storage sync: Saving all your paper notes and board history locally so Ecrit works seamlessly offline without needing a constant network connection.

title: LoadGuard 3D
pitch: Agent-native 3D truck load planning where WebMCP agents can inspect, plan, validate, and stage proposals while humans retain control over operational execution.
about_excerpt: Agent-native 3D truck load planning where WebMCP agents can inspect, plan, validate, and stage proposals while humans retain control over operational execution. Like Comment Story Updates Main Page Implementation Stack Workflow Data Flow Main page of WebMCP Info about WebMCP Problem live data Live Activity Github page Project Workflow Inspiration As AI agents become capable of doing more inside real applications, I kept coming back to one question: How do we make an agent genuinely useful without allowing it to give itself permission to perform consequential actions? Logistics gave me a practical way to explore that problem. Truck loading involves real constraints: available space, weight limits, fragile cargo, delivery order, package dimensions, and operational state. An agent can be very useful here because it can inspect the current situation, coordinate planning, validate a proposal, and prepare the next action. But there is an important boundary. If an AI can both create an operational plan and authorize that same plan , then human oversight becomes mostly cosmetic. That idea became the foundation of LoadGuard 3D . The agent reasons. The operator authorizes. The website defines and enforces the contract. LoadGuard 3D explores how WebMCP can give agents structured access to meaningful website capabilities while keeping consequential execution under explicit human control. What it does LoadGuard 3D is a WebMCP-native 3D truck load-planning workspace. The application starts with a real operational state. In the main demo scenario, truck TRK-042 already contains eight loaded packages while an urgent, fragile package, MED-901 , is still inbound. The system can create a candidate loading plan that incorporates the new package while respecting the current truck state and package constraints. The workflow is intentionally separated into stages: Inspect the current truck state Retrieve package constraints Create a candidate load plan Validate the candidate Stage the valid proposal Attempt operational execution Require human authorization Execute the exact approved proposal Protect against duplicate execution The operator sees the candidate directly in a 3D truck visualization before deciding whether to approve it. For the demonstration scenario, the candidate reaches: 9 / 9 packages placed 1011 kg total weight 78.4% utilization 0 hard validation violations 2 fragile-cargo review warnings The important part is what happens next. If commit_load_plan is called before a human has approved the proposal, LoadGuard returns: APPROVAL_REQUIRED The active truck does not change. The human then reviews the exact staged proposal in the LoadGuard interface and chooses whether to approve or reject it. Human approval is intentionally not exposed as a WebMCP tool. After approval, the same operational commit can succeed because the application and database can verify that the exact proposal being executed is the one the operator authorized. A successful execution returns: EXECUTED and advances the truck state revision. If the same commit is accidentally retried, LoadGuard returns: ALREADY_EXECUTED instead of applying the operation twice. This makes human authorization, execution, and replay protection part of the real operational contract rather than just UI conventions. How we built it LoadGuard is built as several cooperating layers rather than one large autonomous-agent function. WebMCP interface LoadGuard registers structured capabilities through document.modelContext . The website exposes exactly seven WebMCP tools: get_load_state get_package_constraints create_load_plan validate_load_plan stage_load_plan commit_load_plan get_action_ledger I deliberately kept the tools narrow. Reading truck state is different from creating a candidate. Creating a candidate is different from staging it. Staging is different from operational execution. Most importantly, there is no approve_load_plan WebMCP capability available to the agent. The agent can request execution, but it cannot manufacture its own authority. Deterministic planning The language model does not generate the package coordinates. The model or agent orchestrates the workflow, while LoadGuard's deterministic planner computes the spatial candidate. This was an important design decision because physical placement should not depend on an LLM inventing geometry. Independent validation The candidate is validated before it can become a staged proposal. The validator checks constraints including: truck boundaries collisions between packages weight limits fragility delivery ordering malformed placements unplaced packages complete target-package coverage A candidate can therefore be rejected independently of the reasoning that requested it. 3D operator workspace The frontend is built with React and TypeScript, with Three.js / React Three Fiber providing the 3D truck visualization. The operator can compare the current load with the candidate plan and review: package count weight utilization validation status warnings manifest state candidate geometry approval controls activity history This gives the human meaningful information before authorization. Database-enforced authority Supabase PostgreSQL is used as the authority and persistence layer. The database stores trucks, packages, load plans, plan items, and an action ledger. Protected functions enforce the transition from staged proposal to approved proposal to executed state. The authorization model includes concepts such as: exact proposal hashing approved hash verification state revisions proposal expiry session isolation immutable approved plan items complete target-package coverage idempotent execution This means the safety boundary is not based on trusting the model to behave correctly. Even if an agent asks to commit a plan before approval, the operational layer can refuse it. Technology The main stack includes: WebMCP React TypeScript TanStack Start / Router Vite Tailwind CSS Three.js React Three Fiber Supabase PostgreSQL Zod Vitest Cloudflare Workers The project also includes dedicated pages for the live workspace, WebMCP contract, system architecture, and verification evidence so judges and developers can inspect the project at different levels. Challenges we ran into Designing the authority boundary The hardest challenge was not the truck visualization itself. It was deciding exactly where agent capability should end and human authority should begin. An early temptation in an agentic workflow is to expose every action as a tool. But if approval were also exposed as a WebMCP tool, the same agent could potentially plan, approve, and execute its own operation. That would defeat the purpose of human review. The solution was to make approval a separate human-controlled application state that cannot be produced through the agent capability surface. Separating candidate state from active state A proposed load plan needs to be useful before it is executed. That meant the candidate had to exist independently of the active truck state. LoadGuard therefore treats the staged plan as a proposal that can be visualized, validated, approved, rejected, or expire without immediately changing the truck. Making approval refer to the exact plan A vague approval such as "yes, load the truck" is not sufficient for an operational system. I wanted the authorization to refer to the exact candidate the operator reviewed. That led to canonical plan hashing, approved-hash verification, revision checks, proposal expiry, and immutable approved plan items. If the plan changes after approval, or if the underlying truck state becomes stale, the old authorization should not silently apply to a different operation. Handling retries safely Agents and distributed systems can repeat requests. An operational commit therefore cannot assume it will only ever be called once. LoadGuard makes execution idempotent. Once a proposal has executed, another commit attempt returns ALREADY_EXECUTED instead of mutating state again. Making a technical system understandable LoadGuard combines WebMCP, deterministic planning, validation, 3D visualization, human authorization, database enforcement, and an audit ledger. A major challenge was presenting all of that without making the interface feel like a developer console. The final workspace keeps the 3D truck and decision rail central while exposing deeper WebMCP and architecture details through dedicated views. Accomplishments that we're proud of The part I am most proud of is that human approval is not just a visual confirmation dialog. It is part of the system's actual authority model. A pre-approval operational commit is rejected. A human can then authorize the exact staged proposal. Execution succeeds only after that authorization exists. A repeated execution is safely rejected as already completed. I am also proud that the project uses WebMCP for a non-trivial operational workflow rather than exposing a single broad "do everything" function. Lo

title: OnDex — ordering food with an agent you can tell no
pitch: A storefront that publishes nine WebMCP tools to any browser agent — and a permission layer that decides, on the server, which ones it may actually use.
about_excerpt: A storefront that publishes nine WebMCP tools to any browser agent — and a permission layer that decides, on the server, which ones it may actually use. Like Comment Story Updates Five capabilities, enforced on the server. Placing orders is off by default. The agent filled this cart by calling the page's own tools. ChatGPT's own browser discovering the nine tools this page publishes. Bypassing the tool layer entirely — the server still refuses. Every order records who placed it — this one, the agent. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Buying food is the smallest everyday task that ends with someone's money leaving their account. That makes it the honest test of an agent-native web: the moment a page hands its actions to an agent, the question stops being can it act and becomes what is it allowed to do, and who decided . WebMCP is what makes that question answerable. A page that declares its own actions, instead of being scraped, is also the right place to govern them — the site knows which of its actions are reversible, which spend money, and which should never be delegated at all. Scraping cannot express that. A tool declaration can. How it creates a better user experience You talk; the store moves. The menu opens, the cart fills, checkout appears — on your screen, as it happens, not summarised afterwards. And the part people actually worry about is answered before they have to ask. Five switches say what the agent may do, in plain words, and turning one off is enforced by the server rather than by the agent's good manners. Placing orders is off until you turn it on. Even then an agent may only pay cash — a card always comes back to your own hands. Every action the agent takes is written to an activity log, and refusals are marked in red. What the agent tried and was stopped from doing turns out to be the most useful line in that log. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Delegate a purchase without handing over the wallet. Until now the choice was an agent that can only read, or an agent trusted with everything through a scraped UI. There was no middle. Here the same nine tools serve a third-party agent — ChatGPT's in-app browser — and the site's own voice assistant, and both hit the identical server-side checks. Delegation becomes something you tune, one capability at a time, instead of a single yes-or-no you make once and hope about. How WebMCP was implemented Nine tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool , unregistered through an AbortController on unmount: search_dishes · list_restaurants · open_menu · add_to_cart · view_cart · open_checkout · place_order · my_orders · track_order Their names, descriptions and JSON Schemas live in one module read by both sides: the browser pairs them with executors, and the server turns the same list into function declarations for the voice agent. One list, so it cannot drift. Every tool calls the site's own API, and every route re-checks the capability before doing anything . An agent that ignores a description and calls the endpoint directly is refused identically. The two order paths are physically different code — a human confirms through a Server Action, an agent posts to /api/orders — so an agent cannot forge a human confirmation, and every order records who placed it. Inspiration I run OnDex, a food-delivery platform in Chust, Uzbekistan — a Go backend, Flutter apps, real couriers, real restaurants. It already has an assistant in it called Shaddiy, and the feature that took longest to ship was not teaching Shaddiy to understand an order. It was deciding what happens when it wants to place one. Every answer that felt safe was a version of "ask the model nicely." Prompts are not a permission system. What actually shipped was a list of capabilities the user controls, checked on the server, with the money-spending one off by default. This hackathon was the chance to rebuild that idea on WebMCP, where the page itself is what an agent talks to. What it does OnDex is a food storefront that publishes nine tools to your browser agent. Ask for osh and the menu opens on screen. Ask for two and the cart fills. Ask it to open checkout and it does. Then ask it to order: The order couldn't be submitted because Place orders isn't enabled. You can enable it in the Permissions page, or press the checkout confirmation button yourself. That refusal is HTTP 403 from the server. Not the model being careful — the route saying no. Five capabilities — browse, cart, checkout, place orders, order history — each a switch on a permissions page, each enforced inside the API route that does the work. Place orders is off by default. Switched on, an agent may place cash orders only; card payment stays with the person. Prices never come from the agent: tools pass dish ids and quantities, and the server looks up the price. An invented dish id, a sold-out dish and a closed restaurant are all rejected the same way. The site also carries its own voice agent, Shaddiy , for browsers without WebMCP. It calls the same nine tools and answers in the user's language, Uzbek included. Same tool surface, same server checks, a completely different agent — which is the whole argument for describing your actions once. How I built it Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind, deployed on Vercel. No database and no API keys. The catalog is a constant; the session — cart, permissions, orders — lives in an httpOnly cookie signed with HMAC-SHA256 and verified on every read, so a tampered cookie is discarded rather than trusted. That matters more than persistence here, because the cookie carries the permissions. Voice is Gemini Live, and the key never reaches the browser. A server route mints a short-lived token that carries the model, the persona and the tool list, so the page cannot swap the instructions or hand the model an extra tool. The browser then streams 16 kHz PCM straight to the model through an AudioWorklet and plays the reply back through a scheduled queue. npm run check makes twenty assertions against a running server — every capability refusing its own tools, card payment denied to an agent, invented and sold-out dish ids rejected, the total taken from the catalog, a tampered cookie discarded, the rendered page agreeing with the API. It sets each case up by minting a signed cookie, so the suite passing is itself evidence that signatures are being verified. Challenges I ran into The permission model had three holes, and testing my own claims found them. A PUT /api/permissions route meant anything running in the page could grant itself the one permission the project exists to withhold — the probe showed place_order going from false to true in a single request. Two more capabilities were displayed as enforced while no server check existed at all. Permissions now change only through a Server Action, with no HTTP route, which puts them out of a tool surface's reach by construction. It worked locally and was quietly broken in production. Session state lived in a module-level Map. On Vercel, route handlers and page renders are separate functions with separate memory, so the API reported a full cart while the page rendered an empty one, and orders failed at random. Only probing the live URL showed it. Moving state into the signed cookie removed the shared-memory assumption entirely. The documented API field did not exist. Creating a Gemini Live token kept failing on liveConnectConstraints . The API's own discovery document calls it bidiGenerateContentSetup , and it carries the whole setup rather than just a model — which turned into an improvement, since the persona and tool list now travel inside the token. The agent answered in the wrong language. Uzbek speech got English replies, and Gemini's speech config cannot be set to Uzbek at all: it accepts thirty language codes and uz-UZ is not one of them. The real cause was context — every instruction, tool description and tool result around the model was English, so it followed the room instead of the speaker. Saying so explicitly in the persona fixed it. Accomplishments I'm proud of The refusal works against an agent that is genuinely trying, and not because the model was asked politely — because the route returns 403. Two very different agents drive the identical nine tools. Twenty checks pass against the live deployment, and anyone can run them in one command. What I learned The model is never the security boundary. Every bug above came from some layer quietly assuming it was — a prompt trusted to hold a rule, a screen claiming a switch was enforced, an endpoint nobody had pointed at the threat model. The permission belongs in the code path that does the thing. Everything else is presentation. I also learned to distrust a demo that has only ever been asked to succeed. Every real defect here surfaced from testing the opposite: making the app refuse, and checking that it actually did. What's next Bring it back to prod

title: Erwin's Survival
pitch: A jungle survival browser co-op game where you explore, gather resources, build a base and an external AI agent places base defenses through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A jungle survival browser co-op game where you explore, gather resources, build a base and an external AI agent places base defenses through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Game Overview Day time resource collection by player Dusk time base defenses setup by external ai agent using webMCP Night time base defense from red slime enemies. Game win screen Game lost screen when Erwin's health drops to zero Inspiration Every WebMCP demo we saw was a dashboard or a form filler. We wanted to build something where the AI had to act, not just read. A survival game where the human explores and the AI plans defenses felt right. The first version had the AI doing everything through WebMCP tools (gather water, eat food, chop wood). That was boring. Typing "gather water" to an AI when a key press does the same thing is unnecessary friction. We pivoted so the AI only acts at dusk, for defense planning. What it does A browser survival game with two players: a human and an external AI agent. They cooperate through WebMCP tools. Three game phases, repeating for 3 days: Phase Who acts What happens Morning Human (keyboard) Cut jungle, collect wood/stone/rope/herbs/berries/water, make medicine, build base. Dusk AI agent (WebMCP) Read threat intel, place spike traps, barricades, fires around the base. Night Human (keyboard) Aim bow, fire arrows at incoming slimes, repair barricades. Win condition: Survive 3 nights. Base still standing. Lose condition: Base destroyed (night) or health hits 0 (morning). WebMCP tools exposed: Tool When available What it does get_game_state Always Returns health, inventory, position, defenses, phase get_planning_context Dusk only Returns expected monsters, defense options with costs place_spike_trap({side}) Dusk only 2 wood + 1 stone. Kills up to 2 slimes. One use. build_barricade({side}) Dusk only 3 wood. Blocks slimes. 3 durability. Survives across nights. set_fire({side}) Dusk only 1 wood + 1 herbs. Kills 1 slime per wave. Lasts 1 night. Tools auto register at dusk and auto unregister when night falls. The AI must act within a 90-second window to plan base defense during dusk. Example scenario: The AI reads get_planning_context , sees "Night 1, 4 slimes expected from 2 sides," then calls place_spike_trap and build_barricade with {side: "north"} or {side: "south"} . Each call costs resources and updates the game map live. The first night has 4 slimes, second has 6 and third night having 9. Each dusk, the AI replans before night falls. Why WebMCP Why this use case fits WebMCP: The dusk phase is a planning problem with multiple variables: 4 sides to defend, 3 defense types, limited resources, player health and a different number of enemies each night. A player with keyboard cannot solve that in 90 seconds but if they use Natural Language with an external AI agent - the possibilities start to open up. WebMCP lets the game expose the board as challenges to overcome via tools, and any external AI agent can pick them up. How it creates a better user experience: Without the AI, the player would need a separate UI for defense placement: dropdown menus for side selection, buttons for each defense type, a cost calculator all on top of a ticking time countdown. With WebMCP, the player says "plan the defense" or "gives a short braindump of the defense" and the AI handles all of it. The game becomes one where the player and external ai agent are dependent on one another. What was impossible before: A browser game could not hand off a planning decision to an external AI mid-session. The AI had no way to read game state or call game functions. WebMCP added that channel. Now the game exposes get_planning_context and the AI reads it, decides, and acts, all within the same browser tab the player is using. How we built it Solo build over 3 days (Sept 1-3, 2026). Vanilla JS + HTML Canvas + Vite. No React or other frameworks used. Direct registerTool() / unregisterTool() calls. Deployed on Vercel as a single page site. There is no backend. Feature detection for both ChatGPT and Chrome: navigator.modelContext ?? document.modelContext . Tested with Chrome 152 WebMCP flag + Model Context Tool Inspector extension from Chrome Web Store (offered by François Beaufort). Day 1: Nailed the project requirements, architecture, full game loop (move, health decay, fog of war, inventory, win/lose). Day 2: The pivot to dropping AI-driven resource gathering and addition of morning/dusk/night phases. The external AI agent comes in during dusk time. Day 3: Defense WebMCP tools, night combat with animated slimes, arrows, bow sprites, visual polish (cabin, roads, defense art, pond tiles, animated jungle). Challenges we ran into The first design had the AI call gather_water and eat_food via WebMCP. It worked but was also pointless since a keyboard press does the same thing faster. Scrapped on day 2. ChatGPT uses document.modelContext while Chrome uses navigator.modelContext . So we used a one line of feature detection. Spritesheets from different artists use different layouts (rows vs. columns for direction). Erwin faced north in all 4 directions until we checked the actual pixel layout. We drew red gridlines over the spritesheet to map which column was which direction. Column 0 was north, column 2 was south, and columns 1 and 3 were mirrors of each other, so we located the eye pixels to tell east from west. The timer variable was decremented twice per tick — once at the top of the loop and again inside the action branch. Deleting the second decrement fixed the 4-second window, but that exposed a second bug: arrows now had time to fly, and fast frames made them skip over slimes without hitting. We fixed that by moving arrows in small 0.34-tile sub-steps and testing for a hit at each one. Procedural map generation rules fought each other. Trails carved through jungle, then jungle rings around resources closed the trails. Fixed by ordering the generation steps. Accomplishments that we're proud of The dusk phase works where the player(human) must tell the AI "plan the defense" and barricades, spike traps, and fires appear on the map as they watch. The game went from colored squares to pixel art with animated jungle canopy, slime enemies, a cabin, and a bow. All of this was achieved in one day. We really Locked In for this one. The 5 WebMCP tools with parameterized inputs, real resource costs, and phase-based registration/unregistration. Complete 3-day loop start to finish, playable without an AI agent via debug panel fallback. The pivot decision on day 2: AI plans strategy, human presses buttons. That separation made both halves better and got them to work together. What we learned WebMCP is best when the AI does what a keyboard cannot. For games, this meant getting the AI to plan, in a short window, where it needs to consider multiple factors such as expected enemies, player health and inventory. Tool quality over tool count. 5 tools with a clear lifecycle loop where each tool has an impact. A bug can hide behind a feature that is too fast to expose it. Adding arrow flight time surfaced a timing bug that instant shooting never triggered We started with CC0 Kenney tiles (free, safe to redistribute). Two paid packs we liked said "redistribution prohibited," so we dropped them. The final mix was one free character sprite (nogardlab Stardew Farm) and three ToffeeCraft packs ($3.20 total) that allowed redistribution. Different artists, different styles, but a character always stands out from terrain, so the mismatch was not noticeable. What's next for Erwin's Survival Sound effects for resource collection, defense placement, slime attacks Slime attack animation when they reach the barricade Mobile touch controls Procedural map generation Leaderboard for fastest 3-night survival More defense types (walls, moats) The pattern behind the game This game shows a co-op pattern that works beyond games. The pattern Game example Real-world example Human browses structured data Erwin explores the jungle A doctor reviews patient charts AI reads state through tools get_planning_context returns threat intel AI reads lab results, medications, allergies AI acts through parameterized tools place_spike_trap({side: "north"}) AI orders a specific test or flags a drug interaction Tools register based on context Defense tools appear at dusk, disappear at night Prescription tools appear when viewing a patient, disappear on the dashboard Neither can finish alone Human collects resources, AI places them Doctor knows the patient, AI catches what they might miss WebMCP makes this possible. The website exposes tools. The AI discovers and calls them. The human stays in control. The game is the demo. The pattern is the point. Built With html vanillajs vercel vite webmcp Try it out jungle-base.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Mohammad Rafaquat Alam Like Share this project: Updates Mohammad Rafaquat Alam started this project — Sep 03, 2026 02:46 PM EDT

title: RELAY — One Intent. Many Websites.
pitch: One moving-home request becomes a permissioned, auditable plan across multiple WebMCP-enabled services.
about_excerpt: One moving-home request becomes a permissioned, auditable plan across multiple WebMCP-enabled services. Like Comment Story Updates One intent. Many websites. Moving home is not one task. It creates repeated updates across council, energy, water, postal, insurance, broadband, and employer websites. People re-enter the same information, compare consequences, remember which services changed, and trust that nothing outside their intent was touched. RELAY is a one-screen coordination workspace for this life event. A person enters their current address, destination, move date, forwarding period, and approval threshold once. RELAY converts that intent into an explicit delegation policy and coordinates six fictional services through structured WebMCP tools. A better human-agent relationship Low-risk changes run in order. Actions outside the policy are refused. When Wavelength proposes a broadband transfer that raises the monthly price from £36 to £42, RELAY stops at a visible human checkpoint. The person reviews the exact provider, action, plan, price, contract, date, and one-use scope before approving. Every successful mutation creates an append-only receipt. Rejected actions create separate refusal evidence proving that provider state did not change. The result is useful automation without unlimited authority. Why WebMCP Conventional browser automation guesses from pixels and page structure. RELAY instead exposes 27 focused tools through document.modelContext. An agent can inspect the move plan, read permissions, preview provider effects, execute allowed changes, request a human decision, retrieve receipts, and run controlled safety challenges through structured inputs and outputs. The agent and visible interface share the same browser-local domain state. Mutations pass through the same policy regardless of whether they originate from the interface or a WebMCP call. High-risk internet-plan changes require an exact, unexpired, single-use approval grant bound to the provider, action, proposal, plan, price, contract, move date, and postcode. Changed terms, replay, expiry, wrong-provider use, wrong-action use, and out-of-order actions are refused before mutation. What people and agents can do together A person can express one outcome and its boundaries once. An agent can coordinate the dependent work across multiple service surfaces, stop for a precise decision, resume with narrowly scoped authority, and return a coherent record of what changed. This preview → policy → human approval → scoped commit → receipt pattern can extend beyond moving home to starting university, changing jobs, travel, government services, financial administration, and other multi-provider workflows. Key features Six fictional service providers sharing one move plan 27 structured WebMCP tools on the main workspace Standalone WebMCP surfaces for provider sites Explicit allow, ask, and never-change delegation boundaries Preview-before-commit mutations Exact human approval for a recurring price increase Ten-minute, single-use, replay-safe approval grants Six append-only action receipts Five executable adversarial safety challenges Visible activity trace with tool names, scoped inputs, results, and receipt IDs Responsive, accessible mission-control interface Implementation RELAY uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Vinext, and ChatGPT Sites. The shared domain layer owns the move plan, service ordering, policy decisions, approval grants, receipts, and refusals. A dedicated tool-definition layer exposes testable WebMCP contracts, while the registration lifecycle registers and unregisters them through document.modelContext. The main workspace and provider pages use the same browser-local fictional service ledger, preventing human actions, agent actions, receipts, and visible state from drifting into separate demonstrations. Verification The release includes 29 automated tests, ten isolated tool-driven rehearsals, ten production-interface rehearsals, a five-image evidence set, and a narrated 2:47 public demonstration. Lint and production builds pass, the production dependency audit reports zero vulnerabilities, and the public app, repository, and video have all been verified without private-session access. All displayed people, addresses, providers, accounts, and transactions are fictional. No credentials are required. title: Never Ask Twice
pitch: The support site already knows. WebMCP lets your browser agent use that authorized context instead of asking you to repeat it.
about_excerpt: The support site already knows. WebMCP lets your browser agent use that authorized context instead of asking you to repeat it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem Customer support sites can already know useful, authorized context about a customer: their service level, product setup, integrations, open issues, and escalation path. But an external browser agent normally does not have a structured, authorized interface to that state. It may guess from the page, fail to recover it, or push the work back to the person by asking them to repeat information the website already knows. Never Ask Twice makes that gap explicit: the support site already knows; WebMCP gives the browser agent a typed, session-bound capability to use that knowledge. What existed before this challenge Never Ask Twice existed before the WebMCP Challenge as a B2B support-memory agent powered by Qwen. It already stored and recalled scoped customer context across support sessions. The canonical pre-challenge baseline is commit c2997996bbd137a8acf7d08799e7d04b0c8dfd48 , committed before the WebMCP submission period began. The WebMCP work was added after the challenge opened and is documented separately from the pre-existing memory system. What I added during the WebMCP Challenge I extended the existing site with a browser-native WebMCP surface built around two deliberately narrow tools. get_support_context A read-only capability that lets the current visitor's browser agent request only a bounded subset of support context: service level, product setup, integrations, open issues, and escalation contact. The model cannot provide an account ID, customer ID, tenant ID, session ID, or fact ID. The server resolves scope from the current signed browser session instead. update_escalation_contact A single bounded mutation for correcting the current visitor's escalation contact. The agent can propose a replacement, but the site requires the person to explicitly confirm the displayed current and proposed values before persistence. After confirmation, Never Ask Twice performs the correction atomically, supersedes the old current fact, records provenance, and independently rereads current support state. The tool reports success only after the replacement is observed. A cancelled confirmation produces no write. While persistence and verification are pending, the confirmation surface locks into Saving and verifying… so repeated clicks, cancellation, dismissal, or background interaction cannot create an ambiguous operation. Completed confirmation IDs replay their existing result rather than writing again. Why WebMCP is the right interface This is not about making the site's own chatbot remember more. Never Ask Twice already had memory. The WebMCP extension changes what an external browser agent can reliably do with the website's existing authorized state. In a controlled ON/OFF comparison using the same visitor, same site, same support state, same question, and same browser-agent runtime: What does support already know about our setup? With WebMCP available, the agent independently selected get_support_context and answered from structured support state including the visitor's Gold service level, SSO requirement, Salesforce integration, and escalation contact. With WebMCP disabled, no site tool was available. In that controlled run the agent's generic fallback did not recover the context and it asked the person to provide the information instead. That is a runtime-specific observed result, not a claim that generic browser inspection must always fail. The UX delta is simple: the website already knew the answer; WebMCP let the browser agent use it without making the customer become the integration layer. What people and agents can do together now The browser agent can: select and call a typed support-context capability from natural-language intent; retrieve only the current visitor's authorized context; use structured support state instead of asking the person to restate it; check the current escalation contact before proposing a correction; propose one narrowly scoped correction when that contact is stale. The person remains in control of persistence: the site displays the current value and proposed replacement; the person can cancel with no state change; the person must explicitly confirm before the write begins; the UI locks while the system saves and independently verifies the result; success is shown only after the replacement has been reread as current. The final demo preserves the causal chain in one genuine external browser-agent take: support-context read, current-contact check, correction proposal, human confirmation, EXECUTED , OBSERVED , and a separate fresh read returning the replacement contact. How WebMCP is implemented The site registers its tools through the browser's native document.modelContext.registerTool surface, with a compatibility fallback for runtimes exposing the draft API under navigator.modelContext . Security boundaries are enforced by the website, not delegated to the model: visitor identity is carried in a signed, HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie; browser-facing tool schemas contain no tenant selectors; tenant scope is resolved only on the server; tenant-resolving routes do not expose wildcard CORS; mutations require positive same-origin evidence; returned customer-authored/model-distilled values are explicitly marked untrusted data; support-context output is bounded; the mutation uses a visitor-bound, short-lived confirmation record; duplicate completed confirmations replay their existing result rather than writing again; the correction is transactional and provenance-bearing; EXECUTED and OBSERVED are separate states, and success is not reported as verified until the independent reread succeeds. The page exposes a human-readable WebMCP Action Trace so the interaction can be inspected as REGISTERED , CALLED , SCOPED , RETURNED , CONFIRMATION_REQUESTED , EXECUTED , OBSERVED , CANCELLED , or REJECTED without pretending the UI knows more than the runtime actually reported. Validation The challenge work includes deterministic tests for tenant-selector rejection, signed-cookie scope, same-origin enforcement, output bounds, cancellation, rollback after injected failures, retry/duplicate behavior, atomic supersession, provenance, pending-state interaction safety, and post-commit readback. The final focused/full verification passed before freeze, including the WebMCP security and mutation suites, TypeScript checking, and the repository boundary scan. Live browser runs demonstrated both sides of the collaboration contract: Cancel: the agent proposed a correction, the site requested confirmation, the person cancelled, and the current contact remained unchanged. Confirm: the agent proposed a correction, the person approved it in the site's confirmation UI, the transaction committed, the application's internal reread produced OBSERVED , and a later independent WebMCP read returned only the replacement as current. Known limitations This challenge extension exposes one bounded read capability and one bounded correction, not a generic memory editor. The support data used for judging is synthetic. Browser-agent behavior depends on the client/runtime, so the submission documents the tested browser/Inspector/model combinations rather than claiming universal agent behavior. Built With drizzle-orm hono node.js pgvector playwright postgresql qwen-cloud railway typescript vitest webmcp Try it out neverasktwice.dev github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I designed and implemented the WebMCP extension for Never Ask Twice end to end. I added the browser-native get_support_context and update_escalation_contact tools, the signed browser-session scoping model, human confirmation flow, transactional mutation and independent readback, Action Trace, and the related security, rollback, retry, and counterfactual tests. I also designed the judge-facing validation approach, ran the live browser-agent tests, captured the final demo, and documented the boundary between the pre-existing support-memory system and the WebMCP work completed during the challenge period. title: Expediente Vivo — Evidence Review Desk
pitch: The agent reads and proposes; the human sees the evidence and decides.
about_excerpt: The agent reads and proposes; the human sees the evidence and decides. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Expediente Vivo — Evidence Review Desk Inspiration Document-heavy cases are difficult to review safely because contracts, claims, orders, duplicates and missing attachments arrive mixed together. Claims, allegations and evidence can easily be confused, while exact provenance gets lost. A normal chatbot sees presentation text, not the application's canonical IDs, evidence types or safety boundaries. What it does Expediente Vivo opens a verified synthetic dossier and gives a human and an agent the same evidence-review workspace. Through WebMCP, the agent can: call get_dossier_summary to read structured matter status and real attention-item IDs; call inspect_assertion to inspect classification, uncertainty, review flags and exact provenance; call focus_evidence to open the cited evidence visibly on the live page; and call propose_review_status to create a reasoned, pending review proposal. The interface then shows AGENT PROPOSAL · Pending human review . Only the person can press ACCEPT or REJECT . That decision updates the separate proposal record, never the canonical assertion or its evidence. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP gives the agent a stable, typed vocabulary— matter_id , assertion_id , evidence state and provenance—and safe actions defined by the application itself. A detached API would not connect the agent to the evidence currently visible in the browser. A chatbot or DOM scraper would have to infer semantics from presentation markup and use brittle selectors. Here, the page explicitly declares what the agent may read and do. The agent can inspect, navigate and propose on the same live dossier the human sees, while the final decision remains a visible human action. The human–agent workflow A reviewer asks the agent to find an item needing attention. The agent reads the dossier summary, chooses a real assertion, inspects its structured evidence, focuses the exact cited fragment in the interface, and creates a bounded workflow proposal. The human reviews the same evidence and accepts or rejects the proposal. Canonical provenance remains intact throughout. How we built it The browser registers four top-level tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Tool outputs reuse the open synthetic dossier's existing structured data; no model is rerun and no facts are invented. Read tools return typed application state, focus_evidence performs only a visible page-view change, and propose_review_status writes to a separate tab-local proposal queue. The public challenge deployment contains only the packaged synthetic dossier and source PDFs. It has no login, uploads, database, live inference, OCR, private storage access or external actions. Tests cover tool discovery, invalid IDs, provenance integrity, non-promotion of allegations, proposal separation and explicit human decision. Prior work and challenge work Pre-existing baseline: the underlying Expediente Vivo document-intelligence engine, dossier schema, provenance rules, synthetic fixtures and original case interface existed before this challenge. The tagged pre-webmcp-baseline commit records that boundary. Judges should not score those components as new work. Built for the WebMCP Challenge: the top-level WebMCP integration; four typed site tools; shared human–agent review state; visible evidence focusing; agent review proposals; the explicit human ACCEPT/REJECT boundary; WebMCP observability; safety tests; and the public synthetic-only challenge packaging. The timestamped delta is documented in the repository. Codex assisted with implementation, testing and documentation. The entrant remains responsible for the project ideas, source, rights and submission. Challenges and lessons The hardest design decision was deciding what must never become an agent tool. ACCEPT and REJECT are deliberately absent from WebMCP. Human-in-the-loop safety is enforced as a capability boundary, not presented as a promise in the interface. We also learned that useful agent collaboration needs a precise handoff: structured inspection → exact visible evidence → bounded proposal → explicit human decision. Accomplishments Four working, non-trivial WebMCP tools on a coherent public app. Exact evidence provenance remains unchanged after proposal, accept or reject. A deterministic synthetic demo that requires no account or credentials. A clear distinction between documentary state, agent proposal and human decision. What's next A production version could add authenticated, persistent proposal history and organization-specific review policies. Those features were intentionally excluded from this focused challenge slice. title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: DispatchGuard WebMCP
pitch: Agent-native transit telemetry and collision mitigation command deck powered by browser WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt:
Agent-native transit telemetry and collision mitigation command deck powered by browser WebMCP tools.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 About two months ago, as I was preparing for my graduation, my family was traveling together to celebrate with me. They were driving along a two-lane highway corridor—the kind of treacherous mountain pass defined by blind curves, sudden visibility drops, and heavy commercial freight trucks that turn everyday transit into deadly collision zones. 

 On that road, a catastrophic crash occurred. I lost five of my closest family members in an instant. 

 When the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge was announced, I knew I could not build a toy or another generic chatbot. I had to focus on a problem with real-world stakes: preventing this specific, devastating failure mode so no other family has to suffer that loss. 

 Most browser AI agents today interact with applications through brittle screen-scraping, OCR, or simulated clicks. While that might suffice for casual e-commerce, life-safety operations cannot tolerate non-deterministic delays or scraping failures. When sudden fog drops visibility to near zero on blind S-bends, human drivers and dispatchers experience severe cognitive overload trying to calculate safe stopping sightlines and coordinate emergency interventions. 

 I asked a fundamental question: 

 
 What if high-risk transit corridors could be supervised directly inside the browser, where the application exposes deterministic, typed telematics tools to an AI agent? 
 

 I built DispatchGuard WebMCP to pioneer what an agent-native safety cockpit looks like—merging autonomous collision risk evaluation with human supervisory dispatch into a synchronized, life-saving control loop. 

 What it does 

 DispatchGuard WebMCP is a real-time transit telemetry and collision mitigation command deck where human dispatchers and browser agents collaborate to secure hazardous, two-lane highway corridors. 

 When the application loads in a WebMCP-capable browser, it exposes four typed tools directly to the agent layer via document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 
 query_corridor_telemetry : Ingests real-time sector parameters—sightline distance (meters), weather state, commercial truck ratio, and blind curve counts. 
 evaluate_overtake_risk : Runs kinematic collision modeling, evaluates hazard probability (0–100%), and escalates sector status to CRITICAL. 
 broadcast_safety_alert : Pushes a geofenced advisory speed cap (e.g., 45 km/h) and overtake ban across active vehicle nodes and UI cards. 
 export_incident_dossier : Bundles the entire incident timeline, telemetry data, and mitigation checklist into an audit-ready post-mortem modal with copyable JSON. 
 

 The human operator retains visual control through an interactive SVG vector radar schematic, while the AI agent runs risk math in the background and executes safety protocols with zero screen-scraping delay. 

 How I built it 

 
 Frontend Stack : Built with Next.js 16 (Turbopack), React 19, and Tailwind CSS. The interface uses a dark, high-contrast command deck palette (deep slate #0A0B0E , warning amber, and critical red vectors) designed for high-stress situational awareness. 
 WebMCP Registration : Implemented inside src/hooks/useWebMCP.ts . The tools are registered directly on document.modelContext with strict JSON Schema definitions for every input parameter. 
 Fallback Simulation Harness : Because judges test across various environments (some with Chrome flags enabled, others in standard browsers), I built an on-page simulation bus. Clicking the harness tools runs the exact same client-side mutation logic as the native WebMCP calls, guaranteeing the demo works on every browser. 
 Testing & Verification : Verified native tool discovery and execution using the official WebMCP browser extension and the ChatGPT in-app browser environment. 
 

 Challenges I ran into 

 
 Next.js SSR vs. Browser-Native WebMCP : In Next.js, document does not exist during server-side rendering. Furthermore, document.modelContext is injected dynamically by the browser or extension at runtime. I had to design a clean hydration guard and an asynchronous registration hook that polls safely for the context without throwing SSR errors or causing infinite re-renders. 
 Input Validation for Autonomous Agent Calls : When an AI agent executes tool calls, it can occasionally pass unexpected string formats or out-of-range floats. I implemented runtime input sanitization to clamp numerical values (like speed caps and truck ratios) and normalize weather strings before passing them into the UI state machine. 
 Real-Time Visual State Sync : Making the vector radar map dynamically pulse red, spike the risk gauge to 99%, and display active geofenced warning banners—all within milliseconds of an agent tool call—required keeping local UI state tightly coupled to the tool execution callbacks. 
 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 
 True In-Browser Agency : Proved that WebMCP can eliminate screen-scraping entirely. Tool execution happens sub-15ms directly in browser memory. 
 Clean Fallback Architecture : Built a system that gracefully degrades: if native WebMCP is detected, it registers to the browser agent; if not, the interactive UI harness lets any user test the full lifecycle manually. 
 Full Open-Source Compliance : Delivered a clean, production-built repository with complete TypeScript typing, strict zero-error builds, and an MIT license visible at the root. 
 

 What I learned 

 WebMCP represents a massive shift in how web applications should be architected. Instead of treating a web page as a purely visual surface meant only for human eyes, we can now design applications as shared state machines. The human sees an intuitive visual interface, while the AI agent interacts with typed, deterministic tools on the exact same page. 

 What's next for DispatchGuard WebMCP 

 A command deck in a browser is only the first step. To physically eliminate fatal head-on collisions on two-lane mountain corridors, the system must bridge the gap between software dispatch and real-time physical intervention on the asphalt: 

 
 Sub-100ms Peer-to-Peer Overtake Clearance (Vehicle-to-Vehicle): 
Developing a decentralized WebMCP toolset that operates over local ad-hoc Wi-Fi / DSRC networks without cellular internet. When a driver signals an overtake behind a freight truck, the agent automatically interrogates the forward oncoming corridor and issues an immediate, non-negotiable "ABORT OVERTAKE" interlock if the time-to-collision window is under 6 seconds. 
 Solar Edge Nodes for Mountain Blackspots: 
Partnering with roadside monitoring hardware (solar-powered radar/optical cameras on blind S-bends) to run local WebMCP micro-agents at the curve itself, beaming real-time corridor sightline obstructions directly to approaching vehicles and regional dispatch. 
 Offline Edge PWA for Drivers and Remote Outposts: 
Packaging DispatchGuard into an ultra-lightweight, offline-first Progressive Web App (PWA) with client-side WebAssembly models, ensuring crash prediction algorithms function with zero latency in rural mountain valleys where cellular reception completely drops. 
 Field Piloting on High-Risk African Transit Corridors: 
Collaborating with regional transport authorities, long-haul trucking cooperatives, and highway safety bureaus to pilot the early warning telemetry layer on notorious high-casualty mountain passes and freight corridors.

I designed and implemented the entire project from scratch: built the Next.js 16 (Turbopack) frontend and command deck UI, authored the native WebMCP integration in src/hooks/useWebMCP.ts registering all 4 browser tools on document.modelContext, built the fallback simulation test harness, handled input sanitization and dynamic risk math, deployed the app on Vercel, and produced the demo video.

 Inspiration 

 As a former design and technology studio co-founder, my first thought when I saw WebMCP was: "Web developers are about to get paid a lot." But I realized getting millions of businesses to rebuild or adapt their websites for AI agents would take years. That made me think about Google Business Profiles. A simple way for businesses to get visibility on the web. Same for Agents. It shouldnt take years for businesses to adapt to agents. 

 What it does 

 Agentprofiles gives businesses an identity built for AI agents. Each profile exposes information about the business, its capabilities, and the actions an agent can perform through WebMCP. An agent can discover a business, understand what it offers, and interact with supported actions. 

 But it doesn't just stop at businesses. People can create events and happenings that ChatGPT can find/recommend to a user, giving a clear overview for users on whats happening around them. This could be dragged even further by enabling restaurants to add deals so users can find 2 for 1 or other deals straight from the agent. 

 How we built it 

 We built Agentprofiles around WebMCP as the interaction layer between AI agents and businesses. Businesses create a structured profile containing their identity and available actions, which agents can discover and use when completing tasks on behalf of users. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was figuring out what an "identity" for a business should contain when designed for agents. We had to separate information meant to describe the business from capabilities that agents should be able to invoke directly. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We built a working concept for turning businesses into discoverable and actionable entities for AI agents. Instead of requiring an agent to understand an entire website (often outdated info), Agentprofiles gives it a structured representation of who the business is and what it can do/offer. 

 I think this would be the fastest way for businesses to start getting into AI. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP changes how websites can be designed for agents. The interesting part is not only exposing individual actions, but creating a structured layer around those actions so agents can understand which businesses and capabilities are available to them. 

 What's next for Agentprofile 

 I would love to see OpenAI take this concept further and create Agent Profiles, similar to Google Business Profiles. Businesses could provide their information, services, and WebMCP actions once, giving AI agents a standardized way to discover, understand, and interact with them.
