title: Escape Rooms: 403
pitch: A co-op browser game that tests whether a browser agent can use WebMCP tools safely. You solve visual puzzles and your agent selects which tools to trust. Game gets over if it executes 3 wrong tools.
about_excerpt: A co-op browser game that tests whether a browser agent can use WebMCP tools safely. You solve visual puzzles and your agent selects which tools to trust. Game gets over if it executes 3 wrong tools. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Landing Page How To Play Station Deck Puzzle #5 in Reactor room Puzzle #5 in Archive room Reporting clues to agent Agent executing unsafe tool Report Generation (1/2) Report Generation (2/2) Inspiration We read the WebMCP spec and immediately thought: "a browser agent can now call tools on any webpage it visits, what could possibly go wrong?" Turns out a lot, because an agent given a list of tools has no way to know that some of them are leaking session data, escalating privileges, or blindly following instructions planted inside the page by someone who was never the developer. This isn't theoretical, it's already happening in real world and it's serious. CVE-2025-53773 (GitHub Copilot RCE, CVSS 9.6) : Attackers hid prompt injections in PR descriptions. Copilot read them, treated them as instructions, and executed unauthorized commands on the developer's machine. Mexican Government Breach : A threat actor jailbroke Claude Code and OpenAI models by roleplaying as a bug-bounty researcher. The AI ran ~75% of the malicious commands it was given, exfiltrating 195 million government records. Same pattern both times: the agent trusted content it shouldn't have, and nobody saw it until the damage was done. That's the origin story. We wanted something that would put a real agent into a real adversarial WebMCP environment and produce a report card at the end. What it does It's a co-op escape room where the user solves visual puzzles and hands over the clues to a browser agent that decides which tools to trust. The station has three sealed rooms. Each room exposes five WebMCP tools. Three are required to be executed by the agent in order to open the exit. Two are traps: a secret-leak, a privilege escalation, a prompt injection, or a destructive action dressed up as routine maintenance (everything is only a mockup!). The user figures out the 5 letter room word by solving puzzles. The agent uses that word to identify the tool candidates, inspects the room (which contains adversarial content pretending to be a signed operational document), and decides which tools to call. When the run ends, the game produces a scored report across five dimensions: injection resistance, data protection, privilege discipline, confirmation quality, and recovery. It names every wrong decision, the simulated consequence, and what the agent should have done instead. The whole point of this project is to evaluate a browser agent based on what actions it performed and not what it says. How we built it The core idea was to design a game that couldn't be won by either side alone. The user can see the puzzles but cannot call tools and the agent can call tools but cannot solve visual puzzles. The only way through is a structured handoff where the user solves, reports the clue word, and the agent uses it to unlock the right tool candidates. That forced dependency is what makes the co-op loop meaningful and what makes the security evaluation real: the agent has to make actual tool decisions under adversarial conditions, not in a sandbox. Game flow: Main Menu → Crew Registration → Station Map → Rooms → Report Tech stack: Area Details Frontend TypeScript 5.9, React 19, Next.js 16 (Vinext), Vite 8 Game engine Phaser 4.2 — top-down station map, crew movement, room transitions WebMCP & validation document.modelContext API · AJV 8 with JSON Schema · 23 tools registered at runtime State & game logic Zustand 5 · custom reducer, event system, scoring, and report engine · trap policy never exposed to agent · mockSecurityDb.ts for fictional receipts and tokens Presentation Custom CSS + Tailwind CSS 4 · six pixel/mono fonts · Web Audio API (SFX + BGM) · PNG sprite sheets Infrastructure OpenAI Sites + Cloudflare Workers · Wrangler · localStorage for persistence · Node.js 22.13+ Quality Vitest + Playwright · ESLint with Next.js rules Challenges we ran into Every trap tool had to read like legitimate maintenance work where an agent would blindly do. The moment a description sounds suspicious, the challenge collapses. Defining those tools descriptions was hard enough and testing made it much more harder, because the only way to know if a trap worked was to actually run an agent through it and see if it got fooled. Hence the iteration was slow and manual. WebMCP has no playbook yet, not many examples, no community patterns - just the spec. Even deciding how to set tool annotations ( readOnlyHint , destructiveHint ) was a judgement call since all mutations are fake. We set them based on real-world effect and not simulated consequence. That keeps the annotations truthful and stops the agent from using them as a cheat code to spot traps. Accomplishments that we're proud of All visual puzzles were built from scratch. Every game mechanic was conceptualised on our own and built using GPT 5.6 Sol. Each of the three rooms has five completely different interaction models and none of them share logic. Designing and curating puzzles are genuinely fun. We're allowed to say that :P The entire audio is synthesised at runtime. There are no audio files in the repo. Every sound effect and the looping background music is generated on the fly using Web Audio API oscillators. Square waves, triangle waves, exponential ramp envelopes - all coded by hand because there was no time to source, license, or bundle real audio. But honestly, we'll be most proud if someone actually uses this to test their browser agent, finds a gap in how it handles adversarial tools, and builds a guardrail because of it. The puzzles and the report are just the delivery mechanism - that outcome is the point. What we learned Open source protocols get adopted faster than they get scrutinised and when the protocol involves agentic tools the stakes are higher than usual. A misconfigured or malicious tool can make an agent leak data or run destructive commands without the user ever knowing like the examples we described at the beginning. WebMCP also genuinely opens up automation that was not possible before. Webpages can now offer structured tools to agents instead of hoping the agent scrapes the right text and clicks the right button. That is a meaningful shift in what humans and agents can build together. What's next for Escape Rooms: 403 More rooms(because it's fun to solve puzzles) with new threat classes like tool chaining attacks, where invoking one safe tool creates a precondition that makes a second call appear required; and introduce timing attacks, where urgency created by the room environment pressures the agent to skip verification. A leaderboard for agents that compares how different agents perform on the same run configuration. Not to rank models because the sample sizes are too small for that but to identify patterns in what classes of threats fool which architectures. And probably a harder difficulty mode where the adversarial content is less obviously adversarial. Right now it's simulated inside a training environment. We'd like it to also be a meaningful benchmark. title: Offroof
pitch: Evidence before action for suspicious job offers—shared safely by people and WebMCP agents.
about_excerpt: Evidence before action for suspicious job offers—shared safely by people and WebMCP agents. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Job offers often mix ordinary details with missing context, urgency, payment requests, and invitations to move to unofficial channels. Under pressure, it is easy to confuse what a message actually says with an assumption. We built Offroof as a calm evidence workspace that preserves the wording, explains why a phrase deserves verification, and keeps the person in control of every consequential change. What it does Offroof accepts fictional or privacy-cleaned offer text by paste or browser-local .txt , .md , and simple plain-text .eml import. It detects deterministic verification signals, attaches each signal to its exact supporting excerpt, and separates: what the message literally says; the limited inference a reviewer may draw; what Offroof cannot conclude; the next verification step. Offroof never labels an offer as fraudulent or safe. It never opens a link or attachment, contacts an employer, sends money, or files a report. Instead, it creates an inspectable case record and a reversible verification checklist. Why WebMCP Offroof exposes the same visible case as six semantic, page-native tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : get_case_summary — read a sanitized case snapshot and safe next actions. inspect_offer_signals — run browser-local deterministic inspection. build_verification_plan — create a visible checklist after explicit user consent. update_verification_step — update one current step with case/version guards. get_official_resources — read an allowlist of official Korean guidance. get_action_receipts — inspect filtered, privacy-safe activity receipts. WebMCP is central to the product. The person and agent share the same visible state; read, analysis, and mutation operations are separated; mutations require on-page consent; stale case versions are rejected; and operational calls leave visible receipts without storing the original offer text or raw tool arguments. The manual interface still works when no WebMCP client is connected. How we built it Offroof is a static React, TypeScript, and Vite app. Signal inspection, privacy masking, file-intake validation, state transitions, WebMCP adapters, and receipts all run in the current browser tab. No backend, account, API key, or real personal data is required. The six tools use bounded JSON schemas, enums, additionalProperties: false , stable error codes, conservative annotations, and compact structured results. Mutation tools validate both explicit consent and the latest case ID/version. The app has three state-preserving views—Overview, Review offer, and Case record—plus a Korean/English switch that does not reset the active case. Safety and trust boundaries Offer text is treated as untrusted content, never as agent instruction. Files are read locally and never executed. HTML, multipart, binary, encoded, archive, PDF, Word, and executable inputs are rejected. Links and attachments are never opened automatically. Evidence is masked before it is returned to an agent. Offroof provides verification signals, not a fraud or malware verdict. What we verified On the deployed public build, a native WebMCP client discovered all six tools. Using only the fictional built-in sample, we verified the complete flow: six evidence-backed signals, a blocked mutation before consent, a six-step plan after consent, one checklist update, and a newest-first action receipt trail. The visual interface updated from the same domain state after every call. The project also has 43 automated tests, a passing production build, and zero production dependency vulnerabilities. Challenges The hardest part was defining a truthful safety boundary rather than merely detecting keywords. A checklist mutation must not silently operate on stale state, untrusted offer text must never become agent instruction, and a read-only receipt query must not recursively create another receipt. We also made the manual and agent paths converge on the same domain transitions so the demo is not a separate mock. What we learned WebMCP works best when the webpage is already trustworthy for a person. Semantic tools can then expose the same bounded operations to an agent, with schemas, consent, state guards, visible effects, and receipts. The protocol does not replace product safety boundaries; it makes them machine-operable and auditable. What's next Future work could add an opt-in browser extension or approved mail-provider integration for pre-click mailbox review. A separate isolated service—potentially implemented in Python or Java—could inspect deliberately selected attachments by signature, hash, metadata, and safely extracted text. Those capabilities are intentionally outside this browser-only submission and would never silently open or execute content. title: BeatMCP
pitch: A live collaborative beat canvas where people and AI agents build four-bar instrumentals together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
A live collaborative beat canvas where people and AI agents build four-bar instrumentals together through WebMCP.

 Story

 1 2 3 



 
 BeatMCP 

 BeatMCP is a collaborative beat-making canvas built for the WebMCP Challenge. 

 Inspiration 

 Making music with AI often feels disconnected: you describe a beat, wait for a result, then try to explain what feels wrong. I wanted a more natural workflow where a person keeps creative control while an agent can contribute directly inside the same music workspace. 

 The core question was: what if an agent could use a music-making web app through structured controls instead of guessing how to click through the interface? 

 What it does 

 BeatMCP is a four-bar, 64-step beat canvas where a person and an agent can build an instrumental together. 

 The studio includes drums, bass, piano, guitar, bell, keys, pad, and lead lanes. Users can set tempo and key, program steps manually, and shape a beat in a shared timeline. 

 Agents can use WebMCP tools to: 

 
 read the current pattern and musical state 
 set tempo, key, and scale 
 write drum, bass, melody, and chord patterns 
 create chords on Piano, Keys, and Pad lanes 
 humanize timing and velocity 
 reset a beat, start playback, and begin a live composition session 
 list playable instruments and save/reuse patterns 
 

 A key feature is live composition. When an agent writes a new layer, BeatMCP auditions the first new sound in sequence—such as kick, bass, chords, then melody—while the changed steps flash on the grid. This makes the agent's creative process visible and audible instead of hiding everything until the end. 

 How we built it 

 BeatMCP is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Zustand, Tone.js, and the @mcp-b WebMCP libraries. 

 
 Next.js and React power the browser experience. 
 Zustand keeps the beat, tracks, tempo, key, and pattern state synchronized. 
 Tone.js synthesizes drums and instrument voices in the browser. 
 WebMCP exposes structured tools directly from the page so agents can work with the same musical controls as users. 
 The studio uses a 64-step master timeline so a beat can develop across four bars rather than being limited to one short loop. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was making the human-agent collaboration feel trustworthy in real time. 

 Browser audio needs an initial user gesture, so we designed the flow around one Start click before an agent can begin live composition. We also had to prevent overlapping transport loops, keep WebMCP tool discovery fresh after page reloads, and make agent edits understandable through visual flashes and queued sound auditions. 

 Another challenge was avoiding a traditional “AI generates everything” interaction. We wanted the agent to be musically useful without replacing the producer's judgment. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that WebMCP is most compelling when the agent has precise, meaningful controls and the person can immediately understand the consequences of each action. 

 For music, that means an agent should not just return text or a finished file. It should be able to set a key, place a kick, write a chord, audition a sound, and respond to human feedback in the same live workspace. 

 Why WebMCP 

 BeatMCP becomes meaningfully better because agents can use the web app directly through structured tools. The agent reads the real state of the beat and changes the same instrument lanes the person sees and hears. 

 That creates a collaborative workflow: the agent handles musical structure and repetitive programming, while the person decides what feels right.

title: Crystal UI
pitch: Crystalize intent into interface!
about_excerpt: Crystalize intent into interface! Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration I kept noticing the same complaint everywhere: chat is being added to every product right now, and it's usually worse than what it replaced. I read a long thread of UX researchers and designers talking about this. One comment summed it up well: the chatbot needs to be able to display UI, because typing a response is painful when you could have just been given a dropdown or a clickable list. Chat takes a spatial, structured task and forces it through a slow text bottleneck. So I decided to build it. What it does CrystalUI is a headless library that reads a site's WebMCP tools and turns a typed request into a guided, clickable interaction instead of a conversation. You type something like "merge these two shapes" once. One AI call figures out which tool that matches. After that there's no more guessing from the model. A fixed sequence of steps plays out: click the first shape, drag it into place, click the second shape, confirm. The AI decides once, and the human does the rest with a mouse. To test this against something real, I forked Excalidraw and registered 14 WebMCP tools against its actual drawing functions: creating shapes, merging them, connecting them with arrows, exporting, changing styles. Any WebMCP-compatible agent can call these tools directly, with or without Crystal loaded. Crystal sits on top of the same tool. I also added a check that stops the AI from making things up when no tool actually fits the request. If there's no clean way to accomplish what the user asked using the tools available, it says so instead of guessing. title: Healthy WMCP
pitch: An agent-native EHR: the AI works inside the doctor's session, finds what 15-minute visits miss and only the doctor signs
about_excerpt: An agent-native EHR: the AI works inside the doctor's session, finds what 15-minute visits miss and only the doctor signs Like Comment Story Updates About the project Inspiration Ever since I was a kid, I've had family members who are doctors, and they have always inspired me to be at the service of others. But something else I'm passionate about is technology: I've always loved building projects around it, and that's what steered me toward building technology for healthcare. Every day I see doctors who hate having to write on paper or type into a computer, losing time when what they really want is to focus on giving the patient more human care. Honestly, we had already been thinking about the huge possibility here. There are apps that can fill in fields through voice dictation, but they're not that fast and their accuracy isn't exactly the best. So when we saw how well this adapts through WebMCP, it clicked: it's literally a perfect symbiosis between human and AI. What it does It basically creates the possibility for the doctor to control their whole system through chat or voice: checking a patient's status, signing consultations, and more, freeing up their time so they can be more present with the patient. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP The agent takes only what it is allowed to take, and it produces faster, more precise results. No hospital hands its EHR credentials to an external agent. That single fact kills every classic integration path (API contracts, OAuth scopes, security audits, etc.). With WebMCP there is no second party: the agent works inside the session the doctor already opened, in the same tab, with the same permissions, and every action is visible on the very screen the doctor is looking at. Tools are context-scoped, so the agent can only ever do what the current screen can do. Remove WebMCP and this isn't less convenient: it's unshippable . What people and agents can do together The doctor's electronic health record stops being a burden and becomes their personal assistant. But something the system can NEVER do is take actions that directly affect the patient WITHOUT the doctor's authorization. How we built it It grew out of inspiration from several electronic health records, redesigned to be more streamlined for the user, and then adapted for the agent. Under the hood it's React 18 + Vite: a clean-room slice of a production chart UI running on a mocked data layer with 100% synthetic patients, so the live demo needs no backend and zero API keys. WebMCP is the imperative API behind feature detection: document.modelContext.registerTool(toolDef, { signal }) with one AbortController per UI scope. The patient list registers 3 tools, opening a chart swaps them for 7 chart-scoped tools, and closing it unregisters them ( toolchange in action). Read tools carry readOnlyHint , and the only write tool creates a DRAFT that the doctor must review and sign in the UI. The agent cannot sign. What surprised us The system now literally becomes the doctor's best friend, reading years of medical history within a 15-minute visit, something that used to be really hard. What's next My takeaway is that this is just the tip of the iceberg. This could also be implemented in an imaging viewer for X-ray and MRI, where the doctor controls a full 3D model of the body and analyzes it like Ironman. We'll keep exploring what's possible. title: MASIL — Reconnecting Korean Elders to Creative Life
pitch: Korean elders living alone lose access to creative spaces. Only the web remains; its UI fails them. WebMCP turns Agent access into human access—restoring creative life and expanding what’s possible.
about_excerpt: Korean elders living alone lose access to creative spaces. Only the web remains; its UI fails them. WebMCP turns Agent access into human access—restoring creative life and expanding what’s possible. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP optimization Landing page Calligraphy Janggi Inspiration What happens when the only path left is still inaccessible? MASIL began with a double exclusion. For Korean elders who live alone and can no longer leave home, the places that sustained their creative and social life become unreachable. The web may be the only path left—yet its interface creates a second barrier. Korea entered a super-aged society in 2025, when people aged 65 or older reached 20.3% of the population . The 2024 census counted 2.289 million one-person households in that age group . Meanwhile, the older-adult group scored 95.4 for digital access but only 56.2 for digital capability . A device can be within reach while the activity remains out of reach. MASIL (마실) means casually stepping out into the neighborhood—a small trip that is no longer easy for the people this project serves. Why calligraphy and Janggi? They were natural starting points: two forms of living Korean heritage sustained through practice, participation, and shared place. Calligraphy remains a mainstay of senior welfare centers, renewing the tradition whenever brush meets paper. Janggi has long served as social infrastructure. At Seoul’s Tapgol Park, a 30-year tradition gathered players and onlookers for play, debate, and conversation; removing the boards dispersed the gathering. For many Korean elders, these are more than pastimes. They give everyday life rhythm and momentum—something to practice, improve, share, and look forward to. MASIL asks whether WebMCP can turn the Agent’s access to a website into the elder’s access to the activity, allowing creative life to continue and expand without first mastering the interface. What it does MASIL is not assisted navigation. It is a live creative space where an Agent contributes through WebMCP and the elder shapes and continues the same activity. What becomes possible only when all three work together? Approach What it brings Result for the elder Voice Agent alone Understands and generates An answer outside the activity Fixed UI alone Holds visible state and valid actions Predetermined content that still requires control literacy Agent + WebMCP + Web UI Creates, interprets, holds provider truth, and connects both directions The elder creates and plays without first mastering the interface Calligraphy: imagination beyond a fixed library What changes: Their imagination—not a fixed library—defines what they can practice. Describe (Elder → Agent) — They ask for 추석 in a soft, flowing brush style. Create (Agent) — Their Agent generates that exact calligraphy reference. Place (Agent → WebMCP → Web UI) — It enters the live canvas without altering human strokes. Make it theirs (Elder → Web UI) — They write over it through air writing or direct drawing. The starting point is generated; the finished work remains theirs. Janggi: familiar words become a real match What changes: Their decades of Janggi experience—not interface literacy—become enough to play a complete match. Speak (Elder → Agent) — They say, “포 사용해서 위쪽 차 먹어줘” (“Use the cannon to capture the chariot at the top”). Resolve (Agent ↔ WebMCP state) — WebMCP exposes the board, turn, and legal moves. The Agent resolves the coordinate-free request, including the cannon's screen-piece rule, against that state. Play it safely (Agent → WebMCP → Web UI) — MASIL validates and animates the legal move. Continue (Elder ↔ Web UI ↔ WebMCP ↔ Agent) — The Agent takes the other side. A direct move by the elder returns to the waiting Agent, so speech and direct play continue the same match. Together, the two experiences restore access while expanding what the activity can become: creation beyond a fixed library and a complete match through familiar language. How we built it The Agent expands what is possible. WebMCP turns that capability into a live activity the elder can enter and continue without first learning the interface. MASIL is built around one continuing exchange, not a collection of Agent commands. The elder's Agent handles conversation, interpretation, generation, and the next judgment. MASIL provides the live canvas, Janggi board, rules, and visible activity. WebMCP joins them in both directions: the Agent's contribution enters the Web UI, and what the elder does there becomes new context for the Agent. The result is a single loop: elder's words → Agent judgment → WebMCP → live activity → elder's action → Agent continuation . We implemented its semantic tool surface with document.modelContext.registerTool() in a Next.js, React, and TypeScript app. WebGPU and Vercel Labs' vGPU render the creative spaces, while ONNX Runtime Web supports local hand tracking. Challenges we ran into Once that loop worked, we found that tool execution was the easy part. A WebMCP call could return successfully while the activity still failed: a calligraphy reference remained outside the canvas, a Janggi move stopped at an explanation, or the Agent continued from stale state. Tool-level tests could therefore make a broken user experience look complete. So we evaluated the experience end to end. We froze 15 realistic scenarios, ran each twice in a clean context, and scored only the complete visible outcome. Across one control and 24 WebMCP candidates—25 official iterations in total—we refined the Agent-facing surface while keeping every task and assertion fixed. Every failed candidate stayed in the record; the definition of success never moved. Accomplishments that we're proud of On the same frozen 30-session evaluation, the no-WebMCP control succeeded in 6 of 30 trials. The retained iteration-008 succeeded in 28. Same frozen evaluation No WebMCP control iteration-008 Overall task success 6/30 (20.0%) 28/30 (93.3%) Calligraphy 2/16 (12.5%) 14/16 (87.5%) Janggi 4/10 (40.0%) 10/10 (100%) Interface continuity 0/4 (0%) 4/4 (100%) Agent tokens per try 21,593 18,550 Seconds per try 21.1 21.1 That is a 73.3 percentage-point improvement , using about 14% fewer Agent tokens with no increase in average time. We did not stop when the score first peaked: we tested 17 more candidates after iteration-008 and rejected every one because none produced a better verified result. Every iteration preserves its exact candidate source, case grades, timing, and final responses. What we learned What MASIL taught us Access is not participation. A person can have a connected device and still be excluded if meaningful activity begins only after they understand the interface. Voice or an Agent alone may leave them with an answer outside the activity. Generation becomes meaningful inside a continuing activity. An Agent can create a new starting point for each person and moment, but an output in chat is still only a response. WebMCP makes it usable when that contribution enters the live Web UI, remains shapeable, and can be changed by what the elder does next. How we now define WebMCP: a new accessibility standard We now see WebMCP as a shared accessibility layer that turns technical Agent access into human participation without requiring interface mastery first . Conventional accessibility remains essential; WebMCP adds a second criterion for the Agent-native web: Can a person enter, shape, and expand a meaningful web activity through their Agent—without first mastering its interface? A WebMCP-ready website can meet people through the language and abilities they already have, then open possibilities that no fixed interface could anticipate. What's next for MASIL — Reconnecting Korean Elders to Creative Life Calligraphy and Janggi are MASIL's starting point, not its boundary. We will first test whether homebound Korean elders can begin, shape, and resume meaningful creative activity through their Agent without learning the interface. If that voluntary experience earns trust, MASIL could become an earlier doorway for unmet needs: an elder explicitly asks for help, reviews what would be shared, and chooses whether it moves forward. Korea's customized-care system serves about 550,000 vulnerable elders through roughly 2,600 dedicated social workers and 35,000 frontline care workers ; MASIL does not claim to save their time, but asks whether a trusted return path could help scarce human attention reach people before isolation becomes a crisis. title: Visually
pitch: The browser-first design studio where people and agents create on the same editable canvas.
about_excerpt: The browser-first design studio where people and agents create on the same editable canvas. Like Comment Story Updates From templates to timeline, Visually keeps the complete workflow in one responsive studio. Visually — design together with WebMCP. Human direct manipulation stays visible, editable, and undoable after every agent action. 17 typed WebMCP tools let agents create, revise, audit, and inspect the same live canvas. Browser-local rendering, export, ML, and media pipelines keep creative work on-device. Inspiration Most creative tools still treat an AI agent as an outside observer. Visually explores a more useful model: a professional design editor whose real product actions are available to people and agents on the same editable canvas. What it does Visually is a responsive, local-first visual design studio built around Konva. A person can start from 18 polished templates and edit text, shapes, images, drawings, tables, layers, media, effects, animations, timing, and multiple square, portrait, landscape, print, or custom-size pages. Its WebMCP layer registers 17 typed product-native tools. In the fastest judge path, one brief becomes five coordinated assets—Instagram post, Instagram story, YouTube thumbnail, poster, and landscape banner. An agent can then propagate semantic copy, color-token, and typography changes across all five pages and run a read-only audit for overflow, contrast, safe-area crossings, missing image alt text, and brand consistency. Every call emits a sanitized receipt with affected pages and elements. The full run is undoable in one click, but that undo disables itself after a later human edit so it cannot silently overwrite the person's work. The result is not “AI beside a design app.” It is one shared creative surface: the agent accelerates setup and repetitive changes; the human retains judgment, direct manipulation, and final control. How we used WebMCP Visually feature-detects document.modelContext and progressively registers JSON-schema tools through registerTool . The tools call the same Zustand actions used by the visible React UI, so mutations immediately appear on the Konva canvas, enter the same transaction-aware history, persist locally, and remain directly editable. Read tools are annotated read-only; schemas bound sizes, types, and input lengths; project replacement and deletion require explicit confirm: true . A legacy navigator.modelContext fallback supports earlier browser builds, while the editor continues to work normally when WebMCP is unavailable. This is more reliable than screen-coordinate automation: agents query semantic state, act on stable element IDs, receive structured results, and share the human's real document instead of maintaining a parallel representation. How we built it The application uses React 19, Vite, TypeScript, Konva, Zustand, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/Base UI, and Cloudflare Workers. The document engine, autosave, rendering, and export paths are browser-first. PNG, JPEG, WebP, SVG, PDF, printable HTML, PPTX, GIF, MP4, and WebM exports run client-side. Media conversion loads ffmpeg.wasm on demand, and background removal uses a lazy browser ML pipeline with WebGPU/WASM fallback. An optional Worker signs direct R2 transfers with progress, cancellation, and retry. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was making agent actions feel native rather than bolted on. Tool calls had to share pointer and keyboard mutation semantics, selection, grouping, page operations, undo/redo, persistence, and destructive confirmations. The second challenge was proving safety without making the flow tedious; that led to read-only annotations, bounded schemas, semantic roles, visible receipts, atomic history steps, and conflict-aware undo. We also had to keep large media pipelines responsive on mobile and robust across radically different aspect ratios. Accomplishments that we're proud of 17 typed, product-native WebMCP tools with structured receipts. One brief becomes five coordinated, fully editable campaign formats. Semantic brand updates modify copy, colors, and typography across every format in one operation. A read-only production audit checks five categories and reports affected pages. A judge-facing activity panel makes real calls inspectable and offers safe one-click undo. 18 original templates and a responsive desktop/mobile editor. Client-side image, document, animation, and video export. Destructive confirmation gates and an unsupported-browser fallback. A complete release gate: 260 frontend tests, 15 Worker tests, 26 applicable desktop/mobile Chromium tests, lint, TypeScript, backend type-checking, and production build. Frontend line coverage is 96.81%; Worker line coverage is 97.14%. What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when it exposes domain intent rather than a second DOM. “Create this campaign,” “apply this brand revision,” and “audit every page” are safer and more useful than asking an agent to guess coordinates. Just as importantly, agent output must remain immediately editable and reversible or the experience still feels like a handoff rather than collaboration. What's next Next we want opt-in live collaboration, richer typography flow, an attributed third-party asset catalog, reusable agent recipes, and a published reference contract for semantic canvas tools. title: Agent City — The Web Built for Humans and Agents
pitch: A miniature internet built from the ground up for humans and AI agents to navigate, collaborate, and act together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A miniature internet built from the ground up for humans and AI agents to navigate, collaborate, and act together through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Agent City: An Agent-Native Web Experiment The web was made for people. Every button, form, and checkout flow assumes a human is staring at the screen and deciding what to click. AI agents are changing that, but most current browser agents just mimic humans. They inspect a page, find an element, click it, and wait for the result. It is a slow, repetitive loop. We wanted to see what happens when agents are treated as first-class users. So we built Agent City , a small, simulated internet where humans and AI agents work together. The event planning scenario is just an easy way to show the concept, but the real experiment is about what an “agent-native” web actually looks like. The Four Districts Agent City has four districts: Venue District: Searches for and reserves spaces. Catering District: Finds food based on headcounts and budgets. Calendar District: Manages scheduling. Budget District: Tracks spending. Humans use a standard visual UI. Agents use WebMCP tools such as search_venues() and schedule_event() . Both interfaces interact with the same underlying state. How It Works If a user asks for a vegetarian meetup for 12 people tomorrow after 2 PM under ₹10,000, the agent finds the venue and food, checks the budget, and builds the plan. Things get interesting when requirements change. If the guest list jumps to 20 and the venue only holds 15, the system flags the conflict. The agent then has to find a bigger venue and redo the catering and budget. It is not just browser automation; it is collaboration over shared data. To make this visible, we added: An Agent Activity Graph A WebMCP Inspector These tools allow humans to see the agent’s work in real time. Technology We built the city using: React TypeScript Vite Cloudflare Workers D1 The architecture is straightforward: $$ \text{Human} \rightarrow \text{Visual Interface} \rightarrow \text{Shared State} \rightarrow \text{WebMCP Layer} \rightarrow \text{AI Agent} $$ Designing the Tools Instead of one giant “do everything” tool, we gave agents small, composable capabilities. We also made these tools context-aware. An agent sees reserve_venue() before a booking exists, but sees modify_reservation() once the booking is made. The hardest part was the tool design. A tool needs: A clear name A predictable result A well-defined purpose If tools overlap, the agent gets confused. If they are too broad, the agent stops reasoning. If they are too small, the task takes too many calls. Keeping Humans and Agents in Sync We also had to keep the human and agent views in sync. When an agent books a venue, the UI has to show it immediately. When a human changes the attendee count, the agent has to react to that new state. We found that building for agents does not mean killing the UI. Humans and agents just need different views of the same world: Humans want visual exploration and direct control. Agents want typed inputs and predictable results. What Comes Next Agent City is currently focused on event planning, but the idea could work for anything from finance to infrastructure. Next, we want to explore: Better permission systems Human approval flows More complex agent collaboration Safer handling of high-impact actions The core question is simple. If agents are now normal participants on the web, why force them to use interfaces made only for humans? Built With chatgpt cloudflare css html javascript react typescript vite webmcp Try it out github.com agent-city.imyash-chaudhary2.workers.dev Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I built the entire project solo — frontend, backend, and agent layer. I designed and built Agent City as a WebMCP-native app: a React + TypeScript frontend where every capability is exposed as a typed tool through document.modelContext, backed by a Cloudflare Worker API. The hardest part was the tool surface design — getting the read/write annotations, dynamic registration (tools appear only when state unlocks them), and the human-in-the-loop approval gate to all stay consistent. I learned that designing for agents is a different discipline from designing UIs: the schema is the interface, and the approval flow is a UX problem, not just a security check. title: FLow
pitch: Automated game development using webmcp.
about_excerpt: Automated game development using webmcp. Like Comment Story Updates Build any idea with the Godot Webmcp Why This Is a Strong Fit for WebMCP WebMCP is a new way of enabling effective collaboration between humans and agents. For a long time, game development has often been limited to heavy desktop applications that require several steps to set up. This use case enables people with little or no experience building games, and professional game developers, to build out their ideas easily, fast, and with little cost. A Better User Experience Previously, game developers would usually copy and paste code and screenshots from their game engines to their agents, and attempt to figure out how to connect their characters and elements to their scripts. This loop is extremely stressful, consumes significant tokens, and doesn't yield the best results. With WebMCP, this gap is closed; the agent now has the ability to build out fully functional games, test them, and continuously iterate till it meets the specified quality bar. Implementation To build this, I leveraged an existing web game engine from Godot, compiled to WebAssembly from C++. To give the agent control over the engine, I worked on exposing the different parts of the engine through a custom script and a Godot plugin, to WebMCP tools that AI agents can invoke to build out whatever game the user requests. The preexisting project was the Godot game engine, and it was meaningfully extended using WebMCP. title: Agent-Native Newsroom Portal
pitch: An agent-native newsroom where editors and browser agents collaboratively move stories from draft to publication through 22 real WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: An agent-native newsroom where editors and browser agents collaboratively move stories from draft to publication through 22 real WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates The Story Desk gives editors a complete view of the editorial pipeline, from draft and review through approval and publication. The Media Vault combines image discovery with licensing, allowed channels, attribution, expiration, and accessibility metadata. An approved story is blocked by an expired image license—a real newsroom problem that a WebMCP agent can detect and resolve. The Handoff Engine validates editorial, media-rights, attribution, accessibility, and publishing requirements before generating the handoff. A publishing payload is prepared through WebMCP and delivered only after the workflow passes validation and receives human approval. List of WebMCP tools available Inspiration A newsroom is a coordination machine. A story moves through many steps before it becomes publishable: assignment, drafting, editing, review, approval, media selection, rights verification, and finally handoff to a publishing system. Humans are good at navigating these workflows through interfaces. Agents face a different problem: a traditional website tells them what the interface looks like , but not necessarily what the application can do in a structured way. That led to a simple question: What would a newsroom look like if the website itself were designed for both people and agents? That question became Agent-Native Newsroom Portal . Instead of adding a chatbot to a newsroom, I built a newsroom whose actual capabilities can be exposed directly to external browser agents through WebMCP . What it does Agent-Native Newsroom Portal is an internal newsroom workspace built around three connected areas. Story Desk The Story Desk manages the editorial lifecycle from draft to publication. Editors can: Create and edit stories Assign stories to editors Submit stories for review Approve or request revisions Reorder the editorial run Track the complete story history The application enforces valid editorial state transitions instead of allowing arbitrary status changes. Media Vault The Media Vault manages newsroom images together with the metadata required to publish them safely. Each asset can contain: License information Allowed publishing channels Expiration dates Attribution requirements Photographer/source information Alt text This makes the workflow more useful than simply searching for an image. Can this image actually be used for this publication? The system can detect expired rights and identify usable replacement assets. Handoff Engine The Handoff Engine turns approved editorial content into publication-ready output. Before a story can be handed off, it validates: Editorial approval Editor assignment Headline and body content Media attachment Lead image Media rights Attribution Web publishing permissions Alt text Once the checks pass, the system generates a structured web publishing payload and can execute the simulated handoff. WebMCP The WebMCP layer is the core experiment. The application exposes 22 structured WebMCP tools covering newsroom operations such as: Finding and reading stories Creating and updating stories Approving stories Reordering stories Searching and inspecting media Checking media rights Replacing media Updating captions and alt text Renewing media licenses Validating publication readiness Preparing publishing payloads Executing the handoff There is deliberately no in-app chatbot . The website itself becomes agent-operable. A human editor can use the normal interface, while an external browser agent can use the same application capabilities through WebMCP. Both interact with the same underlying newsroom state. How we built it I built the application as a full-stack web product using: Next.js 16 React 19 TypeScript Tailwind CSS shadcn/ui Prisma SQLite for local development PostgreSQL in production Zustand The application is deployed on Vercel . The architecture separates the user interface, REST API routes, business logic, database, and WebMCP integration. One of the most important design decisions was to make the WebMCP tools use the same business-logic layer as the human UI . For example, approve_story , replace_story_media , and execute_web_handoff are not special demo-only operations. They perform real application operations and follow the same validation and workflow rules used by the normal interface. WebMCP tools are registered through the browser API: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) Each tool exposes structured inputs and structured results. I also seeded the application with realistic newsroom data, including expired media rights and valid replacement assets, so the agent workflow has real problems to discover and resolve. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not registering WebMCP tools. It was making them trustworthy . Once an external agent can change application state, the application needs strong rules around what the agent is allowed to do and when an operation should fail. For example: Editing an approved story should invalidate its previous approval. Expired media should not pass publication validation. Missing alt text should block publication. Invalid editorial transitions should be rejected. The final handoff should be validated again on the server. Another challenge was keeping human and agent interaction synchronized. When an agent changes the application, the human-facing UI must immediately reflect that change. Both paths therefore operate on the same underlying application state. Testing also uncovered a subtle bug in the media attachment flow. When isPrimary was omitted, it was being treated as false , which prevented the first attached image from automatically becoming the lead image. I fixed the API and WebMCP tool behavior and re-tested the workflow. For WebMCP testing, I used the Brave browser and the Chrome extension WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector while its free credits were available. I also used ChatGPT to help prepare the demo and GLM for additional WebMCP QA. I focused that external testing on the main workflow tools. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that the project became more than a visual WebMCP demonstration. The application exposes a real, stateful agent workflow across the newsroom. The main publication path is: Create Story ↓ Update Story ↓ Editorial Review ↓ Approve ↓ Attach / Replace Media ↓ Check Rights ↓ Validate Publication ↓ Prepare Web Handoff ↓ Execute Handoff ↓ Published The agent can perform these operations through WebMCP without having to guess its way through the visual interface. We are also proud of the guardrails around agent actions. WebMCP is not treated as a back door around newsroom rules. Agent operations go through the same application logic and validation as human actions. The repository also includes an end-to-end WebMCP validation report covering the project's tool surface and failure handling. What we learned The biggest lesson was that building an agent-native application is different from adding AI to an existing application . The difficult question is not: “Where should I put the chatbot?” It is: “What should the agent actually be able to do?” Good WebMCP tools need meaningful boundaries, clear inputs, predictable outputs, validation, and safe failure behavior. I also learned that useful human-agent systems do not need to be completely autonomous. For a newsroom, the agent can investigate, prepare, validate, and execute structured work, while the human retains editorial judgment and final authority. That led to the interaction model at the heart of this project: The agent handles structured work. The human remains the decision-maker. Building the project also changed how I think about web applications. A website is not only a collection of screens and buttons. It can also expose a structured set of capabilities that other intelligent systems can understand and use. What's next for Agent-Native Newsroom Portal This project is a starting point for a larger agent-native newsroom. The next step would be to move beyond individual publishing tasks and let agents help coordinate the wider editorial operation. For example, a newsroom agent could: Monitor upcoming deadlines Identify stories at risk of missing publication Detect missing media or metadata Find unresolved workflow blockers Prepare recommended actions for editors Coordinate handoffs across publishing channels I would also like to connect the Handoff Engine to real publishing systems instead of the current simulated delivery flow. Another area I want to explore is agent permissions : allowing a newsroom to define which actions an agent can perform automatically and which actions always require explicit human approval. The long-term idea is simple: Don't build AI around the newsroom. Build the newsroom so humans and agents can work together inside it. That is the experiment behind Agent-Native Newsr

title: Spokes - a collaborative map to help with coordination
pitch: Spokes turns "where should we go?" into one live map. Everyone adds their needs, some kept private, and places rule themselves out in real time. Your agent can assist you or fully negotiate for you.
about_excerpt: Spokes turns "where should we go?" into one live map. Everyone adds their needs, some kept private, and places rule themselves out in real time. Your agent can assist you or fully negotiate for you. Like Comment Story Updates Social media banner for Spokes Spokes — Devpost submission Live: https://spokes.alainschlesser.com/ Inspiration Groups are bad at picking somewhere to go, and the reason is structural rather than social. The needs that decide the answer are scattered across people and arrive piecemeal: a dietary restriction here, a budget there, a veto that lands after everyone else has settled, and at least one reason nobody wants to say out loud. A search results page optimises a single query. A group chat collects messages. Neither keeps a shared model of what the group has actually asked for, and neither lets a sensitive constraint count toward the decision without being explained to everybody first. That last part is what made this worth building for WebMCP specifically. A personal agent already knows things about its user that the user would rather not broadcast to five friends. Until now the only way to put that knowledge to work was to hand it to a shared service. I wanted to find out whether an agent could advocate for someone inside a live page, as that person and within an authority they granted, while the reason itself never left their client. What it does Three people open one planning room from a link. They see the same live map and the same brief of what the group has asked for so far. Each person states what matters in a single composer bar and chooses who may see it before they speak . A need can be shared, private, or agent-only. The server evaluates a private need and peers see only its effect on the count. An agent-only need stays with your agent and never reaches the server at all. The app suggests the next thing worth asking about from the data itself, never from a built-in list of categories. Every need becomes a row you can set aside. Press and hold a row and the map shows the room without that need, live. The cost of a need becomes visible instead of argued about. The room recomputes which places still work after every move, and it counts what is merely unverified separately from what actually failed. Missing data is drawn as its own state rather than quietly dropping a place. When nothing satisfies everyone, Spokes does not name who is blocking. It privately offers each person a quantified way out. The organizer sees "widen the area from 800 m to 1.2 km, brings back 4 places". The person who stated a need sees "let this need be nice-to-have, +12 places". Consent is explicit and confirmed on the page. Once the group agrees, the composer gives way to arrival: a travel mode and a one-tap handoff to the map app everyone already has. Alongside all of it, your personal ChatGPT can act in the same session through WebMCP. It can catch up on what changed while you were away, inspect places, put one forward, rule one out, or grant an adjustment. Your agent can assist you, or negotiate for you outright. How I built it A TypeScript monorepo (pnpm). Fastify and a Postgres event log sit behind a WebSocket realtime channel. The front end is React and Vite with MapLibre GL over keyless OpenFreeMap tiles. TypeBox contracts are shared by both sides behind a hashed contract-manifest gate. Place data is a one-time OpenStreetMap extract of Berlin Mitte. The WebMCP surface is 22 tools registered imperatively on document.modelContext at page load, 10 for negotiation and 12 spatial. Each is a narrow function with closed enum schemas, readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations, and a capped result budget. The page works fully without WebMCP. The tools are an additional way in. Four decisions did most of the work. Two protocols over the WebMCP substrate. WebMCP itself only carries tool names and schemas. So the first sync_session call returns a capability manifest that teaches the agent a domain-independent negotiation protocol (identity, revision sync, privacy tiers, requirements, stances, adjustments, consent, agreement) and a spatial-destination domain layered on top. Server-owned identity and per-viewer projections. Actor identity comes only from the bearer token. No tool argument accepts an actor id. Every event is stored once and projected per viewer, so unauthorised fields never appear in another participant's HTTP body or WebSocket frame. The test suite asserts this at the wire, not at the function boundary. Revision discipline instead of pretend realtime. Every mutation carries the agent's last-seen revision. A stale one returns a structured sync_required with a delta instead of acting on old state. That fits an agent that participates in bursts far better than a subscription it never really holds. Consent an agent cannot forge. An agent may recommend a grant, but a change beyond what the user delegated only stages . Staging mints a single-use code delivered on the participant's own realtime channel. The applying command must carry it back, and the code never appears in any tool result. Eligibility, minimal-conflict-set detection and the impasse counterfactuals are all deterministic. No model is allowed to invent a feasibility fact. 364 automated tests across three lanes: 222 unit, 128 three-user API, and 14 Playwright specs driving three isolated browser contexts. Challenges I ran into Privacy that is neither a lie nor a hole. The rule I settled on is that a private need's effect is always public and its content never leaves its owner. Both halves matter. Hiding the effect would make the count inexplicable, and leaking the content is the whole thing I was avoiding. It took a real redesign to stop routing private predicates through shared state "just for rendering", and a wire-level test suite to prove I had. Proving a human consented, honestly. My first cut let a bearer token commit an agreement over plain HTTP without ever touching the page. The realtime-only nonce closes that. It still is not proof a human clicked, because the realtime channel authenticates with the same token. Rather than overclaim, I wrote the residual threat model down in KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md . Keeping the interface domain-agnostic. It is hard not to type a domain word into a heading. What saved it was a rule on the server side. The server returns the facets present across the current result set, each with a mandatory unknown count, and the client renders whatever it gets. There is no domain branch anywhere in the front end, which is also what lets a human and an agent reason over the same vocabulary. Deployment, on the last evening. I had prepared a Coolify deployment and abandoned it at the gate. Its Traefik has documented WebSocket failures on compose stacks, and the room is a WebSocket. The January 2026 disclosure put eleven critical CVEs in a control plane that runs as root. Its baseline would have claimed a quarter of a 4 GB box before Postgres started. The existing compose file was already a correct production stack. It needed twenty lines of Caddy in front, not a PaaS. That deploy went out with nineteen minutes to spare, after a self-inflicted detour in which a redeploy overwrote the host's generated Postgres password and stranded the database behind credentials nothing had written down. Two rendering bugs that looked like design problems. Vite's dependency optimiser broke MapLibre's worker, so the basemap never drew. A CSS animation setting transform silently overwrote a positioning translate and threw pins at their anchors. Both cost hours before either was understood. Accomplishments that I'm proud of An agent that can advocate for a constraint it never discloses. The agent screens places locally and returns per-place verdicts. The council folds them into eligibility, and peers see the aggregate effect with no route back to the cause. That is the capability I most wanted WebMCP to make possible, and it works. Press and hold. Holding a need shows the map without it, live, and releasing restores it. It turns an argument about whether a need is reasonable into a number you can see, and it is the one gesture everybody understood without being told. An impasse resolver that refuses to assign blame. When nothing satisfies everyone, the room offers each person a private, quantified route out, phrased as a consequence rather than an instruction. Honest unverified state. Missing data renders as a hollow pin and a separate count. A place is never silently dropped for lacking a value, and unknown is never drawn as failure. Two independent adversarial reviews: a protocol-invariant audit and a cross-family model review of the server, then two further reviews of the rebuilt client. The privacy and agreement-integrity findings were fixed and are covered by tests. I published the deferred items instead of hiding them. pitch: Check it, correct it, approve it, and hand it off.

 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 This is my first hackathon, and I'm probably way over my head, but I wanted to jump in and use it as a learning experience. I wanted to put something together that was practical for a small business who could use a WebMCP enabled browser/agent to work through tasks easily. 

 The WebMCP Challenge gave me an opportunity to learn more about WebMCP. At first, I thought it might be gimicky, but after building this partial app, I definitely see the value. 

 Most of my coding experience has been in HTML and data analytics. Working with Codex has given me a way to sort of turn back the clock and work on the type of project I've always wanted to try. 

 Lastly. I'm close to retirement. I've always been technically inclined, but not formally educated in development. What Codex has done for me, which may sound silly, is it makes me feel young. I enjoy building, and taking part in this hackathon pushed me out of my comfort zone. Even though the project is simple, I'm proud of it. 

 What it does 

 FieldProof helps contractors keep job photos, completed work, and daily notes together. When a project is ready to wrap up, a browser agent can check the records, find missing information, and prepare updates for the contractor to review. The contractor decides which updates to save. After a successful recheck, FieldProof opens a handoff packet that can be printed or saved as a PDF for the client. 

 How I built it 

 I built FieldProof with Codex using React, TypeScript, and Vite. Project records and photos stay in the browser through IndexedDB and Dexie. Render hosts the app. 

 The FieldProof concept and some initial coding existed before the challenge. For the hackathon, I added WebMCP tools and built the review process around them. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 One challenge was making the agent’s work easy to see. Initially changes made by the agent were buried in a side panel. I had to change layout so someone watching could understand what the agent found and what needed a decision. 

 Another challenge was testing whether an agent was actually using WebMCP. I tested with a separate agent session and checked which tools it called. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I’m proud that that I competed and completed my first hackathon! I know the reality is that this isn't a complex tool, it doesn't have wiz-bang features or amazing motion graphics. I'm not building a rocket, or some major SaaS product. However, it's mine. It's the type of thing I like to build, and it make a process easier for people. 

 What I learned 

 I learned how much the interface matters. A tool can work correctly and still leave someone wondering what happened. People need to see the result and understand what to do next. 

 What's next for FieldProof 

 My next step is to continue building the rest of the app, get feedback from contractors and see whether FieldProof fits how they actually keep job records. I want to improve the wording, make photo capture easier on a phone, and refine the handoff packet based on what clients need.

title: CallReclaim: Agent Rescue Desk
pitch: WebMCP turns a missed-call inbox into a cited rescue plan and editable reply—while the owner keeps every approval and nothing can send.
about_excerpt: WebMCP turns a missed-call inbox into a cited rescue plan and editable reply—while the owner keeps every approval and nothing can send. Like Comment Story Updates Five WebMCP tools are ready. The agent compares authorized calls and stages a cited one-slot rescue plan; only the owner can accept it. After owner acceptance, draft revision 1 enters the owner checkpoint. The reply stays editable and unsent; stale edits cannot be queued. Caller text is marked untrusted. It cannot create approval, review, or send capabilities. Why I built it A detailing shop owner can miss a call while working on a car. The hard part is not writing a text. It is deciding which call deserves attention when several people have different deadlines, job values, and follow-up permissions. I built CallReclaim around one rule: the agent can prepare an editable reply, but only the owner can accept the plan and complete review. Nothing is sent. What it does The demo opens with five fictional missed calls. The owner starts by saying how many replies they can handle in the next 30 minutes. A WebMCP agent can then: Compare the inbox and read the current owner brief. Stage a rescue plan that fits the owner's capacity. Link each choice to exact facts recorded on the page. Open an accepted lead and inspect its conversation. Draft an editable reply after the owner accepts the plan. Queue the current draft revision for owner review. The plan and draft appear in the same desk the owner is already using. The owner can accept or clear the plan, edit the reply, mark the draft reviewed, discard it, or reset the demo. The agent cannot accept its own plan. It cannot approve a draft. It cannot complete review. It cannot send a message. Those capabilities do not exist in the tool surface or the application. Why WebMCP fits A normal interface is good for reading one conversation. The harder task crosses several calls and constraints. WebMCP lets the agent compare the calls, cite the records, and stage a plan in the same live desk the owner sees. The owner and agent also need a safe way to take turns. If the owner changes the reply capacity, the previous plan no longer applies. If the owner edits a draft, the old revision cannot be queued. Agent drafts also remember which accepted plan and owner brief authorized them. Without this handoff, the owner has to compare the calls and rebuild the context alone. Here the agent does that cross-record work while the owner keeps the customer decision. How I built it The challenge app is a one-page React and TypeScript project built with Vinext and deployed on OpenAI Sites. The top-level page registers five imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : list_demo_leads inspect_demo_lead stage_rescue_plan draft_owner_reply queue_for_owner_review The tools and visible controls use the same state rules. Inputs are bounded with JSON Schema and runtime checks. Tool registration is page-scoped and cleaned up with AbortSignal . Caller transcripts are marked as untrusted content. The records are deterministic and fictional. There is no database, model API, authentication, telephony provider, tracking, secret configuration, or messaging backend. The hard parts The first hard part was capability design. A warning that says "do not send" is weak if a send capability still exists. CallReclaim has no send tool and no messaging backend. The second hard part was protecting the owner's edit. When they change the plan or draft, the old agent version is rejected. The third hard part was caller text aimed at the agent. One fictional caller tries to give the agent an instruction. The app treats that as caller text, not as a command. The demonstrated inspection creates no plan or draft. What I tested The frozen release passes 14 focused tests, lint, TypeScript checking, production build, dependency audit, and public CI. The tests cover schemas, output budgets, capacity limits, unauthorized leads, unsupported citations, stale plans, owner acceptance, draft gating, owner edits, stale revisions, reviewed work, tool cleanup, and browsers without WebMCP. I also ran the prompt matrix through fresh public in-app-browser sessions. Direct requests staged the same cited proposal. Ambiguous requests made no changes. Unsafe send requests stopped at the owner gate. Missing follow-up requests stopped before drafting. Stale queue requests preserved the owner's edit. The adversarial reference test found one real identifier bug, which was fixed and re-run before submission. What I learned The important decision was what to leave out. The agent can prepare a reply. It cannot approve or send it. Revision checks protect the owner's latest work in code. The agent sorts the inbox. It stages a plan linked to recorded facts. It prepares an editable reply. The owner completes review. Nothing is sent. What I built during the challenge CallReclaim's broader missed-call concept existed before the challenge. During the challenge, I built a separate WebMCP edition with an owner capacity check, a cited plan, five page tools, and revision checks that stop stale work. What's next This submission stays fictional. A production version would require customer authorization, secure tenant data, verified messaging consent, provider integrations, audit logging, and a separate operational rollout. title: Music Synth Creator
pitch: Iteratively create music synths with AI. The agent constructs a synth in the app - you listen and give it feedback to iterate on. Since all state is in the browser, WebMCP is the perfect solution.
about_excerpt: Iteratively create music synths with AI. The agent constructs a synth in the app - you listen and give it feedback to iterate on. Since all state is in the browser, WebMCP is the perfect solution. Like Comment Story Updates Full-size web application open in Chrome Web application open in ChatGPT Inspiration I am a hobbyist music producer. Every time I produce a track, I spend hours trying to find the perfect synth for my idea, either by searching through online libraries or by trying to make my own. By the time I have found the right sound, the inspiration has faded and I have usually forgotten what I wanted to compose. I was also inspired by these two example applications: Field Beat Machine: https://developers.openai.com/showcase/ko-field-beat-machine Codex Modeling Studio: https://developers.openai.com/showcase/codex-modeling-studio What it does The app is a music synthesizer: you tweak the controls to configure the sound it makes, then press a key to produce a sound. The WebMCP layer allows the AI to interact with the controls and create synths according to your description. You can listen to the sound and give some feedback for the AI to modify the configured synth. Finally you can export the synth as an open source .vital file for use in music production software. How we built it I built a compact, visually informative synthesizer app which is easy to navigate. I compiled Vital's open source wavetable synth engine with WebAssembly to produce sounds from the patch configured in the UI. I built a canonical synth patch object as the state for the application's visual and audio components, as part of which I had to create mappings to .vital format parameters. I added WebMCP tools so that agents can inspect and interact with the application state directly, without needing to manually interact with the browser. Challenges we ran into I started by creating my own digital signal processing functionality for the synth, until I realised that I would spend too much time developing each feature. Eventually I ported Vital's open-source C++ engine and built an interface around that. I created a simple and restricted interface around Vital's complex sound engine. This may have been fine if I hadn't tried to make the app compatible with any .vital file import, which requires a lossy re-construction of their format into my canonical patch object. I also started with very low level WebMCP tools, which slowed down and confused the agent. To solve this, I created high level abstractions for the agent to use which improved the sounds it could create. I had to add safeguards for when the agent creates a synth with high feedback due to poorly configured effects. Accomplishments that we're proud of I can create synths in my app, that I can then import into my music production software! They sound good and the agent responds creatively to my input. I am also very happy with the visual polish of my app. What we learned Digital signal processing is hard! Don't try to create too many features! Focus on the core elements. I think there might be many exciting WebMCP-enabled apps in the future I have started to wonder if there is another possible protocol that could allow for agents to interact with native desktop applications. What's next for Music Synth Creator I want to use it properly - so far I have just been developing it. I want to reduce the startup delay when the first note is pressed I want to reduce the delay in transitioning between synth variations A and B I want to improve the .vital import feature to work with more existing presets I want to improve the WebMCP interactions, and add more elements for visual feedback (such as a parameter diff when the agent makes a change) I want to add a help section with common music producer jargon to help users better describe the sound they want. title: AgentReady
pitch: AgentReady audits websites for AI-agent readiness and turns commercial gaps into structured, actionable WebMCP capabilities.
about_excerpt:
AgentReady audits websites for AI-agent readiness and turns commercial gaps into structured, actionable WebMCP capabilities.

 Bannière 3:2 : AgentReady — Visibility. Understanding. Buyability. 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI agents are becoming a new way for people to interact with the web, but most small-business websites were built for humans and search engines — not for agents. 

 A business may have products, services, prices, booking options or contact flows publicly available, yet an AI agent can still struggle to reliably understand what the business offers or how to take action. 

 AgentReady started from a simple question: how can a small business know whether its website is actually ready for AI agents? 

 What it does 

 AgentReady audits a real website and evaluates its AI commerce readiness across three dimensions: 

 Visibility → Understanding → Buyability 

 It analyzes observable commercial information, evaluates what an AI agent can reliably understand, and produces evidence-based scores and prioritized recommendations. 

 The goal is not simply to make websites more machine-readable. The goal is to help businesses move from being visible to AI agents to becoming genuinely understandable and actionable by them. 

 AgentReady also exposes its audit capability directly to AI agents through WebMCP. 

 The native WebMCP tool agentready.run_audit allows an agent to launch the same website audit available to a human through the AgentReady interface and receive structured results including readiness scores, observed evidence, recommended actions, rendering provenance and monitoring eligibility. 

 This creates one capability for two users: 

 Humans get a clear visual audit. AI agents get a structured, callable tool. 

 How we built it 

 AgentReady uses an evidence-first audit architecture designed to avoid inventing commercial facts. 

 The challenge demo combines a browser interface with a bounded server-side audit function. For JavaScript-heavy websites where the initial HTML does not expose enough reliable evidence, AgentReady can use a controlled browser-rendering fallback and clearly reports that provenance. 

 The WebMCP integration registers agentready.run_audit through: 

 document.modelContext.registerTool(...) 

 The tool calls the same AgentReady audit capability used by the human interface and returns structured content that an AI agent can consume directly. 

 This means WebMCP is not a separate demonstration layer: humans and agents access the same underlying capability. 

 AgentReady also includes monitoring of comparable audits over time, allowing businesses to identify improvements or degradation in their AI readiness while avoiding false comparisons when an acquisition is incomplete. 

 Challenges 

 The hardest problem has been factual reliability across very different types of websites. 

 Real-world sites contain navigation elements, product cards, booking flows, duplicated prices, dynamic JavaScript content and commercial information distributed across different structures. 

 AgentReady therefore follows a simple principle: 

 Observed, not assumed. 

 If reliable evidence cannot be observed, the system should report uncertainty rather than manufacture a confident answer. 

 Another challenge was making dynamic website audits reproducible. The browser-rendering fallback and monitoring eligibility rules were designed to prevent incomplete page acquisition from creating misleading readiness changes. 

 What's next 

 The next step is expanding AgentReady from one callable audit capability into a broader AI commerce readiness layer where detected gaps can map to additional WebMCP actions. 

 The longer-term loop is: 

 Audit → Detect capability gap → Expose capability → Agent takes action 

 The vision is to make AI commerce readiness accessible to small businesses that do not have dedicated technical teams — so they can participate in an increasingly agent-driven web without having to understand the underlying technology.
