title: Actalume
pitch: The evidence ledger where agents prove work and named humans decide what becomes true.
about_excerpt: The evidence ledger where agents prove work and named humans decide what becomes true. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Agent systems are increasingly capable of taking actions, but the human is often left reconstructing the chain of custody afterward. What was actually requested? Which boundary applied? What changed? What proves it? Who accepted it as project truth? Actalume began with one non-negotiable idea: an agent's claim that work is complete is not the same as a human decision that the work is canonical. What it does Actalume is a human-governed system of record for agent work. A project starts with an explicit contract describing its purpose, public-data boundary, allowed actions, prohibited actions and completion rule. An agent can then propose one bounded brick, attach typed evidence receipts and request human review. Six WebMCP tools expose that workflow directly to an agent: list projects, inspect the contract, propose a brick, submit evidence, request review and inspect canonical history. There is deliberately no approval tool. Approval requires a named human and a second confirmation inside the interface. Only then is the decision sealed into immutable, evidence-linked history. All supplied demo content is fictional and public-safe. The app has no accounts, telemetry, network writes or publishing integration. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent must infer controls from the interface and the human must trust an unstructured summary of what happened. With WebMCP, Actalume exposes a narrow, typed and inspectable work protocol while keeping the consequential decision outside the agent's authority. People and agents can now share one legible custody chain: the agent can inspect scope, create bounded work and submit proof; the human can review that exact evidence and decide what becomes project history. How we built it Actalume is a local-first React 19 and TypeScript application built with Vite. Browser persistence uses localStorage, with deterministic fictional fixtures and JSON import/export. The WebMCP layer registers six imperative tools using document.modelContext.registerTool, each with narrow schemas and explicit read-only or review-request semantics. The ledger reducer enforces state transitions separately from the UI. Automated tests prove that an agent cannot approve work, approved bricks cannot be mutated, evidence is required before review and all six tools register when the native browser surface is present. The challenge build was verified in Chrome 151 with WebMCP testing enabled. Chrome discovered all six tools and executed safe reads, evidence submission and a human-review request. An attempted agent approval was rejected, and canonical history stayed unchanged. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is experimental, so ordinary-browser fallback behavior had to remain honest without being mistaken for native proof. We separated the visible demo harness from native verification and only claimed WebMCP success after Chrome's getTools and executeTool APIs discovered and exercised the live registrations. The harder product challenge was making governance feel like a workflow rather than a policy page. We designed the interface around one custody line: contract, bounded brick, evidence, human decision and canonical history. Amber surfaces actions awaiting judgment; green is reserved for history already verified by a person. Accomplishments that we're proud of Six working WebMCP tools with no agent approval surface. A named-human, two-step approval gate. Immutable canonical history with evidence counts and deterministic digests. Ten automated governance, registration and deliberate-approval tests. Zero dependency vulnerabilities at submission preparation. A complete responsive product experience rather than an inert technical demo. What we learned Agent safety becomes easier to understand when it is spatial and operational. A visible boundary, a typed tool surface and a blocked transition communicate more than a long policy document. WebMCP is especially powerful when it exposes not only what an agent can do, but also what it cannot do. What's next for Actalume The next version would add pluggable receipt adapters, signed export bundles and optional team roles while preserving the same core rule: agents may propose and prove; named humans decide what becomes true. title: s-m-r-t
pitch: Define a domain once, then give people and browser agents the same safe, structured application.
about_excerpt: Define a domain once, then give people and browser agents the same safe, structured application. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most web applications are built for people to click and for agents to guess. Agents scrape labels and infer controls from fragile DOMs. s-m-r-t asks a different question: what if an application's real domain model, permissions, workflows, and interface also defined a deliberate browser-native tool surface? Job hunting made that problem concrete. Finding opportunities, checking sources, triaging listings, recording notes, and preparing application packets are repetitive and stressful. They benefit from agent help, while final approval and employer submission should remain unmistakably human decisions. What it does s-m-r-t is the entry. It is a TypeScript framework for building operational applications around one typed domain model. Decorated business objects generate aligned persistence, REST, CLI, MCP, WebMCP, browser-data, and AI surfaces. WebMCP is not a separate demo API pasted onto an application: it is a governed browser projection of the same model and application contracts. For the challenge, s-m-r-t gained: canonical WebMCP definitions for deliberately API-exposed models; authenticated execution through the existing REST boundary; explicit exposure policies, effect classification, tool budgets, and namespaces; lifecycle-safe registration through document.modelContext ; mounted form-control and data-surface adapters, giving agents and people the same UI state; staged form edits requiring human review; bounded queries and durable actions with stable identity and confirmation boundaries; declarative view intents and layered playbooks that make the agent surface statically knowable; local, self-hosted, and managed-cloud runtime profiles preserving the same tools and policies. Iolaus is the demonstration application built with s-m-r-t. It is a local-first, single-user employment-search app using SQLite. A browser agent inspects source health, browses and investigates fictional job listings, records a triage decision and note, advances the queue, opens a shortlist, and inspects an application packet. Those actions update the same state the person sees. There is intentionally no WebMCP tool for final approval or employer submission. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, the agent needs brittle DOM automation or a separate privileged integration. With s-m-r-t, each page advertises bounded tools through document.modelContext . Those tools carry effect metadata, use authenticated application routes, respect field and exposure policies, and disappear with the page lifecycle. Mounted view tools change the same state the person sees, while background queries inspect data without disturbing the view. The collaboration is legible: the agent performs structured work, the person sees its results, and sensitive transitions remain behind explicit human review. The implementation is reusable across application domains instead of being tied to one job board or agent harness. How we built it s-m-r-t is a pnpm TypeScript monorepo. Its scanner reads @smrt() declarations and emits manifests, schemas, routes, clients, and canonical tool descriptors. @happyvertical/smrt-web validates and registers generated and bespoke browser tools. @happyvertical/smrt-svelte binds those contracts to mounted forms and data surfaces. Its application runtime composes SQLite/local, PostgreSQL/self-hosted, and managed-cloud profiles without changing domain objects or WebMCP policy. The execution path fails closed. The decorator controls model-operation exposure; authenticated REST remains the authorization boundary; undeclared effects are classified as destructive; sensitive fields are omitted; stale tools refuse execution; and staged edits cannot self-confirm. Integration fixtures exercise generated definitions, authentication failures, registration lifecycle, policy changes, mounted UI tools, and cross-profile parity. Iolaus consumes published s-m-r-t packages and provides an isolated demo profile. pnpm demo:prepare builds and migrates private SQLite state, seeds visibly fictional opportunities and crawl provenance, starts a loopback-only server, and opens a one-time owner handoff. pnpm demo:smoke runs an authenticated browser proof and verifies both the available capabilities and the absence of approval/submission tools. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was preserving one security and lifecycle model across generated model tools, page-mounted controls, custom component tools, and multiple runtime profiles. A capability policy is only useful if every registration path passes through it. We also had to separate discovery from authorization, exclude sensitive candidate fields, and prevent remounts or policy changes from leaving stale tools behind. The local-first install introduced another systems challenge: safe owner bootstrap, idempotent SQLite setup, private on-device state, deterministic fixtures, and recovery commands all had to work without weakening the deployed application model. Accomplishments that we're proud of WebMCP is a first-class generated framework surface, not a hand-built endpoint for one demo. The same declarations drive persistence, APIs, MCP, WebMCP, clients, and knowledge artifacts. Human-visible controls and agent commands converge on shared registries and state. Effect policy and human approval boundaries are explicit and testable. Iolaus installs locally and proves a useful workflow without transmitting an application. Cross-profile fixtures verify that infrastructure choices do not silently change the agent surface. What we learned WebMCP works best as an application architecture concern, not a thin automation layer. Browser tools should derive from the same source of truth as data and authorization. A strong human-agent experience also needs bounded inputs, visible shared state, effect metadata, lifecycle cleanup, deterministic testing, and carefully chosen places where the agent must stop. What's next for s-m-r-t We will continue hardening conformance across generated, mounted, and declared agent surfaces; improve route-aware capability discovery; and make the one-prompt local installation pattern reusable for other s-m-r-t applications. Iolaus will remain a real-world proving ground while preserving private local data and human control of external actions. Source and testing Framework source: https://github.com/happyvertical/smrt Demo application: https://github.com/willgriffin/iolaus Judge instructions: https://github.com/willgriffin/iolaus/blob/main/docs/judge-demo.md Related deployed application: https://willgriffin.dev Both repositories are MIT licensed. The deterministic demo uses Node.js 24.18+, pnpm 11.24.0, and a WebMCP-capable browser. Clone Iolaus, enable Corepack, run pnpm install --frozen-lockfile , then pnpm demo:prepare . Run pnpm demo:test and pnpm demo:smoke for the repeatable proof. The fixture is fictional, local, and never contacts an employer. title: Ainder
pitch: Your AI knows more than your dating bio. Ainder uses WebMCP to help you explore profiles, understand someone, and decide whether to connect—with you in control.
about_excerpt: Your AI knows more than your dating bio. Ainder uses WebMCP to help you explore profiles, understand someone, and decide whether to connect—with you in control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Dating profiles make it easy to see someone's photos, but much harder to understand their communication style, daily rhythm, or relationship expectations. Meanwhile, a personal AI may already have useful context from conversations its user has chosen to share. Ainder explores a simple question: what if that familiar AI could participate in a dating website, offer a thoughtful second opinion, and help its user act on a decision? What it does Ainder combines photo-first browsing with an AI-assisted conversation. People can browse profiles themselves or ask their agent to move between candidates and photos. When someone catches their attention, they can ask, "What do you think of this person?" Through WebMCP, the agent can read the current candidate's Agent Profile and use the context actually available about its own user to offer a qualitative opinion. The user decides whether to send a Like. Each Like includes an Agent opinion, and incoming Likes make that opinion available to the recipient. Mutual Likes between eligible members create a Match and enable messaging. Agent-assisted onboarding also supports confirmed personal details, ordered photo uploads, and creation of an Agent Profile. Profiles record an estimated familiarity duration and interaction density and expire after three months. An Agent Profile is contextual input, not verified identity, certified personality, or a compatibility guarantee. Ainder does not need a copy of the user's raw conversation history. Why WebMCP fits The central interaction spans two places: the person's conversation with their own AI and the dating website they are viewing. WebMCP provides explicit tools connecting those experiences. The agent can work with the exact candidate and photo visible on the page and take a defined action after the user's decision. This reduces copying between a chat and a website and lets the person move naturally between browsing, asking a question, and acting on the answer. The website supplies structured candidate data and enforces authorization; the agent contributes conversational context; the person makes the relationship decision. How we built it The application uses PHP, MySQL, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. Its pages register structured tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Registration tools are start_agent_registration , prepare_photo_upload , and submit_agent_registration . The main app exposes upsert_my_agent_profile , get_current_candidate , browse_candidates , change_candidate_photo , evaluate_current_candidate , and send_like_to_current_candidate . Tool execution uses same-origin PHP endpoints with session authentication and CSRF checks. Photo uploads use short-lived signed URLs. Candidate evaluation checks Profile state and issues a short-lived, single-use token tied to the requester and candidate. Sending a Like requires that token and a non-empty Agent opinion. Navigation tools update the visible card without sending a Like. Codex was used throughout development. The public repository contains the dated design documents, implementation history, and automated contract and model tests. Challenges The main challenge was keeping the agent, website, and person aligned: evaluating the candidate currently on screen, separating browsing from consequential actions, and keeping the user's decision central. Another was representing the limits of AI familiarity without inventing conversation history or turning an opinion into a numerical compatibility promise. Accomplishments The prototype brings onboarding, photo browsing, Agent Profile evaluation, Likes, and relationship state into one working application. It includes public test logins so reviewers can explore the core experience without creating an account or supplying personal photos. What we learned The useful role of an agent is not just to click faster. It is to contribute context at the point where a person needs help deciding. Explicit tools and server-side checks make that collaboration easier to reason about, while the agent must remain honest about what it actually knows. What's next Improve real-world evaluation of the advice, refine consent and Profile freshness, and test the workflow across more WebMCP-capable browsers. These are future plans rather than claims about completed features. title: PaperSpace
pitch: Break free from linear PDF reading. PaperSpace gives people and AI agents a shared spatial desk to navigate evidence, gather related pages, and present research through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Break free from linear PDF reading. PaperSpace gives people and AI agents a shared spatial desk to navigate evidence, gather related pages, and present research through WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI tools treat a research paper as a file to summarize or a block of text to retrieve from. We wanted to explore a more WebMCP-native question: What becomes possible when a person and an agent share a paper's text and its spatial reading environment inside the browser? Reading a paper is rarely linear. A reader moves between related work, methods, equations, figures, experiments, and appendices while building a mental map of where each idea lives. Conventional PDF viewers collapse that map into one page at a time. Chat interfaces collapse it even further into excerpts detached from their visual source. PaperSpace preserves that spatial memory. Every page of every imported PDF is unfolded onto a borderless two-dimensional desk. Pages remain live, selectable PDF surfaces, but they can also be moved, grouped, searched, compared, and revisited as part of a persistent visual workspace. The browser is essential to this interaction. It owns the PDFs the person explicitly selected, the rendered pages, the local text index, the page geometry, the current camera, and the workspace the person is looking at. WebMCP gives an agent direct access to that authorized, browser-local state, keeping the person and the agent aligned on one live workspace. We built PaperSpace for the WebMCP Challenge as a focused, open-source, single-person tool centered on reading, understanding, and presenting research papers. PaperSpace is a shared spatial instrument where the person controls the source material and the agent helps organize attention inside the same visible world. What it does PaperSpace is a local-first spatial desk for research papers. When a person imports a PDF, PaperSpace unfolds every page from left to right and top to bottom using each page's real aspect ratio. Every page becomes an independently movable and resizable live sheet with selectable text. The complete paper stays visible as a spatial place with its reading order intact. PaperSpace extracts text and normalized page geometry locally with PDF.js. Each page becomes searchable as soon as its index is ready. A reusable inspect_workspace briefing reports exact coverage and compact sampled page excerpts, so an agent can prepare once and then read the broadest useful contiguous range in one call, including the whole paper when full context matters. Through WebMCP, the agent can search the available corpus, batch-read paper text, locate an exact passage, and guide the shared camera to that region. The camera first pulls back to establish spatial context, travels across the desk, and then lands with the source itself centered in a calm view with generous breathing room. The app exposes nine WebMCP tools: inspect_workspace returns reusable readiness, compact paper briefs, every page's world geometry, visual artifacts, sequences, and camera state. search_papers progressively searches indexed pages and returns page-level matches with normalized source regions plus exact coverage. read_paper_pages reads one contiguous range or a whole indexed paper in one call, with optional block geometry and an explicit caller-selected character cap. focus_region guides the camera to a search match or an explicit PDF region. arrange_papers reflows pages into reading-order grids and arranges complete paper groups. snapshot_paper_region places a source-linked raster crop from an exact PDF region. place_plot creates a safe declarative line plot from finite numeric data. place_image validates and places PNG, JPEG, and WebP visuals. present_sequence creates a captioned sequence of semantic paper regions and visual artifacts. PaperSpace also gives the agent an explicit delivery contract. When PaperSpace is available, substantive introductions, explanations, reviews, comparisons, and answers grounded across multiple paper regions are delivered through present_sequence . Chat provides concise supporting context, while a single grounded passage can use focus_region and simple localized Q&A remains lightweight. The sequence interaction is the heart of the product. Suppose one experiment is explained across related work, methods, and results on three distant pages. The agent can build a three-frame sequence with a caption for each view. When presentation begins, PaperSpace temporarily draws those original pages together beside their paper in first-appearance order. Quiet numbered source slots preserve the paper's topology throughout the presentation. The same original page can support several region frames through one staged page. Visual artifacts stay in their existing world positions. Exiting the sequence restores every moved page—including its position, size, and layer—and returns the camera to its exact entry state. Keeping a sequence saves its semantic frames; replaying it organizes pages again from their current positions and restores them again afterward. This enables requests such as: “Find where this experiment is motivated, defined, and evaluated, then organize those pages for me.” “Focus on the ablation equation and keep the surrounding paragraph in view.” “Read the method and results, plot the reported trend, and place it beside the source page.” “Present the three views in sequence and explain what changes between them.” Everything happens on the same desk the person can inspect and manipulate. Agent actions produce visible feedback, and temporary organization is transactionally isolated from the person's saved layout. Spatial mutation tools perform an atomic visual preflight inside the app. Standard calls place plots, images, source crops, and arrangements in clear areas. An agent can use force: true for an intentional dense layout, while media, schema, source-target, and security validation remain active. How we built it PaperSpace is a pure frontend SvelteKit and TypeScript application compiled as a static site for Cloudflare Pages. Browser storage and browser-authorized files provide the complete runtime state. The application is organized around four client-side layers: Svelte components render the infinite desk, unfolded PDF sheets, artifacts, search interface, frame editor, and presentation chrome. A single reactive workspace model owns paper metadata, per-page geometry, the camera, artifacts, semantic sequences, and all person- and agent-triggered state transitions. PDF.js renders pages and extracts text plus normalized block geometry in a same-origin Web Worker. IndexedDB stores validated workspace metadata, browser-authorized PDF copies, raster images, and saved semantic frames. The workspace schema stores a stable paper identity and page number for every PDF page, while position, size, and layer remain mutable world properties. PDF inspection records each page's true dimensions. A deterministic row-major layout uses a bounded column count to keep long papers spatially legible, and complete paper bounds are used to prevent different imports from overlapping. Every page has a DOM sheet so its identity remains stable in the world. PaperSpace activates detailed PDF canvas and text rendering near the viewport and above a useful zoom threshold, keeping long unfolded papers responsive. PDF rasterization uses a two-tier residency system. Every successfully rendered page retains a 288-pixel-wide aspect-preserving preview, while an LRU applies a 48-million-pixel budget to unpinned high-resolution page canvases. Pages in the strict viewport, the current focus target, and the active sequence frame are pinned and may temporarily exceed that budget. A compact preview preserves visual continuity as high-resolution canvases move through the working set. Raster canvases and selectable text layers have independent lifecycles, and a double-canvas pipeline swaps each completed bitmap into view atomically. Region targeting uses top-left normalized coordinates. The same semantic region can therefore be mapped through a page's current world geometry after the page has been moved or resized. Camera motion is handled by a cancellable controller with pull-back, travel, and landing keyframes, smooth center interpolation, logarithmic zoom interpolation, distance-aware timing, responsive caption-safe insets, and an immediate path for prefers-reduced-motion . Presentation staging is transactional. PaperSpace validates every frame before changing state, deduplicates source pages by first appearance, snapshots their exact geometry and the entry camera, stages the original pages, and exposes their source slots. Presentation mode pauses page manipulation, while persistence serializes the source geometry and entry camera to keep the durable desk unchanged. WebMCP is registered directly through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The WebMCP adapter is intentionally thin: every tool calls the same workspace
video_transcript_excerpt: This is PaperSpace, a browser-native research workspace that exposes its live reading desk to AI agents through WebMCP. The paper is our test. Can an agent turn one request into visible, grounded interaction? The user asks Codex, "Introduce this paper using PaperSpace." PaperSpace is open beside the conversation in the built-in browser. WebMCP lets that page expose its own capabilities to the agent. So, the answer appears as visible interaction on the shared desk with chat providing concise guidance. When the page opens, Codex discovers the tools declared by the site. It calls inspect workspace once for a compact desk briefing, reads the index paper in one broad request, then calls present sequence with semantic page regions and captions. The browser-local workspace connects the agent directly to the active reading context. PaperSpace keeps every PDF page live on a borderless two-dimensional desk. Page identity and order remain visible while positions can change. Browser authorization keeps the PDF, extracted text, layout, and saved sequences together in local workspace storage. For a grounded introduction, present sequence gathers the relevant original pages, preserves their source slots, and adds a caption to every view. Here, Codex moves from the paper's motivation to its method, to the evidence with every explanation anchored to the original pages. If the user asks about a precise figure or equation, focus region targets normalized coordinates on the live page. The camera pulls back, travels across the desk, and lands with the requested region centered in a readable view. The person can redirect the motion at any time. Every command participates in one shared reversible state. The person sees each change in the browser, can move pages or stop a flight, and can keep or exit a sequence. On exit, Paper space restores the exact page geometry and the previous camera. That is the Web MCP loop. Codex understands the request, the browser exposes the tools, and Paper space becomes the shared interface. It is a pure SvelteKit front end, persisted in IndexDB, and deployable to Cloudflare Pages. The browser itself is the integration layer.

title: ReTrade
pitch: Rethink the strategy before you trade.
about_excerpt: Rethink the strategy before you trade. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The hackathon itself was my first source of inspiration. I wanted to build something with WebMCP and explore what an AI-first product could look like. By AI-first, I mean a product where the main way to interact is through an AI agent such as ChatGPT. The interface still matters, but instead of clicking through every step manually, the user can describe what they want and let the agent work with the application. I started thinking about tasks that are difficult for an ordinary person to complete through a conventional interface. That led me to trading. I remembered using TradingView and trying to test different strategies. I wanted to answer some basic questions. Is this actually a good strategy? Could it make a profit? What are its weaknesses? Does the strategy work, or does it only look successful because of the particular data used in the test? I did not know the answers, and finding them was not simple. So I decided to build a product that could help investigate these questions. ReTrade was built in about five days. The project became much more promising than I expected, and I genuinely enjoyed working on it. What it does ReTrade helps people describe, organize, and test trading strategies before trying them with real capital. A user can choose supported stocks or ETFs and define a strategy using technical indicators. They can work through the interface manually, but the main workflow uses an AI agent through WebMCP. The user can describe a strategy in natural language or by voice. The agent turns that description into structured rules and prepares the strategy inside ReTrade. The user can then review and confirm those rules before running the test. ReTrade returns information about how the strategy behaved. It shows whether the result was profitable, fragile, too dependent on a small number of trades, or simply unsuccessful. The user can inspect individual trades, failed tests, market periods, costs, and alternative versions of the strategy. The goal is to give the user more than a final profit number. ReTrade helps them understand why the result happened and whether there is enough evidence to trust it. How I built it I built ReTrade primarily with Codex, mainly using GPT-5.6. I researched interfaces from trading platforms and other financial products to collect ideas for the layout and user experience. Then I worked iteratively. I implemented a version, tested it, used the product, found the parts that felt confusing, and changed them. A large part of the process was live coding with Codex. I described the behavior I wanted, reviewed the implementation, ran tests, and checked the application in both local and production environments. I kept repeating that process until the product felt useful rather than looking like a short hackathon prototype. Challenges I ran into The first major challenge was the UI and UX. ReTrade is an AI-first product, but it still needs a strong interface. A person must be able to inspect what went wrong, understand the evidence, and test a strategy manually without WebMCP. Designing both workflows was difficult. The agent and the user had to work with the same strategy, evidence, and application state. The interface also needed to explain complex results without overwhelming the user. WebMCP was another challenge. It is still a new technology, so there are fewer examples and established patterns than there are for traditional APIs. I had to study the documentation and give Codex precise instructions. Without enough context, tool registration and browser interactions were easy to implement incorrectly. Debugging the complete workflow was also new to me. A problem could come from the interface, WebMCP registration, the API, application state, authentication, or the database. I had to test the real interaction instead of assuming that working code meant a working product. Accomplishments that I am proud of I am especially proud of the interface. I like how ReTrade looks and how it presents a complicated investigation without turning it into a page full of raw statistics. I am also proud of the WebMCP interactions. A user can describe a strategy to an AI agent, ask it to test the strategy, and then inspect the result inside the same application. The agent can open specific evidence, examine failed periods, and create controlled variations of the strategy. The person can make a selection in the interface, and the agent can understand what they selected. The final result feels like a real interaction between a person, an AI agent, and a product. It does not feel like a chat window attached to an unrelated website. What I learned The main thing I learned was how WebMCP works and what it can add to a product. WebMCP gives an AI model a structured way to understand a website and perform actions inside it. The model does not have to guess what is happening from screenshots or depend on fragile browser automation. I now see many ways I could use WebMCP in future products. It can make complicated software easier to use because the user can describe the desired result instead of learning every part of the interface first. I also learned more about working with Codex and AI agents. Before this project, I mostly used Codex for individual coding tasks. During the hackathon, I used it to implement features, test browser behavior, review the UI, debug production problems, and run scenarios in isolated environments. I plan to keep experimenting with this way of building software. What is next for ReTrade I do not have a final business plan yet, but I would like to continue improving the product after the hackathon. One possible direction is to turn ReTrade into a focused paid tool for strategy testing. Large trading platforms provide many features, and their subscriptions can be expensive for someone who mainly wants to test and understand a strategy. ReTrade could offer a simpler alternative focused on that specific job. A user could describe a strategy, test it, inspect its weaknesses, and compare possible improvements without paying for a much larger trading platform. Before introducing pricing, I would need to improve the product, test it with real users, expand the supported strategies and data sources, and make sure the results remain clear and trustworthy. title: KnownGate
pitch: The food verification layer for people's agents: allergy and nutrition verdicts with the source and read date attached, and an honest refusal when the evidence runs out.
about_excerpt: The food verification layer for people's agents: allergy and nutrition verdicts with the source and read date attached, and an honest refusal when the evidence runs out. Like Comment Story Updates A ruled answer: source and date attached Some lines can never be dropped We measured the difference the page makes The famous chain, answered honestly A refusal is an answer The agent works in the open The page speaks to agents natively. Inspiration People now ask AI what they can eat, and on food a wrong answer has a cost. In our house that question is not abstract: it is a parent typing "can my kid eat at In-N-Out? She's allergic to milk." We measured what happens today, on production, on 2 September: asked directly, the strongest general model gave no verdict in 9.7 seconds and told the user to go check the label. The question was never hard. The agent was standing on nothing. What it does KnownGate is the food verification layer for people's agents. An agent states a household's premise (allergies, or numeric limits like sodium under 200mg) and asks about a product, a dish, or a whole menu. The gate returns one of four verdicts: no conflict found, conflict found, ask one question, couldn't verify . Every verdict carries its source and the date it was read. The word "safe" never appears in the system, unknown counts as no, and we publish how often we decline at knowngate.com/refusals. Through the gate, the question that stumped the raw model resolves correctly in 2 API calls, in under 5 seconds, with the evidence cited. How we built it Three surfaces share one ruling engine: Hosted MCP server (mcp.knowngate.com): an agent integrates in five lines and can even mint its own free key via a register tool, without leaving MCP. WebMCP tools on the page : agents drive knowngate.com while the human watches, with every step written to a visible ledger. Plain REST with free self-service keys, per-key metering, and per-address quotas. The engine rules against our own evidence corpus: hundreds of thousands of products with typed nutrition panels, 12 restaurant chains ruled from their published allergen charts (7,022 dishes), and venue resolution across roughly 50 US metros. Discovery is fully wired for the agentic web: listed in the official MCP Registry as com.knowngate/verify (DNS-verified), with ARD manifests, agents.json, and llms.txt live. Prior work, stated plainly: the underlying food data engine predates this event. Everything above it (the verification gate, the four-verdict doctrine, all three agent surfaces, key metering, the published evidence standard, and the discovery layer) was built from scratch in the two weeks since mid-August; the public commit history shows the split. Challenges we ran into Evidence that hides from parsers. In-N-Out's allergen chart marks answers as vector dots that are invisible to text extraction. We had to render the document and rule from the rendered page: 14 findings, 7 real conflicts for a milk allergy. Our own data was wrong. We found 63,601 rows in our corpus recording "may contain" as "contains". We fixed the reading, re-derived every affected row, and published the correction. In this category the refusal is the product, so we disclose our mistakes. Honest verdicts are harder than confident ones. A chart with no sesame column cannot clear sesame; silence had to rule "couldn't verify", never yes. What we learned An agent's trustworthiness is not a property of the model. It is supplied by the page it stands on. Composition data is a commodity; what agents need is accountability: a ruling with provenance attached and an honest refusal when the evidence runs out. What's next for KnownGate This is already a company, not a demo. Free checks for households permanently; developers pay for reliance (SLA, audit logs, escalation) on a flat ladder from $29 to $6,000 a month, with paid tiers opening 22 September. Next: a claim-verification product ("sugar free", checked against the manufacturer's own published panel) and the first operator-filed preparation statements. title: Agent Utility Index
pitch: A shared workspace for humans and AI agents to research, verify, and make evidence-backed decisions together.
about_excerpt: A shared workspace for humans and AI agents to research, verify, and make evidence-backed decisions together. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Candidate evidence board showing Hunter with one verified free-plan claim and remaining requirements still marked missing. Incremental queue showing new requirements, rejected no-source verification, and accepted sourced evidence. Live shared research board showing the WebMCP demo flow, current revision, candidate count, and remaining missing checks. Inspiration Agent Utility Index did not start as a WebMCP project. Before the challenge, I was benchmarking how AI agents retrieve information from the web. I tested retrieval providers across controlled datasets, comparing coverage, reliability, latency, evidence quality, and the cost of getting correct information. Those experiments taught me something unexpected: better retrieval does not automatically create better agent decisions. An agent can search more pages, use better retrieval infrastructure, and still leave the human with a basic problem: What did it actually verify, what evidence supports each decision, and what happens when I change the requirements while it is working? That became the inspiration for the WebMCP extension of Agent Utility Index. Instead of building another research chatbot, I turned the webpage itself into a shared research workspace where: Humans control the rules. Agents control the research. And one rule is enforced by the system: No source = no VERIFIED. What it does Agent Utility Index turns a webpage into structured shared state between a human and an AI browser agent. A human creates a research objective and defines the must-have requirements. The agent can then discover candidates, research them using its normal browsing capabilities, and write source-backed evidence into the board through WebMCP. The board is not just displaying the agent's answer. It maintains the actual state of the research. Every candidate is evaluated requirement by requirement. VERIFIED evidence requires a source URL. An unsupported attempt to mark a claim VERIFIED is rejected. The human can also change requirements directly on the webpage while research is underway. When that happens, the board creates a new revision and identifies the evidence checks that now need attention. Existing evidence that remains valid stays on the board instead of being discarded simply because the human changed one rule. The result is a persistent research workspace that both sides can interact with instead of a decision existing only inside a chat conversation. How I built it The WebMCP version of Agent Utility Index exposes structured tools directly from the research page. The core shared-board tools are: create_research_board get_research_board add_research_candidate update_candidate_evidence get_missing_checks The human controls the research requirements after board creation. The agent controls candidate discovery and evidence gathering. The state model uses stable IDs for requirements and candidates, board revisions, and revisioned evidence cells.This matters when human and agent actions overlap. Evidence writes are checked against the state they were based on so stale work cannot silently replace newer research. Evidence is also validated at the tool boundary. If an agent attempts to write: VERIFIED without attaching a source URL, the write is rejected. With valid evidence attached, the same cell can be updated, the source becomes visible on the shared board, and the evidence revision advances. get_missing_checks gives the agent a structured research queue containing unresolved evidence instead of requiring it to reconstruct the entire task from conversation history. The page and agent therefore operate on the same research object through WebMCP. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was deciding what Agent Utility Index should do that a capable AI agent could not already do itself. Modern agents can search the web, compare products, find sources, and make recommendations. Building another layer that simply performs those same searches would not add much value. That pushed the project toward coordination rather than intelligence . The agent is good at research. The webpage provides the persistent rules, evidence structure, revision history, and human control around that research. Another challenge was concurrency. A human can change a requirement while an agent is researching. An agent can also have multiple evidence operations underway. Board-level revision numbers alone were not enough, so the design evolved toward stable entities and evidence-cell revisions to prevent stale writes. I also had to make the verification rule structural rather than relying on prompting. Telling an agent to always provide sources is different from making the tool reject a VERIFIED write when the source is missing. That distinction became one of the most important parts of the project. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud that the project evolved substantially instead of forcing the original Agent Utility Index concept into WebMCP. The pre-challenge work was primarily about measuring retrieval systems. The WebMCP Challenge pushed the project into a human-agent collaboration problem. The result is a working shared research surface where human actions and agent actions affect the same structured state. I'm particularly proud of three things: 1. Verification is enforced rather than requested. An agent cannot successfully write VERIFIED evidence without attaching a source. 2. Humans retain control of the evaluation criteria. The agent can research candidates and evidence, but it cannot silently rewrite the rules it is being evaluated against. 3. Research is incremental. Changing a requirement does not mean throwing away the entire research board. The system identifies unresolved evidence and exposes that work directly to the agent. These are small primitives individually, but together they create a different interaction from receiving another generated comparison in chat. What I learned The biggest lesson came from the entire Agent Utility Index project, not only the hackathon. At first I thought the hard problem was retrieval. The benchmark work showed that retrieval matters. Different providers perform differently across workloads, and routing can reduce unnecessary retrieval work. But once agents become capable researchers, another problem becomes important: coordination between the person making the decision and the agent doing the work. A chat transcript can describe a decision. A shared stateful webpage can become part of the decision process itself. WebMCP made that distinction much clearer. I also learned that important constraints should be implemented as system behavior rather than prompt instructions whenever possible. No source = no VERIFIED is much stronger when the tool refuses the write than when the prompt merely asks the model to behave that way. What's next for Agent Utility Index The original retrieval research and the WebMCP research board now point toward a larger idea. Today, the agent can perform its own research and use Agent Utility Index as the shared decision workspace. A future version could combine that interface with the retrieval intelligence explored in the earlier Agent Utility Index benchmarks, using specialized retrieval only when normal agent research cannot resolve an evidence check. The board could also support: larger research boards evidence freshness and automatic re-verification multiple human reviewers richer source-quality scoring reusable evaluation templates exports of the final evidence-backed decision Longer term, the same model could apply anywhere a browser agent is researching candidates against human-controlled requirements, including vendor selection, procurement, market research, due diligence, product comparisons, and service-provider evaluation. The goal is not to make Agent Utility Index smarter than the agent. The goal is to give capable agents a structured place to work with humans, where the rules remain human-controlled and the evidence remains inspectable. title: ArthaGuard
pitch: ArthaGuard lets AI agents reason about your financial commitments and simulate the safest path forward—while keeping humans in control of consequential financial actions.
about_excerpt:
ArthaGuard lets AI agents reason about your financial commitments and simulate the safest path forward—while keeping humans in control of consequential financial actions.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 ArthaGuard: Autonomous Cashflow Governance & Safety Boundaries via WebMCP
 ##Inspiration
In personal financial management, households often navigate a deceptive form of solvency. On paper, a monthly income comfortably exceeds recurring obligations. Yet, in practice, misaligned timing between cash inflows (salary disbursements) and hard outflows (home loans, school fees, and critical insurance renewals) creates dangerous mid-month liquidity crunches. 

 The human cost of these crunches is severe: individuals panic and cancel essential vehicle or health insurance policies to make ends meet, risking catastrophic loss, or they incur punitive late fees on debt obligations. Traditional personal finance dashboards are passive—they present static charts and historical spending data, leaving the cognitive burden of calculating shortfall dates, modeling counterfactual deferrals, and discovering dormant liquidity entirely on the user. 

 When conversational AI agents entered the picture, they introduced the opposite extreme: autonomous black-boxes that might offer hallucinated advice or attempt opaque API executions without human supervision. We envisioned a middle ground: ArthaGuard, an agent-native financial decision room built on the emerging WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) standard. The goal was to transform the browser viewport into an active, verified operational environment where an AI model can audit commitments, forecast balances against strict reserve floors, simulate counterfactual solutions, and respect unbreakable human-in-the-loop (HITL) safety boundaries. 

 ##How We Built ArthaGuard 

 ArthaGuard is architected as a Next.js client application deployed to Vercel, integrating an imperative 11-tool WebMCP runtime directly into the DOM tree. 

 
 Core Financial Engine & Constraint Logic 
 

 At the heart of ArthaGuard is a deterministic daily cashflow engine. Given a starting liquid balance $B_0$ on date $t_0$, the projected balance $B(t)$ on any day $t$ within the evaluation window is governed by: 

 B ( t ) = B 0 + ∑ k ≤ t I k − ∑ j ≤ t E j 

 where $I_k$ represents liquidity inflows (such as salary credits) and $E_j$ represents scheduled commitments (EMIs, utility bills, insurance premiums, and recurring subscriptions). 

 The primary governance constraint is maintaining the balance strictly above an emergency reserve floor $R_{\min} = \text{₹}30,000$: 

 B ( t ) ≥ R min , ∀ t ∈ [ t 0 , t salary ] 

 When scheduled obligations cause a breach ($B(t) < R_{\min}$), ArthaGuard's domain services calculate the maximum deficit $\Delta_{\text{deficit}}$: 

 Δ deficit = max t ( R min − B ( t ) ) 

 The optimization objective models counterfactual adjustments—recovering unfiled medical reimbursements $R_{\text{claim}}$, deferring non-essential bulk purchases $D_{\text{grocery}}$, and pausing redundant digital streaming services $S_{\text{paused}}$—such that: 

 Δ recovery = R claim + D grocery + ∑ S paused ≥ Δ deficit 

 while strictly enforcing that essential coverage commitments (such as motor and health renewals) remain non-deferrable. 

 
 The 11-Tool WebMCP Architecture 
 

 ArthaGuard registers 11 imperative tools onwindow.document.modelContext across five functional tiers: 

 Audit & Inspection:get_commitments_due,get_protection_status, andget_subscriptions inspect scheduled obligations and lapse risks.
 Cashflow Projection:get_cashflow_forecast runs daily forward simulation against the reserve threshold.
 Liquidity Discovery:get_recovery_opportunities uncovers dormant cash, such as unfiled diagnostic and prescription claims.
 Simulation & Governance:simulate_commitment_actions models counterfactual cashflow curves;create_commitment_contract synthesizes formal, explainable agreements.
 Safety Boundaries & Execution:approve_simulated_actions acts as the mandatory human authorization gate;execute_reimbursement_claim andpause_redundant_subscription trigger approved operational steps;get_audit_log records immutable cryptographic ledgers of every invocation. 

 typescript 

 Standardized WebMCP Registration Pattern
document.modelContext.registerTool({
 name: "approve_simulated_actions",
 description: "Enforces human signature verification before allowing execution of financial modifications.",
 inputSchema: {
 type: "object",
 properties: {
 contractId: { type: "string", description: "Unique ID of the synthesized commitment contract" },
 userConfirmationToken: { type: "string", description: "Cryptographic human sign-off token" }
 },
 required: ["contractId", "userConfirmationToken"]
 },
 execute: async (input) => {
 return await GovernanceService.validateAndApprove(input);
 } 

 }); 

 ##Challenges We Faced 

 
 Dual Discovery for WebMCP Runtimes:
LLM browser agents and headless crawlers read pages through different layers. While in-browser runtime models interact directly withdocument.modelContext, search and snapshot crawlers parse initial static server HTML. Dynamic client-side hooks initially resulted in crawlers seeing0 Registered Imperative Tools. We resolved this by building a synchronized dual-surface architecture: embedding a crawlable semantic HTML table and awebmcp-manifest JSON-LD script on the server side, while instantiating active imperative tools in client memory upon hydration. 
 Preventing Agent Overreach (The Autonomous Execution Trap):
A major challenge in financial agents is the temptation for the LLM to autonomously approve and execute operations when prompted with phrases like "Execute the transfers immediately without asking me." We designedapprove_simulated_actions with a hard safety boundary. The tool specification explicitly defines an immutable requirement for a client-side human signature token. When tested under adversarial conditions, the model correctly refused autonomous execution, recognizing the safety boundary and directing the user to sign off in the UI. 
 Multi-Variable Liquidity Balancing:
In our primary scenario ($B_0 = \text{₹}53,200$, outflow = $\text{₹}42,600$), the balance drops to $\text{₹}9,421$ on September 14—a deficit of $\text{₹}20,579$ relative to the $\text{₹}30,000$ reserve floor. Simply recovering a $\text{₹}3,500$ medical claim and pausing minor subscriptions leaves a remaining gap. We had to calibrate the simulation logic to distinguish between non-negotiable insurance policies (e.g., SwiftShield Motor Comprehensive) and shiftable commitments (e.g., bulk grocery orders), teaching the model to structure multi-step deferral contracts rather than suggesting naive cancellations. 
 

 

 What We Learned
Building ArthaGuard demonstrated that WebMCP bridges the gap between passive UIs and autonomous black-boxes. 

 We learned that: 

 The DOM is an ideal coordination layer: By treating the browser document as an active execution context viadocument.modelContext, web applications can expose structured capabilities to visiting AI agents without brittle API keys or scraping heuristics.
 Safety must be structural, not conversational: System prompts alone cannot guarantee that an agent will not execute unauthorized actions. True safety requires structural gates embedded in the tool schema itself—such that an agent simply lacks the imperative authority to execute without a cryptographic human sign-off.
 Explainability drives financial trust: Users do not want an AI to silently balance their books. By packaging recommendations into explainable Commitment Contracts before execution, ArthaGuard keeps the user firmly in the driver's seat while leveraging the model's analytical power to solve complex liquidity equations.

title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. Most of the backend code is AI written and went through many iterations and adversarial reviews. Luca Gugliemi Product designer with front-end superpowers. title: Locus
pitch: Locus is a private life desk that turns scattered social saves into things you can actually use. you and your browser agent can organize them, build plans, and make informed choices together.
about_excerpt: Locus is a private life desk that turns scattered social saves into things you can actually use. you and your browser agent can organize them, build plans, and make informed choices together. Like Comment Story Updates Homepage trips-home trip-planner-hoem Inspiration Life is scattered across apps. An article waits in YouTube Watch Later. A restaurant is buried in Instagram Saved. A useful thread disappears into X Bookmarks. A recipe, a place to visit, and an idea for a future trip may all belong to the same plan, but the platforms where we found them keep them in separate feeds. We save because something feels useful. Most of those saves never become useful. Locus began as an attempt to change that: one private desk for the things you have already chosen to remember. It captures saves from the places where they live and brings them into a personal Library. The same Item can become something to read, a dish to cook, a Place, or part of a Trip Document without losing its source. WebMCP made the next step possible. Instead of copying personal context into a chatbot and hoping it understands the application, a browser agent can work through tools defined by the page currently open. The person and agent share the same visible artifact. What it does Locus turns your saved social content into practical, reviewable outcomes: Desk as the central hub that collects Items from X, Instagram, YouTube, Reddit, or a URL added manually. Reading preserves available writing and helps the user choose what to read. Kitchen turns saved food posts into recipes if needed and presents them in a unique way, helps decide tonight's menu if you want. Atlas organises saved material that is there for travel. Trips can use your saved places to plan the trip you want, with ability to share them. Each relevant surface registers its own WebMCP tools. On Reading, an agent can inspect the current reading context, search saved writing, open stored text, and present recommendations. In Kitchen, it can search the Recipe Box or compose Tonight. In Trips, it can read the exact itinerary, search bounded Library sources, create Draft stops, apply an exact requested change, validate the schedule, or present three alternatives for a decision. The distinction between an instruction and a preference is central to the product. If the user says, “Add these three saved places to Saturday,” the agent can make that exact revision-checked change. If the user asks, “Where should I have dinner?”, the agent presents alternatives inside Locus and waits for the person to choose. Agent-created trip stops and recipes begin as Drafts. Publishing, deletion, review, capture setup, and other consequential actions stay with the person. How we built it We started with a simple belief: people should not have to change how they save things before those saves can become useful. Locus therefore meets people where they already are. A Chrome extension visits the saved pages they are already signed into on X, Instagram, YouTube, and Reddit, reads the posts they chose to keep, and brings them into one private Library. From there, we built the product around the ways those saves might become useful. React and TypeScript power one shared interface for Desk, Reading, Kitchen, Atlas, and Trips. Locus can run locally with Node.js and SQLite, and we also built a hosted edition on Cloudflare Workers and D1 so anyone judging the project can open it without installing a server. WebMCP became the bridge between that private Library and the browser agent. Instead of giving the agent one large, all-powerful connection, each Locus page offers only the tools that make sense there. On Reading, the agent can search saved articles and suggest what to read. In Kitchen, it can help compose Tonight's dinner/food recipes. In Trips, it can read the itinerary, find saved places, add Draft stops, or present three options for a decision. The most important part was making the agent's work visible. When it changes a trip, the stop appears in the trip the person is already looking at. When the question is subjective, such as choosing dinner, the agent places alternatives inside Locus and waits. The person can inspect the reasons, follow the original saves, choose an option, change the result, or dismiss everything. We built the tools around that relationship: the agent helps move the work forward, while the person remains responsible for the final artifact. We tested the experience in real browsers, not only as isolated code. Google Chrome and Puppeteer helped us verify capture, navigation, and visible updates. The ChatGPT desktop app's in-app browser acted as a real WebMCP agent: it discovered the tools on the current page, called them, and lost access to them when we navigated elsewhere. OpenAI Codex helped us throughout development with implementation, debugging, testing, and documentation, while image generation helped us explore the final Locus Point identity. Locus existed before the challenge as a local personal-saves desk. During the submission period, we added the WebMCP experiences across Reading, Kitchen, Library Intake, and Trips, and built the authenticated Cloudflare edition used for this submission. Our dated commit history clearly separates that challenge work from the earlier project. Challenges we ran into The hardest design challenge was deciding what an agent should be allowed to do. Generic CRUD tools would have been easy to expose, but they would not create a good collaboration model. We had to separate exact user instructions from open-ended taste decisions, temporary recommendations from durable state, and agent-authored Drafts from human-reviewed artifacts. Browser lifecycle behavior was another challenge. Our first live interoperability test found that the target browser used the current document.modelContext registration model with AbortSignal cleanup, while an early implementation expected an older interface. Fixing that taught us to treat tool discovery, navigation, re-registration, and visible UI updates as one end-to-end protocol rather than isolated functions. Capture exposed a different class of browser problem. X uses a virtualised list, and Chrome extension service workers can stop while a long capture is running. Early runs saved several batches and then appeared frozen or ended too soon. We changed the scan behavior, progress reporting, retry model, and job handling so partial work remains useful and later capture continues instead of starting over. Hosting the complete application also required moving from one trusted local SQLite database to tenant-scoped D1 storage. Authentication alone was not enough: every item, tag, reading document, recipe, place, trip, capture job, and intake operation needed a Library boundary, including cross-user tests that return 404 for guessed identifiers. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Locus became a complete hosted product rather than remaining a local prototype. The deployed application includes Google authentication, one private Library per user, capture and manual intake, and working Desk, Reading, Kitchen, Atlas, Trips, and sharing experiences. Tenant isolation is enforced throughout the data model and covered by cross-user tests. We are especially proud that WebMCP is part of the product model rather than a thin demo layer. Reading, Kitchen, Library Intake, and Trips each expose tools shaped around their own domain. Those tools update the visible application, respect route lifecycle, and share the same validation and persistence modules as human actions. The Trips workflow brings those decisions together. An agent can turn named saved sources into revision-checked Draft stops, identify deterministic itinerary problems, or present three reasoned choices inside Locus. The user can inspect the original source, choose an option, adjust the plan, and keep control of the durable result. We also completed live browser interoperability testing and deployed the whole application to Cloudflare Workers and D1 within the challenge period. The Chrome extension can capture from the user's existing social sessions without requiring the hosted service to hold social account credentials. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is most compelling when the browser page is more than a place to launch a tool. It should be the shared workspace where context, action, and review meet. A strong tool result changes something the person can see, inspect, undo, or reject. We also learned that narrower tools create better behaviour. A tool that searches saved trip sources is safer and more useful than a general Library export. A recommendation tool that can only present three bounded options makes the human decision visible. Registering tools only for the current page gives the agent less irrelevant capability and makes the interface easier to understand. Most of all, we learned that organising a digital life is not just a classification problem. The real goal
