 Merchant 3: Paper & Ink Bookstore — untrustedContentHint protection against prompt injection 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 Today's agentic web demos fall into one of two traps: 

 
 Brittle Screen Scraping : Agents using vision or accessibility trees to click coordinates and type blindly into DOM elements, which break the moment a CSS class, layout, or modal changes. 
 Walled-Garden Aggregators : Agents restricted to closed ecosystem APIs where independent neighborhood businesses must surrender 30% take rates and hand over customer relationships to centralized platforms. 
 

 When the W3C and Chrome WebMCP standard ( document.modelContext ) emerged, we saw the foundation for a third, better future: the open web itself as the native agent runtime . 

 We asked ourselves: Could an AI agent coordinate a real-world multi-stop morning errand across three completely independent, standalone neighborhood businesses—a specialty coffee shop, a boutique grooming studio, and an indie bookstore—with zero backend integration, zero proprietary API keys, and pure on-page tool discovery? 

 That question led to Open Web Concierge . 

 

 What It Does 

 Open Web Concierge is an autonomous multi-vendor assistant that plans, negotiates, and executes unified errands across the open web while keeping the human firmly in control. 

 
 Dynamic Instruction-Driven Scoping : The user speaks naturally (e.g., "I want an iced cold brew with oat milk" , "Book a haircut with Marcus at 11:15" , or a multi-stop Saturday routine). The agent dynamically parses intent and activates only the merchant services requested, gracefully omitting non-relevant stops with zero wasted spend. 
 User Identity Profile & Live Form Reflection : The Concierge maintains the user's default credentials (Name, Email, Mobile No., Gender). As the agent navigates each merchant website, it emits live synchronization events over a shared errand bus—allowing the user to watch the merchant's counter form or booking calendar populate live on screen with an active sync indicator. 
 Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Security Gates : The agent never silently commits funds. Before finalizing any transaction, a modal confirmation gate halts execution, presenting itemized pricing, timing, and merchant verification for explicit user approval. 
 Live Cross-Side Checkout Reflection : Once authorized, dual-layer real-time synchronization ( BroadcastChannel and reactive storage) immediately posts the confirmed order to the merchant's Active Barista Queue , Client Appointment Log , and Front Register Holds across independent windows and tabs. 
 Auditable Receipts : Upon completion, the Concierge compiles an itemized trip log with verifiable order IDs and costs, exportable as Markdown or JSON. 
 

 

 How We Built It 

 We built the application as a production-grade multi-page web ecosystem using React 19 , Vite 6 , and Tailwind CSS , adhering strictly to the Chrome & W3C WebMCP specification: 

 
 Merchant Tool Registration on document.modelContext :

 
 Artisan Roast Café ( /cafe/ ) : Exposes check_menu ( readOnlyHint: true ) and order_coffee (with strict parameter schemas and customer contact info). 
 Luxe Grooming Studio ( /salon/ ) : Exposes check_availability ( readOnlyHint: true ) and book_slot for stylist and calendar scheduling. 
 Paper & Ink Bookstore ( /bookstore/ ) : Exposes search_catalog ( untrustedContentHint: true ) and reserve_book for front-desk holds. 
 Concierge Orchestration Hub ( / ) : Exposes get_errand_briefing and log_completed_step . 
 
 Prompt Injection Defense via Chrome Hints :

 
 Following WebMCP security guidelines, search_catalog marks query results with untrustedContentHint: true . This informs the consuming LLM that merchant book blurbs and user reviews are untrusted third-party content, neutralizing indirect prompt injection vectors. 
 
 Idempotency Protection :

 
 Implemented client request tokens ( clientRequestId ) cached in a 15-second sliding window to prevent accidental double-billing or duplicate holds from rapid agent loops. 
 
 Bi-Directional Errand Bus :

 
 Combined the HTML5 BroadcastChannel API ( webmcp_errand_bus ) with reactive window storage listeners to ensure sub-millisecond, cross-tab synchronization between the Concierge hub and open merchant tabs without requiring an intermediary WebSocket server. 
 
 Built-in WebMCP Inspector :

 
 Included an interactive on-page drawer allowing judges and developers to inspect live registered schemas, test parameter validation, and trigger manual tool executions. 
 
 

 

 Challenges We Faced 

 
 Contextual Linguistic Disambiguation : Natural language is messy. In a prompt like "Book a haircut with Marcus" , the word "book" is a scheduling verb, not a request for literature. We engineered a contextual parser that accurately distinguishes verbal actions ( "book an appointment" ) from literary nouns ( "read a book" , "buy a novel" ) to prevent erroneous merchant activations. 
 Zero-Flicker Live Form Population : Connecting cross-tab React state to live agent actions without causing form resets or race conditions required decoupling tool discovery from UI input bindings, synchronizing through a predictable broadcast event contract. 
 Eliminating "AI Slop" Aesthetics : We committed to an authentic, human-crafted design language. We eliminated all emojis, avoided generic gradient pills, and designed a neutral, high-contrast dark palette ( #0C0C0C , #121110 , #141414 ) inspired by Swiss editorial typography and physical ledger boards. 
 Cross-Window Consistency : Ensuring that checkouts made in the Concierge immediately reflect in the merchant's Barista Queue or Appointment Log across separate browser tabs and embedded multi-views required implementing dual-channel sync ( BroadcastChannel with storage event fallbacks). 
 

 

 What We Learned & The Future of the Open Web 

 WebMCP represents a paradigm shift for web development. For the last 15 years, the web has been pressured into walled gardens and mobile app silos because machines couldn't reliably interact with standard HTML. 

 By standardizing document.modelContext , the open web becomes the agentic web . A local family-owned bakery or indie bookstore can become fully AI-operable in an afternoon simply by exposing standard tools on their existing website. No platform monopolies, no 30% tolls, and no closed ecosystems—just humans, agents, and merchants collaborating over the open protocols of the web.

pitch: The WebMCP-powered marketplace where humans and AI agents shop together.

 Inspiration 

 Online shopping involves many steps: searching for products, applying filters, checking specifications, comparing options, finding offers, adding items to a cart, and finally deciding whether to purchase. 

 We asked ourselves: 

 
 * What if an AI agent could actually work with a shopping website instead of simply telling the user what to buy? And can the work become easier for the users as, complex [part will be handled by the AI agent, and the approval part will be under the Humans. * 
 

 Traditional websites are primarily designed for human interaction. An AI agent may be able to read information or navigate the interface, but it does not have a reliable, structured way to use the website's capabilities. 

 This inspired us to build AgentCart , a WebMCP-powered marketplace where humans and AI agents can shop together. 

 Our goal was to explore what happens when a website is designed not only for humans, but also as an active tool interface for AI agents. 

 

 What it does 

 AgentCart allows a user to give an AI agent a natural-language shopping goal. 

 For example: 

 
 "Find me the best laptop for programming under ₹70,000. Prioritize performance and battery life." 
 

 The agent can then: 

 
 Search available products 
 Filter them according to the user's requirements 
 Inspect product specifications 
 Compare the strongest candidates 
 Find the best available offer 
 Add the selected product to the cart 
 Calculate the final price 
 Request human approval before completing the purchase 
 

 AgentCart currently exposes eight WebMCP tools: 

 
 search_products 
 filter_products 
 get_product_details 
 compare_products 
 find_best_offer 
 add_to_cart 
 calculate_cart_total 
 request_purchase_approval 
 

 The WebMCP integration is implemented using: 

 document.modelContext.registerTool() 

 A key part of AgentCart is human-in-the-loop control . The agent can research, compare, optimize, and prepare a purchase, but it cannot complete the simulated purchase without explicit human approval. 

 No real payment or transaction takes place. 

 

 How we built it 

 AgentCart was built using React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Zustand . 

 We created a structured electronics product catalog containing product information such as price, brand, category, rating, stock, specifications, features, and offers. 

 The WebMCP integration is implemented in the frontend using document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool has a defined name, description, input schema, and execution function. 

 We designed the tools around the actual shopping workflow rather than exposing only a single generic AI action. 

 The application also includes an Agent Activity panel that makes the agent's workflow visible to the user, for example: 

 search_products → filter_products → compare_products → find_best_offer → add_to_cart → request_purchase_approval 

 We used Git and GitHub for source control and deployed the application using Vercel . 

 The final purchase flow is simulated so that the complete human + agent interaction can be demonstrated safely. 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of our biggest challenges was making WebMCP tool registration reliable. 

 Because the application can initialize more than once, we needed to prevent duplicate tool registrations. We implemented registration safeguards and checks for already-registered tools. 

 Another challenge was making the agent workflow respond differently to different natural-language requests. We did not want every prompt to produce the same demonstration. 

 We therefore implemented dynamic handling for: 

 
 Product categories 
 Budget limits 
 Ratings 
 Battery requirements 
 Cheapest-product requests 
 Comparison requests 
 Offers 
 Purchase and approval workflows 
 

 We also had to carefully separate agent autonomy from human control . The agent can perform research and prepare a cart, but the final consequential action requires explicit human approval. 

 Finally, we focused on making the WebMCP functionality understandable through the user interface instead of hiding the interaction behind the scenes. The Agent Activity panel helps users see what the agent is doing. 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that AgentCart goes beyond simply demonstrating that WebMCP tools can be registered. 

 We built a complete shopping workflow around multiple meaningful WebMCP tools, connecting product discovery, filtering, comparison, offer optimization, cart preparation, and human approval. 

 We are especially proud of the human + agent collaboration model . The agent handles the repetitive research and optimization work while the human remains responsible for the final purchase decision. 

 We also built the project as a working, deployed web application rather than only a technical proof of concept. 

 Most importantly, we created an experience where the WebMCP implementation directly changes what the website can do with an AI agent. 

 

 What we learned 

 Building AgentCart taught us that making a website agent-ready is very different from simply adding an AI chatbot. 

 We learned how WebMCP can allow websites to expose structured capabilities that AI agents can use directly. 

 We also learned that tool design matters. Clear tool names, descriptions, input schemas, and appropriate read-only or state-changing behavior are important for reliable agent interaction. 

 Another important lesson was the importance of human-in-the-loop design . Giving an agent the ability to research and prepare actions does not mean it should automatically perform every consequential action and the important action like the approval and payment processing should be taken by Human only. 

 We also learned how frontend state management, WebMCP tool execution, dynamic workflows, and user-facing activity visualization can be combined into one agent-ready web experience. 

 

 What's next for AgentCart 

 AgentCart currently focuses on demonstrating the core WebMCP-powered shopping experience with electronics. 

 The next step would be expanding the marketplace with more product categories and richer real-world data. 

 We would also like to explore more advanced agent capabilities such as personalized preferences, multi-item shopping goals, budget optimization, shipping comparisons, and more sophisticated approval controls. 

 Beyond shopping, the same WebMCP interaction pattern could be applied to other multi-step web experiences such as travel planning, restaurant reservations, service marketplaces, and productivity applications. 

 Our broader vision is a web where websites are not only pages that humans read and click, but active environments that AI agents can work with while humans remain in control. 

 

 Final Thought 

 Before WebMCP, an AI agent could tell you what to buy. 

 With WebMCP, the web can actually work with the agent. 

 AgentCart is our exploration of what that future could look like.

title: Filika
pitch: Filika lets AI agents turn website issues, confusing flows, and blocked tasks into actionable feedback for product teams.
about_excerpt: Filika lets AI agents turn website issues, confusing flows, and blocked tasks into actionable feedback for product teams. Like 3 Comment Story Updates Hero Demo Page Login Page Onboarding Dashboard Complaints Feedback Detail Profile Menu Filika: WebMCP feedback infrastructure for modern web applications Inspiration Website problems are often discovered in the moment but never reach the people who can fix them. A customer may get stuck in checkout, an employee may be unable to complete a task, or an agent may encounter confusing behavior while helping someone. Turning that experience into an actionable report usually requires leaving the task, finding a support channel, and manually reconstructing what happened. Filika makes that handoff part of the browsing experience. What it does Filika is a WebMCP-native feedback system for web applications. A website registers the static filika_submit_feedback tool with document.modelContext . When a browser agent encounters an observed bug, blocked task, confusing behavior, or concrete product idea, it can submit a structured report containing a title, description, expected behavior, and reproduction steps. The report is delivered to a maintainer workspace where teams can review, search, filter, and export it to GitHub. Why WebMCP matters Without WebMCP, an agent has no reliable, structured way to hand an observed problem back to the product team. It would need to guess its way through a website's support UI, generate an unstructured message, or stop at a conversational summary. With Filika, the website intentionally exposes one narrowly scoped feedback capability. The agent can act at the moment it sees the problem, while the product team receives feedback in a consistent format that is ready for triage. This creates a better experience for both sides: people and agents can continue working instead of filing a separate ticket, and maintainers receive clearer reports with reproducible context rather than vague descriptions. How we built it Filika is a TypeScript monorepo built with Bun, Next.js, React, PostgreSQL, and Drizzle. The browser SDK uses document.modelContext.registerTool() to register the static filika_submit_feedback WebMCP tool. Its closed JSON schema accepts only bounded, structured feedback fields. The collector API validates every request, verifies the configured website origin, limits payload size and timeouts, detects duplicates using idempotency keys, and stores accepted reports in PostgreSQL. The maintainer workspace lets teams create applications, configure allowed origins, install the generated SDK snippet, inspect incoming feedback, and export approved reports to GitHub issues. A public demo storefront includes intentional failures so judges can test the WebMCP flow themselves. Privacy and safety Filika deliberately does not collect ambient page content, browser history, screenshots, cookies, local storage, or credentials. Tool metadata is static, input schemas reject unknown fields, and browser or collector data is treated as untrusted until validated. Demo Open the demo, ask a WebMCP-enabled browser agent to complete the sample shopping task, let it encounter the intentional failure, and ask it to submit feedback with Filika. Then open the workspace to see the submitted report and its reproduction steps. title: GoPic for Agents
pitch: Turn a real-world sign into the right place. GoPic uses visual evidence, location context, and WebMCP tools so agents can identify and ground real-world businesses from storefront photos.
about_excerpt: Turn a real-world sign into the right place. GoPic uses visual evidence, location context, and WebMCP tools so agents can identify and ground real-world businesses from storefront photos. Like Comment Story Updates GoPic turns a storefront photo into structured OCR, place candidates, and a grounded result for WebMCP agents. What it does Inspiration Travelers constantly see useful information in the physical world — storefronts, restaurant signs, shop names, addresses — but turning that visual clue into the correct place on the web is still surprisingly awkward. OCR can read text, but reading text is not the same as identifying the right real-world place. Businesses can share the same name, signs can use unfamiliar scripts, and users may not know what to type into search. GoPic already explored this problem as a mobile visual-search product. For the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to take the next step: expose that visual sign-to-place workflow directly to AI agents. What it does GoPic for Agents lets a human provide a storefront or sign photo and an optional location hint. GoPic then: analyzes the visible sign text, combines the visual evidence with location context, returns structured place candidates, identifies the strongest grounded result when the evidence is sufficient. The same workflow is exposed to compatible agents through three WebMCP tools: gopic_get_sign_context gopic_analyze_sign gopic_get_place_candidates This allows an agent to discover and invoke GoPic's capabilities directly from the webpage instead of guessing how to interact with the UI. How I built it The challenge website is a lightweight HTML, CSS, and JavaScript experience designed for both humans and WebMCP-enabled agents. WebMCP tools are registered using document.modelContext.registerTool() . The analysis flow is: Human photo → WebMCP tool → Supabase Edge Function → visual analysis → structured OCR and place candidates → grounded result The backend runs as a Supabase Edge Function. API credentials are stored only as server-side secrets and are never exposed to the browser or committed to the public repository. The public demo endpoint also includes origin checks, image type and size validation, and rate limiting. Challenges I ran into One challenge was separating simple OCR from actual place grounding. A sign may contain a business name, branch information, an address, phone number, and descriptive text, and not all of it should be treated as a place name. Another challenge was making the same workflow useful to both humans and agents. The page needed to remain understandable as a normal website while also exposing structured actions that an agent can discover and execute. I also spent time tightening the public demo architecture so that API credentials were not exposed and the live implementation matched the public source repository. What I learned WebMCP changes the role of a website. Instead of being only a visual interface that an agent has to interpret, the page can explicitly describe the actions it offers and the structured data those actions return. That makes it possible to combine human intent — "this is the sign I care about" — with an agent's ability to act quickly on the web. What's next The larger vision for GoPic is to make real-world visual information directly actionable. A traveler should be able to point at a sign, menu, storefront, product label, or other physical-world clue and let an agent understand what it is, identify the relevant real-world entity, and continue the task on the web. For this challenge, the focus is intentionally narrow: See the sign. Find the real place. title: Relocates.io
pitch: Where can all of us live? A map that answers it for a whole household — and negotiates when it can't.
about_excerpt: Where can all of us live? A map that answers it for a whole household — and negotiates when it can't. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration We had one weekend of viewings, in a city none of us had lived in, and a spreadsheet. The question was simple and nothing could answer it: where can all four of us actually live? Property sites filter by price and bedroom count. But nobody is unhappy about a bedroom count. They're unhappy because the school run takes forty minutes, and because that got decided once, in a hurry, from three timezones away, and then paid for every morning for three years. So we guessed. Everybody guesses. It's a constraint satisfaction problem and it deserved a solver, so we wrote one. Every requirement becomes a comparison over a 250-metre grid of the real city: real schools from Google Places with their real ratings, real gyms, real parks, and real terrain, so a hill costs the minutes it actually costs. Where everyone's requirements overlap, a volume lights up over the photorealistic map. Then it goes to zero. Six honest requirements from four people usually don't fit in one city. Every tool we'd used treats that as a dead end. Empty list, try removing a filter. But "nowhere works" is genuinely useful information, as long as you also say which two requirements are fighting and how much one has to give. So the page tests dropping each requirement, then every pair, then sweeps the blocking thresholds to find the smallest concession that reopens the map. It draws both options at once, in the colours of the two people involved. That's the point where WebMCP stopped being a technology choice. The solver can tell you bending one limit reopens more ground than bending the other. It can't tell you that one of those limits is a bad knee and the other is a fourteen-year-old walking to school by herself. It can't know that the cheaper concession is the harder one to live with. Somebody has to say "hers is cheaper, but hers is the medical one" — and a slider is never going to say that. But it doesn't work from a server either. The agent offers two futures, the page draws both over the real city, and the person picks by looking at them. What's being compared is a shape on a map, not a number in a response. The state and the solver have to sit where the person's eyes already are. The loop runs both ways too, which is the part we didn't expect to matter as much as it does. People don't wait their turn. They drag a threshold while the agent is still talking, delete something, accept an option on their own. Those edits are real and they aren't the agent's. So the page logs who changed what and hands the agent everything a human did since its last turn. What it does Relocates.io finds the part of a city where everyone in a household gets what they need at the same time, draws it on a photorealistic 3D map, and when that region doesn't exist, tells you exactly which requirements collide and how far one has to move. You can describe your household to an agent or build it by hand. Both drive the same state. Pick a city. It builds a 250 m grid and loads the terrain. Add people, then their requirements. Not filters — requirements that belong to someone, each carrying their own reason in their own words. "She walks alone, it's her independence." "It's his knee, not a preference." That sentence matters later. Watch where they overlap. The intersection is contoured and extruded over the real buildings. The area in km² is the number on screen. When it hits zero, you get options, not an error. The page finds what's blocking, works out the smallest movement that reopens the map, and draws both candidate futures at once with the area each one buys. You choose. Click one and it resolves. Both numbers were already on screen — what the agent adds is which concession is cheaper, which is easier, and why those aren't the same. Then check a real listing. Paste an address, get pass or fail on every requirement with the margin, plus the nearest spots that would have worked. Or search homes restricted to inside the feasible region, so it can't return somewhere that fails one of your family. The 3D isn't decoration. If you can't fly out for a third viewing, the two things you most need to see are what a street looks like and how steep it is, and a flat map shows neither. Walking times run through Tobler's hiking function over real elevation, so a kilometre uphill costs about 40% more than a flat one. The hill you can see is the hill that makes the school walk eleven minutes instead of seven. Same dataset drives the picture and the arithmetic. How we built it Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Google Maps Platform, WebMCP. About 4,600 lines. No server, no database, no API routes. Browser tab ├── Grid 250 m lattice over the search area ├── Layers one Float32Array per question — walk time, commute, grade ├── Solver masks · marching squares · diagnosis · relaxation sweep ├── Map3D photorealistic tiles + pooled extruded volumes ├── WebMCP 18 tools on document.modelContext └── Cache IndexedDB — a city is learned once Everything runs in the browser through the Maps JS SDK and caches locally. Nothing about the household leaves the page. That started as a constraint and turned out to be the reason the whole thing works: an agent can reach into live state and get an answer in the same tick. Places and Elevation are real. Commute times are modelled from distance and mode rather than routed, and we say so on screen. We skipped the Routes API on purpose. Real routed commutes meant thousands of billed matrix elements per origin and several seconds of latency on every threshold change, which would have killed the thing that makes the sweep feel like an instrument. Two functions carry the project. diagnose.ts answers why there's nowhere to live. With a dozen requirements over a few thousand cells there's no need to be clever, so it tests every leave-one-out combination, then every pair if none of those work. Exhaustive and exact. frontier.ts answers how far a requirement has to bend, sweeping its threshold across the grid for the smallest movement that opens any cell, then the area gained at every step after. It returns a curve, not a point, so the agent can describe what a concession costs. Both measure off the grid. Neither estimates. That's the whole technical claim, so it lives in the code rather than in a paragraph. The map uses Map3DElement with regions as extruded Polygon3DElement volumes and drawsOccludedSegments on, so buildings never hide the answer. Those are DOM nodes, not batched geometry, so they're pooled at startup and mutated in place. Three things about the tools mattered more than the rest. Descriptions say when to call something, not just what it does: "call this whenever the area is 0, before telling the user anything." Every requirement carries a required rationale field. And get_state returns humanChanges , so the agent finds out what a person did while it wasn't looking. Challenges we ran into deck.gl doesn't work over photorealistic tiles. The obvious stack was a dead end. Overlays float above the terrain instead of sitting on it. We dropped deck.gl for native Polygon3DElement , which Google renders against the same terrain as the tiles. Found it with a throwaway HTML file before writing any real code, which saved a day. Google has no ratings for schools. Gyms, parks and supermarkets all return them. Secondary schools returned zero out of eight. Our "4★ or better" filter emptied the pool, so every school requirement became permanently unsatisfiable and the map went permanently blank. Saying "nowhere qualifies" would have been a lie with a straight face, so the filter now drops itself, says so in a banner, and reports the caveat to the agent. Nobody agrees where WebMCP lives. Drafts disagree on navigator.modelContext versus document.modelContext . We built against navigator , and an agent looking at the live page told us exactly what that produces: "exposes WebMCP capability, but currently provides no WebMCP tools." It now checks document first, awaits each registration, and tears down with AbortSignal . Photorealistic tiles take no style array. No saturation: -100 , so the grey-out when there's no answer had to be a CSS filter on the container. It greys the regions too, but during a conflict there are no regions to keep coloured, so that worked out. The numbers sit in an unfiltered layer above. Cutting things. Routes API, air quality, saved sessions, multi-city. All had to go to keep one sequence working reliably: requirements, conflict, two futures, a choice. Accomplishments that we're proud of The empty state is the product. Treating "nowhere works" as the interesting case is the idea everything is built around, and it held up against real data from a real city. Every number is real. Every km² and every minute comes off the grid. The agent is told never to state a figure it didn't get from a tool, and the tools are shaped so it never nee
video_transcript_excerpt: Finding a place for a family usually means juggling dozens of open tabs, trying to guess where everyone's daily life actually intersects. Relocates.io solves this geometrically. We input a family of four relocating to San Francisco. David commuting to Google, Sarah, Leah, and 8-year-old Tom. The agent parses the household and registers the profiles directly into client state. Now we define their daily mobility constraints. David needs transit within 30 minutes. Leah needs a 15-minute walk to high school. Tom needs 10 minutes to primary school, plus a nearby gym and park. The browser intersects these travel boundaries on device, 29.38 square kilometers across five candidate zones. Now the hard constraint. Sarah has an injured knee. Any pedestrian incline over a 6% grade is physically out of the question. That medical requirement is treated as non-negotiable, factoring San Francisco's elevation profiles into the pedestrian routes. >> The viable terrain immediately collapses by more than half down to 13.44 square kilometers. Hills eliminate most of the city. Instead of negotiating back and forth in chat, I open the drawer and adjust the sliders myself, granting Tom 17 minutes and tightening the park to six. Web MCP immediately detects my manual edits and synchronizes the agent state. The polygon updates dynamically to 11.88 square kilometers, highlighting five qualifying neighborhoods, including the Presidio. We drop straight into 3D terrain to verify street inclines before signing a lease. Compromise isn't an argument anymore. It's just geometry.

title: Pulse: Voice-Steered Drums
pitch: Hands on the pads, voice on the loop: Pulse lets musicians improvise live with AI-guided tempo, swing, and sounds via WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
Hands on the pads, voice on the loop: Pulse lets musicians improvise live with AI-guided tempo, swing, and sounds via WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 I can't play a single instrument. So I built one that plays itself. 

 I can't play a single instrument. Not really. I can find middle C on a piano if you give me a minute, and that's about where my musical talent ends. 

 So when I sat down to build something for the WebMCP Challenge, a drum machine was the last thing I expected to make. 

 Here's what changed my mind: one sentence buried in Codex's docs — "Website-provided tool definitions and results are untrusted content." It's a throwaway security note, but it describes something bigger. For years, an AI agent trying to use a website has had exactly one option: stare at the page and guess. Parse the HTML, look at the buttons, click where it thinks is, hope for the best. The website never gets a say in how it's operated. 

 WebMCP flips that. The page can just tell the agent what it does. Not "here are some buttons," but set_tempo, mute_track, with real schemas, wired straight into the app. 

 I wanted to test that idea somewhere unforgiving. Music felt right, because you can't fake a groove. If an agent's tempo lands on 240 instead of 124, you hear it immediately. There's no ambiguity to hide behind. 

 So I built Pulse: a browser drum sequencer with a mouse-and-grid interface anyone can click around in, and seven WebMCP tools — tempo, swing, pattern length, mute, sound, step, and a read-only pattern-state query — wired into the exact same engine underneath. Not a demo layer, but the same sequencer. 

 The moment that actually got me was when I opened ChatGPT and said: "Set the tempo to 124, make Track 4 a cowbell, mute Track 3." The grid on my screen lit up and rearranged itself in real time. There was no "AI mode." The square that lit up was the exact same square my mouse lights up. I built a visible tell for this on purpose: when a tool call changes something, the control flashes violet for a second, so you can actually see the agent working instead of taking my word for it. Open the live app right now and see for yourself. 

 I'm still not a musician, and maybe I never will be. But I made a loop tonight that I was proud of, entirely with my voice, because the website told the agent exactly how to operate it instead of leaving the agent to reverse-engineer the interface. That's the whole idea behind Pulse: when a page can describe its own capabilities, the gap between "someone who can use this" and "someone who can't" starts to shrink — for agents. For people like me. 

 What Pulse does 

 Pulse exposes six WebMCP tools directly from the browser: 

 set_tempo
set_swing
set_pattern_length
mute_track
set_track_sound
toggle_step 

 A musician can interact with the sequencer normally using the visible controls, or an AI agent can manipulate the exact same sequencer through WebMCP. 

 For example, I can tell ChatGPT: 

 “Make the pattern two bars, set the tempo to 124 BPM with 20% swing, change Track 4 to cowbell, toggle steps 4 and 12, and mute Track 3.” 

 The agent discovers the matching site tools, calls them, and the changes immediately appear on the live drum-machine grid. 

 There is no separate “AI version” of Pulse. 

 Why WebMCP is a strong fit 

 Without WebMCP, an agent controlling Pulse would have to reason about the presentation layer: 

 Where is the tempo control?
Is this button Track 3 or Track 4?
Does clicking this grid square turn a step on or off?
How should a slider be manipulated? 

 With WebMCP, the page answers those questions itself. 

 Pulse exposes typed application capabilities directly from the page. The agent operates on concepts such as tempo, swing, track, sound, pattern length, and step instead of screen coordinates. 

 That makes the interaction more precise for the agent while preserving the visual, tactile interface for the person using the instrument. 

 Humans and agents working together 

 The most interesting thing about Pulse is that the human and the agent are not using two different systems. 

 Both operate on the same application state. 

 A person can start a loop manually, ask an agent to change the groove, continue editing with the mouse, ask for another modification, and keep playing. 

 The WebMCP invocation that lights up the grid follows the same state path as the click that lights it up from my mouse. 

 The agent is not simulating the use of Pulse. It is using Pulse through a capability surface deliberately provided by Pulse. 

 That is what I think matters about WebMCP beyond this demo: websites can become active participants in defining how agents interact with them. 

 How I implemented WebMCP 

 Pulse is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, the Web Audio API, and WebMCP. 

 The six WebMCP tools are registered in the live browser page and execute against the same Sequencer instance used by the visible controls. 

 For example, the UI tempo control and the WebMCP set_tempo tool ultimately operate on the same sequencer logic. 

 The WebMCP layer does not proxy commands through a separate AI backend. The tools live inside the page, beside the application state they control. 

 The application is deployed publicly on Vercel over HTTPS and can be exercised through ChatGPT’s built-in browser or Google Chrome with WebMCP testing enabled. 

 Building it 

 The implementation process was not completely clean, and that ended up being one of the most useful parts of the project. 

 I initially used hand-written WebMCP registration code before discovering the official integration hook and migrating to it. 

 I spent real time reading Chrome’s secure-tools documentation, revisiting my tool descriptions, and learning constraints I did not even know existed when I began. 

 The warning that website-provided tool definitions and results are untrusted also forced me to think more carefully about the trust boundary between an agent host and a page it did not write. 

 Codex was my primary development partner throughout that process: helping trace the WebMCP integration, reason about the tool surface, migrate implementation details, validate schemas, debug browser behavior, and verify the final production build. 

 Those details are not glamorous, but they are what “the future of the open web” looked like from inside the build: not a keynote slide, but a series of small, specific decisions about what a page should expose and how much an agent should trust it. 

 What I learned 

 WebMCP changed how I think about the relationship between websites and agents. 

 The important abstraction is not “AI clicking websites faster.” 

 It is applications exposing a semantic capability layer alongside their human interface. 

 The visual UI remains valuable for people. The WebMCP tool surface becomes the precise interface for agents. Both operate over the same underlying application. 

 That feels substantially more robust than teaching increasingly powerful models to reverse-engineer every website they encounter. 

 Known limitations 

 toggle_step intentionally implements toggle semantics rather than absolute “step on” or “step off” semantics. Calling it twice therefore reverses the change. For deterministic judging or demos, refreshing Pulse before running the provided multi-step prompt gives a known starting state. 

 Play/Stop is also intentionally not exposed as a tool in the current version because browser audio requires an initial user gesture. 

 What’s next 

 Pulse currently exposes six musical operations, but the same architecture could support higher-level capabilities such as creating fills, saving patterns, loading presets, manipulating velocity, generating variations, or exposing reusable musical structures. 

 More broadly, I want to explore the same model in applications where agents currently rely heavily on UI interpretation. 

 Pulse is a small demonstration of a much larger idea: 

 When a website can tell an agent exactly what it offers, the agent no longer has to guess. 

 

 
 Built With 

 next.js react typescript vercel web-audio-api webmcp 
 

 
 Try it out 

 
 
 
 pulse-webmcp.vercel.app

title: MemoryBook
pitch: A collaborative digital memory book that lets AI understand contributions and use WebMCP to organize, create, and edit the book directly.
about_excerpt:
A collaborative digital memory book that lets AI understand contributions and use WebMCP to organize, create, and edit the book directly.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Memory books are built from many small pieces: photos, stories, memories, events, and messages submitted by different people. Collecting those contributions is relatively easy. Turning them into a coherent and meaningful book is much harder. 

 MemoryBook explores a different approach. Instead of using AI only to generate text or answer questions, the application exposes meaningful book operations through WebMCP. This allows an AI agent to understand the contents of the book and actively help organize and build it. 

 The goal is to make AI a useful collaborator inside a real web application while keeping the user in control. 

 What it does 

 MemoryBook is a collaborative digital memory book application where people can submit memories and photos and an organizer can turn them into a finished book. 

 Through WebMCP, an AI agent can interact with the application using structured tools. 

 The current integration allows the AI to: 

 
 retrieve the current MemoryBook status and context 
 list submitted contributions 
 analyze which important school-year events are missing 
 propose a thematic spread based on the submitted memories 
 build that thematic spread directly in the MemoryBook 
 reorder pages in the book 
 

 This creates an end-to-end workflow in which the AI can first understand the collected material, reason about it, propose an editorial decision, and then make an actual change to the book when requested. 

 How we built it 

 MemoryBook is a full-stack web application built with React, TypeScript and Vite on the frontend, with a Node.js/Express backend and PostgreSQL for persistent data. 

 The visual editor supports editable text, drawing, images, layers, undo/redo, page navigation, saving and page previews. 

 For the WebMCP integration, I designed tools around meaningful user intentions instead of low-level interface controls. 

 These include tools for retrieving book context and status, listing contributions, checking event coverage, building a thematic spread, and reordering pages. 

 The AI therefore does not need to simulate mouse clicks or manipulate individual interface elements. It can discover structured capabilities exposed by the website and use them to work with the same MemoryBook data as the normal user interface. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge was connecting AI actions to a real, persistent editor rather than creating a scripted demonstration. 

 WebMCP operations had to work with the same pages, contribution data, saved state and previews used by the normal application. 

 Another challenge was choosing the right level of abstraction for the tools. Low-level controls would make the AI responsible for operating the UI. Higher-level WebMCP tools allow it to work with concepts that actually matter to the user: contributions, missing events, thematic spreads and page order. 

 Reliable saving and synchronization were also important because an AI-created page must behave like any page created or edited manually. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The most important accomplishment is a working end-to-end WebMCP workflow. 

 The AI can inspect real submitted memories, analyze their coverage, propose a thematic spread, and then build that spread directly in the MemoryBook. 

 The resulting content is not just an AI response in a chat window. It becomes part of the actual editable book. 

 The project also demonstrates that WebMCP can support both read-only analytical operations and actions that modify application state, while allowing the user to decide when an operation should be executed. 

 What we learned 

 Building MemoryBook changed how I think about AI integration in web applications. 

 An embedded chatbot can answer questions about an application. WebMCP enables something different: the website can expose what it is capable of doing, and an AI agent can use those capabilities as tools. 

 The most useful model is not necessarily AI replacing the interface. 

 A person may prefer a visual editor for creative decisions. An AI agent may be better at reviewing many contributions, identifying missing themes and organizing information. Both can work with the same underlying application and book. 

 What's next for MemoryBook 

 MemoryBook is currently a working prototype focused on demonstrating the WebMCP workflow. 

 The larger direction is a complete collaborative memory-book platform where groups can collect memories and photos, organize them with AI assistance, visually edit the result, and produce a finished digital or printable book. 

 Future development can expand the collaboration workflow, improve AI-assisted layout and organization, and add production-ready publishing and export capabilities. 

 WebMCP can make this process substantially easier by allowing AI agents to handle organizational and repetitive editorial work while keeping people in control of the final book.

title: kepler.gl webMCP
pitch: Empower AI agents like Codex to build, style, and explore interactive kepler.gl visualizations using WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Empower AI agents like Codex to build, style, and explore interactive kepler.gl visualizations using WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Kepler.gl WebMCP - demo 1 GIF Kepler.gl WebMCP - demo 2 (gif) Kepler.gl WebMCP - demo 3 Xun Li @Foursquare Inspiration Kepler.gl is a popular open source project for GPU-accelerated geovisualization, rendering millions of data points, trip animations, and flow maps via simple JSON configs. However, while modern AI agents like Codex/Claude code excel at spatial data preparation, preprocessing and analysis, they lack rich mapping tools—relying instead on flat, static plots. Bridging this gap used to require tedious manual friction: exporting data/results from the agent, opening kepler.gl, and rebuilding layers by hand. kepler.gl WebMCP eliminates that friction. Powered by the WebMCP standard, it exposes kepler.gl’s map controls directly to AI agents. Now, users can simply ask Codex(or Chrome webMCP puglin) to map their analysis and watch a live, interactive kepler.gl visualization build automatically with zero setup. What it does Open https://deploy-preview-3678--keplergl.netlify.app/demo in a WebMCP-enabled browser e.g. Codex browser and ask it to discover the site tools automatically. To create a map, ask in plain language and the agent composes the commands against the live map. Here are some examples: A map from your analysis data/results, in any style you can describe. "Get all roads in San Francisco and create a map using road types. Then make two more maps: 'winter SFO' using winter theme colors, and 'Van Gogh SFO' using Van Gogh Starry Night theme colors." The agent loads the data, feed to kepler.gl, add a new map layer, colors the roads by type — the skill turns "winter" and "Van Gogh Starry Night" into proper palettes. Animation with simulation/real data semantics. "Simulate 4 taxis moving on real driving routes in San Francisco, animate them on the map, and color them by company (Uber, Lyft, Waymo, Tesla)." The agent builds a trip layer by creating real driving routes along real streets, animates it over time, and colors each taxi by its company in kepler.gl. Everyday, personal data. "Create a flow map using the geotags and timestamps of the photos in my travel folder." The skill maps this to a flow layer, turning consecutive photo locations across a trip into origin–destination movements — a daily-life use case, not an expert feature. Here is a simulation that everyone can run: Every ask ends with a live, interactive kepler.gl map in the same browser — layers, colors, and animation all driven by the agent in real time. How we built it One contract, written once. Everything hangs on @kepler.gl/mcp package, which defines 12 map.* commands — data (load, save, create-table, add-column), layers (add-layer, update-layer-color), views (set-basemap, split-view, get-boundary), time filters, and dataset context. Each command has a ZOD input schema that converts once to JSON Schema (served to both MCP and WebMCP), policy metadata (read-only hints, risk), and results formatted as human-readable text for the model, not for an API. See the source code of kepler.gl/mcp at: https://github.com/keplergl/kepler.gl/pull/3678 Challenges we ran into Building on a moving target. WebMCP is an evolving draft standard with active UI, permissioning, and discovery developments. We mitigated this moving specification by shipping flexible adapters for both MCP and WebMCP API endpoints. The agent can’t see the map. Every command alters a visual surface where the ultimate source of truth is the rendered pixels. Right now, our tool outputs narrate the action taken rather than the visual result—closing that loop with screenshots and viewport deltas is our clear next step. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole kepler.gl map became a callable package. We extracted a mature map surface into @kepler.gl/mcp — twelve commands, dependency-light, with the kepler skill shipping inside. The same code now runs in a chat panel (kepler.gl AI assistant), an MCP relay, and browser WebMCP. What we learned Correctness comes from structure, not prompting. A structure with a combination of SKILL set and a limited number of tools is better than converting every function into tool. Write results for the model, not the API. Type-safe failures that die as an opaque UnknownError teach an agent nothing. It is better to return the details that say what went wrong to help agent work with the Kepler.gl webMCP. What's next for kepler.gl webMCP Close the visual loop. Let the agent see the map it's building — screenshots and viewport deltas as first-class command results — so it can verify its own work like a human would. Publish @kepler.gl/mcp to npm so any team can embed the same callable map surface in their own site or MCP server. Grow the ecosystem pipeline, so the "data processing → analyze → map → understand" conversation in Codex or other harness tools keeps expanding. title: WebMCP Operator Workspace
pitch: A shared workspace where WebMCP agents discover context-aware tools, prepare visible work, and apply sensitive actions only after human approval.
about_excerpt: A shared workspace where WebMCP agents discover context-aware tools, prepare visible work, and apply sensitive actions only after human approval. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration## Inspiration A website should be able to tell an AI agent what it can do, rather than making the agent infer every operation from visual controls. We built WebMCP Operator Workspace to explore a practical question: how can a human and an agent share an operational workspace while keeping capabilities contextual and sensitive decisions human-controlled? What it does The application presents a fictional hotel refrigeration incident across two pages: Case Workspace and Asset Inspector. In Case Workspace, an agent can read the incident, prepare a work plan, draft a customer update, select equipment components and prepare contextual observations. Prepared work appears in the interface for the human to review. The capability surface changes with context: Case Workspace initially exposes 11 tools. Selecting a component activates two additional tools, bringing the total to 13. Clearing the selection withdraws those tools, returning to 11. Navigating to Asset Inspector exposes six tools for that page. For sensitive proposals, the application separates preparation from approval. Applying a pending proposal is blocked. A human reviews it and clicks Approve in the page. The agent can then apply that proposal once; repeating it is rejected. There is no registered WebMCP tool to approve a proposal. On Asset Inspector, the agent can prepare an inspection note, but the final form save remains a human UI action. How we built it The project is a standalone application built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, hosted on GitHub Pages. It registers structured capabilities through document.modelContext.registerTool(). Contextual tools are withdrawn using AbortSignal, and each document registers its relevant tool surface. A semantic capability tree describes declared pages, interface regions and capabilities. It distinguishes application contracts from runtime observations: observing an unexpected tool does not automatically add it to the application's authorized surface. Navigation uses declared page identifiers rather than arbitrary URLs. Proposal handling uses explicit states and single-use approval consumption. The reviewed candidate passed 49 automated tests covering application contracts and behaviors, including approval states, replay rejection and contextual lifecycle scenarios. GitHub Actions runs the test suite. Challenges we faced The main challenge was separating three concepts: discovering a capability, preparing work and having authority to apply a sensitive proposal. Contextual tools must disappear when their context ends. Registration failures must not leave a partially active surface. Navigation must expose the destination page's capabilities rather than preserve stale assumptions. We also needed the interface to distinguish a prepared draft from a saved note, and an approved proposal from an applied action. What we learned WebMCP is useful not only for exposing operations, but also for making the agent-facing interface reflect the current application context. Visible shared state helps the human understand what the agent prepared. Explicit approval states make the transition from proposal to application understandable and testable. Accomplishments We combined contextual tool registration, a multipage capability surface, visible agent-prepared work and a human approval workflow in one publicly accessible application. The result demonstrates a complete application-level sequence: proposal, blocked premature application, human approval, single application and replay rejection. How to try it Open the live application with a WebMCP-compatible agent client and enter the workspace. Ask the agent to read the case, select condenser_fan, prepare an observation and clear the selection. Next, request a sensitive-action proposal and observe the blocked attempt before approving it manually. Ask the agent to apply the approved proposal and then repeat the same proposal to test replay rejection. Finally, navigate to asset-inspector and prepare an inspection note without submitting the human form. The application does not require our developer tunnel, proprietary Universal MCP runtime or credentials. An ordinary browser can display the human interface, but agent invocation requires a WebMCP-compatible client. Scope and limitations All incident, customer and equipment data is fictional. State is in memory and local to the active page; reloads and navigation do not promise persistence. Drafts do not send messages. Applying a proposal records a local demo event; it does not dispatch a technician or operate real equipment. The approval boundary demonstrates application workflow enforcement, not server-side authentication or protection against arbitrary browser automation. The accompanying video is an AI-generated explanation created with NotebookLM, not a screen recording of execution. What's next We would explore further usability testing and carefully scoped operational integrations. Persistence, identity and server-enforced authorization would require additional design before production use. title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. pitch: Recover missed leads with WebMCP while humans control the final booking.
about_excerpt:
Recover missed leads with WebMCP while humans control the final booking.

 Story

 Inspiration 

 Small service businesses lose valuable enquiries when calls are missed, follow-up is delayed, or customer details are scattered across disconnected tools. Recovering one lead can require several repetitive steps: identify the opportunity, understand the request, prepare a response, qualify the need, find availability, obtain approval, book the appointment, and update reporting. 

 Palm92 Lead Recovery OS explores a more useful open web where a person and an AI agent can complete that workflow together without surrendering human control. 

 What it does 

 Palm92 exposes seven structured browser-native WebMCP tools: 

 
 get_unrecovered_leads 
 get_lead_details 
 prepare_follow_up 
 recover_lead 
 find_available_appointments 
 prepare_appointment 
 get_recovery_summary 
 

 An agent can discover missed enquiries, inspect structured lead details, draft a follow-up, record an explicit fictional customer response, qualify the requirement, check appointment availability, and prepare an appointment. 

 The agent cannot complete the final booking. Palm92 pauses at a visible human approval checkpoint. Only the person can approve the final demonstration booking, after which the dashboard updates. 

 The governing principle is: AI investigates. Humans decide. 

 Why WebMCP 

 This workflow is a strong fit for WebMCP because it involves connected browser actions, structured business data, business context, and a consequential final decision. Instead of forcing an agent to infer controls from page layout, Palm92 makes safe capabilities explicitly discoverable through document.modelContext.registerTool . 

 The tools share the same in-browser state as the human-facing dashboard. Inputs use narrow JSON schemas and tool annotations describe their effects. This creates a coherent experience in which the agent handles investigation and preparation while the human retains authority. 

 Challenge-period work 

 Palm92 existed as a lead-recovery dashboard before the challenge. During the challenge period it was meaningfully extended with seven client-side JavaScript WebMCP tools, shared browser state, structured schemas, tool annotations, an agent-driven recovery sequence, automated checks, and a human-only approval boundary. The dated commit history and CHALLENGE_CHANGELOG.md distinguish this work from the earlier dashboard. 

 Demo result 

 The demonstration uses the fictional Daniel Reed kitchen-quote enquiry, valued at £2,400. After the approved recovery flow: 

 
 Calls recovered increase from 61 to 62 
 Appointments increase from 23 to 24 
 Recovered pipeline value increases from £7,050 to £9,450 
 

 All customer names, telephone numbers, records, and values are fictional demonstration data. No real customer is contacted and no external calendar is booked. 

 How it was built 

 Palm92 is a browser-based JavaScript application hosted on ChatGPT Sites. WebMCP tools are registered client-side through document.modelContext.registerTool . The tool layer and interface use the same state, so agent actions remain visible and understandable to the person. 

 Codex supported implementation planning, WebMCP tool refinement, debugging, safety checks, automated testing, repository preparation, demo editing, and validation of the end-to-end workflow. ChatGPT was used to test agent discovery and execution through the in-app browser's Site tools. 

 How to test 

 
 Open the live application in the latest ChatGPT desktop app using GPT-5.6 Sol or GPT-5.6 Terra. 
 Select Site tools in the address bar and inspect the seven Palm92 tools. 
 Ask the agent to find today's highest-value unrecovered lead and help recover it. 
 Let the agent inspect the lead, prepare the follow-up, qualify the opportunity, check availability, and prepare the appointment. 
 Confirm that the agent stops before booking and requests human approval. 
 Approve using the visible Palm92 control. 
 Confirm that the dashboard updates once to 62 recovered calls, 24 appointments, and £9,450 pipeline value. 
 

 No credentials are required. 

 Limitations and next steps 

 The current build uses fictional in-browser demonstration data and does not contact customers, update an external CRM, or book an external calendar. A production version would require secure identity, permissions, encrypted server-side integrations, consent controls, durable audit storage, monitoring, and configurable organisational policies.

title: Hand Off Helper
pitch: Live multiplayer ops room where a human support lead and an AI agent work the same support or incident case on the same page.
about_excerpt:
Live multiplayer ops room where a human support lead and an AI agent work the same support or incident case on the same page.

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 I am tired of "AI everywhere" and help nowhere. 

 You open a support chat because a charge posted twice. You get a polite paragraph. You ask for the refund. You get another paragraph. You ask for a person. You get a form. Twenty minutes later the money still has not moved and you still cannot see who owns the case. 

 That is the loop I wanted to break. Not "more chatbot." A page where an agent can actually do the work, I can see every step, and I still have to approve anything that spends money or emails the customer. 

 What it does 

 Handoff is a multiplayer ops room for one live support case. 

 I am Jordan, the human lead. The agent is on the same board. We share CASE-1042: Maya Chen, duplicate Pro annual charge, $2,388, chargeback risk. 

 The agent does not scrape the UI. The page registers WebMCP tools, so it can get_case , draft_customer_reply , propose_refund , issue_refund , send_customer_reply , page_oncall , and resolve_case . Drafts show up in public. Refunds sit behind an Approve / Reject card. If I reject, that is a first-class event. Nothing irreversible happens in the dark. 

 Live site: https://handoffhelper.com 

 How I built it 

 Vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No Next.js. No backend. State lives in the page. 

 Tools register with document.modelContext.registerTool , with navigator.modelContext as fallback. Each tool has a JSON schema. Read-only tools are marked readOnlyHint . Destructive tools open an on-page approval gate before they commit. The same store drives the UI, the timeline, and the tool results, so what the agent does is what I see. 

 I shipped it on Cloudflare Pages at handoffhelper.com so judges do not hit a login wall. 

 Challenges I faced 

 WebMCP was new to me. I had used the phrase "MCP" and assumed server-side Model Context Protocol. This challenge is the browser spec: the page exposes tools to the model. 

 That distinction ate time. I had to learn registerTool , the schemas, readOnlyHint , and what happens when modelContext is missing. Early on the public URL was a ChatGPT Site that required login. Useless for a judge. I bought handoffhelper.com and moved the static files to Cloudflare. 

 The other hard part was the human gate. It is easy to let the agent "just send the email." It is harder to make approve / reject visible, blocking, and logged under two identities. I wanted the kill switch to be obvious, not a hidden confirm in the model transcript. 

 What I learned 

 Agents are fast at draft and lookup. They should not be trusted with money or customer email until a person says yes. 

 If the tools are sloppy, the model asks extra questions and the demo dies. Tight descriptions ("do not call issue_refund until propose_refund exists") mattered more than extra features. 

 And a public URL with no login is part of the product. If a judge cannot open the page, the tools do not exist.

An agent that finds and negotiates your next purchase, while you stay in control.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 AEON — The Agent Economy, Human Controlled 

 Inspiration 

 AEON started with one question: 

 
 How much authority should an AI agent have when real money is involved? 
 

 AI agents are moving beyond answering questions. They can search, use tools, negotiate, and increasingly act on our behalf. 

 That made me interested in a bigger idea: what happens when agents become participants in the economy too? 

 AEON is my exploration of that future. 

 The principle is simple: 

 
 Let the agent do the work. Keep the decisions that matter with the human. 
 

 

 What It Does 

 AEON turns a natural-language request into a commerce mission. 

 For example: 

 
 “Find me a smartphone under ₦500,000. Get the best deal you can, but ask me before purchasing.” 
 

 AEON can: 

 
 Understand the goal, budget, and constraints 
 Search and compare products 
 Build multi-product baskets 
 Negotiate with seller agents 
 Check actions against the user's authority 
 Stop for human approval 
 Execute only after approval 
 

 The journey is: 

 Search → Evaluate → Negotiate → Govern → Approval → Execute 

 

 Human-Controlled Authority 

 The core idea behind AEON is that capability should not automatically mean authority . 

 An agent may be capable of negotiating or purchasing, but the user decides what it is allowed to do. 

 For example: 

 
 Budget: ₦500,000 
 Negotiation: Authorized 
 Purchase: Human approval required 
 

 Even if AEON negotiates a valid deal within budget, it still stops before purchasing. 

 The human gets the final say. 

 

 WebMCP 

 AEON uses WebMCP to expose structured capabilities such as: 

 create_mission 
 search_products 
 compare_products 
 negotiate_offer 
 request_purchase_approval 

 WebMCP provides the capabilities. 

 AEON defines the mission. 

 The Constitution defines the boundaries. 

 The human controls consequential actions. 

 

 How I Built It 

 AEON is built with: 

 
 React 
 TypeScript 
 Vite 
 WebMCP 
 

 The system includes natural-language mission parsing, marketplace search, product comparison, multi-product baskets, seller-agent negotiation, governance, human approval, execution, and observability. 

 

 Challenges 

 The hardest part was making everything behave like one coherent agent system. 

 I had to solve issues around: 

 
 Mission state leaking between runs 
 Approval state not matching the UI 
 Negotiation finishing too early 
 Keeping the technical trace aligned with the visible journey 
 Handling missing budgets, invalid input, no results, multiple products, declined deals, and new missions 
 

 A lot of the final product came from fixing these edge cases. 

 

 What I'm Proud Of 

 AEON demonstrates a complete agent-commerce loop: 

 Natural language → Search → Evaluation → Negotiation → Governance → Human approval → Execution 

 I'm especially proud of: 

 
 Agent-to-agent negotiation 
 Multi-product missions 
 The Constitution Firewall 
 Human-controlled execution 
 WebMCP-powered capabilities 
 

 

 What I Learned 

 Building an agent is not just about giving it more tools. 

 The harder questions are: 

 
 What should it understand? 

 What should it be allowed to do? 

 When should it stop and ask the human? 
 

 I also learned that transparency does not mean showing everything. Users mainly need to understand what the agent is doing, why it is doing it, and when their decision is required. 

 

 What's Next 

 I want to explore AEON as part of a broader agent economy where humans, agents, and merchants can interact safely. 

 Future directions include: 

 
 Real marketplace integrations 
 Better agent-to-agent negotiation 
 Persistent user constitutions 
 Granular spending permissions 
 Merchant agents 
 Identity and transaction verification 
 Prompt-injection protection 
 Stronger audit trails 
 Safer payment handling 
 

 If agents are going to participate in real economic activity, trust cannot be added at the end. 

 It has to be part of the architecture from the beginning. 

 AEON — The Agent Economy, Human Controlled.
