title: Actuo Expense Manager
pitch: Turns out AI agents can act like human can, just had to teach two apps that don't know each other to actually talk.
about_excerpt: Turns out AI agents can act like human can, just had to teach two apps that don't know each other to actually talk. Like Comment Story Updates Landing page Expense List Add Expense Page Settings page list all function calls history and settings for custom agent settings (Model selection and BYOK Config) Agent Page listing all available tools and a custom chatbot agent that calls 3rd party app tools embedded with <iframe allow="tools">. Dashboard page with a 3rd Party Utility with WebMCP enabled embedded with <iframe allow="tools"> for converting currencies Inspiration I deliver a lot of talks around new and upcoming features of web, across the Indian Developer Community, which involves me spending a great deal of time investigating new features of web platforms so that I can pass them on to our community. Recently I came across WebMCP, and a very simple concept drew my interest. An AI agent shouldn't have to work out what a button does by randomly clicking around a page; instead it should be able to carry out the same actions as a human user, using an actual contract and the same authentication and rules. It seemed like a good idea to base a proper project on it rather than just go through the documentation. My aim was not to launch a well-polished startup; I only wanted to use the standard from beginning to end, discover its shortcomings on my own, and create something tangible to contribute back to the community. That exploration eventually became Actuo. What it does Actuo is a multi-tenant expense management application which includes features such as organizations, roles, budgets, approval workflows, and support for multiple currencies. I designed it in such a way that each significant action taken by a user through the user interface also corresponds to a real WebMCP tool that is registered directly via document.modelContext . Read-only tools: For example, there's search_expenses , get_budget_status , get_spend_summary , and fetch_categories . I've also included a generate_report tool which can be cancelled during the process by means of an AbortSignal , the result being that the server actually gives up on the task rather than the browser simply ignoring the result. Mutating tools: The submit_expense tool has the ability to mutate data; I showed this by using the WebMCP declarative API with no JavaScript involvement, simply employing a regular HTML form on the Add Expense page and including the appropriate tool annotations. State-gated tools: The approve_expense tool appears in the list returned by getTools() only when a signed-in admin has pending expenses that need approving; once the queue is empty the tool disappears. Custom Agent powered by Gemini API: A custom agent can use a functions/tools from third party currency converter app embedded using <iframe allow="tools"> to convert the expense value to base currency. Following snippet can fetch those tools and we can use Gemini API function calling if we are building our own agent. Navigation Tools: Built in navigation tools allowing agents to act exactly like human and navigate between pages while performing tasks. Sample prompts to try Sign in, open the Copilot orb, and paste any of these, each is chosen to hit a different tool or WebMCP aspect from the table below. Try this What it exercises What did we spend on software this month? get_spend_summary — read-only, runs instantly, no confirmation How much budget is left for Travel this month? get_budget_status — read-only Show me all pending expenses from last week search_expenses — read-only, untrusted-content badge What categories do we have set up? fetch_categories — read-only File a ₹1,200 lunch at Barista submit_expense — mutating , stops for confirmation before writing Export last month's expenses as CSV — then hit Cancel while it runs generate_report — cancellable , AbortSignal end to end (as priya@actuo.demo , with pending items) Approve all pending expenses under ₹2,000 approve_expense — state-gated , only registered for owner/admin with a non-empty queue (on /agent ) Convert 200 EUR to INR Cross-origin: discovers and calls a tool from Cambiaro , an independently deployed converter app Sign in as arjun@actuo.demo (member) and try the approval prompt again and approve_expense won't even appear in the tool list, since it's gated server-side by role, not just hidden in the UI. // getting tools for own app await document.modelContext.getTools(); // getting tools for 3rd party app embedded with <iframe allow="tools"> await document.modelContext.getTools({ fromOrigins: ['https://cambiaro.programmersingh.dev'] }); The aspect that interested me most to develop was the /agent screen since it demonstrates interoperability between different origins rather than merely within a single application. It presents as an independent WebMCP-enabled site the currency converter I developed called Cambiaro. Actuo does not own the code for Cambiaro; instead, Actuo calls getTools({ fromOrigins }) on Cambiaro and receives back the actual tool descriptions across the origin boundary, together with all the security annotations remaining unaltered. I confirmed this in real time between two deployed URLs and as a result of calling Cambiaro's currency tool from Actuo the embedded widget on Cambiaro's side was actually updated. How I built it For the frontend I used Angular with support for SSR and PWA, on the backend I used NestJS and for the database I used Supabase. The specifications for each tool are defined just once in a common file as a JSON Schema. This same schema is registered on the client side and employed by the server when validating each incoming request. Thus there is a single source of truth regarding what a tool actually accepts. I always followed one strict rule during the project. Anything that WebMCP makes available at the discovery level is solely for the purpose of improving the user experience and ensuring interoperability, not to serve as a security boundary. Although it is useful to hide the approve_expense function from the discovery level for a non-administrator, the backend still independently checks the caller's role in the database on each and every call, no matter what the client discovers. Challenges I ran into Definitely the most difficult aspect was getting the cross-origin feature to work. It took a great deal of trial and error to work out the settings for exposedTo , fromOrigins , and the iframe's allow="tools" permission policy between the two separately deployed applications. A tool remains invisible to origins other than its own unless its registration specifically lists the consuming origin; that is why Actuo has to pass along its own origin to Cambiaro when the frame loads if the handshake is to work. A further difficulty consisted in making the state-gated tools genuinely secure rather than merely hiding them visually. It is one thing to hide a tool from a list, but much more effort is required to ensure that its disappearance is supported by an independently enforced check, and to prove this by writing tests for someone who is attempting to spoof a role claim. What I learned The most important thing I've learned is that looking at the examples in the specification does not prepare you for the kind of experience you'll actually have when developing a real application. It wasn't until I had gotten deep into the code that I realised how much of the fascinating WebMCP surface area only becomes available when you have actual users, genuine roles, and live data. Features such as state-gating, cancellation, cross-origin discovery, and security annotations simply don't appear in the single-page toy demonstrations. That's precisely the kind of insight I hope to bring back to my GDG talk; I don't just want to show the API, I want to demonstrate what happens when you actually try to use it. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Making the cross-origin connection work in both directions. When you invoke the currency converter from Actuo's /agent screen, the currency converter doesn't simply return a fixed figure; you can actually see the state change on Cambiaro, which is a completely separate and independently deployed application. It was only when two applications with different codebases and release cycles started genuinely communicating with each other using just the WebMCP origin handshake that this stopped being merely a specification I was reading and became something real that I could demonstrate. Creating state-gated tools that are truly secure, not just appearing so. While it's a pleasant user experience that the expense approval tool doesn't appear on the frontend when you're not an admin, I made certain that this wasn't just a visual illusion. Each time a request is made, the backend independently checks the user's role. I also prepared specific tests to detect anyone attempting to forge their role claim. My aim was to be able to state with confidence that the application is genuinely secure, not mer

title: Field Assist
pitch: Field Assist lets Codex and a human expert turn a live phone camera into verified, object-tracked guidance—pointing users to the correct physical control.
about_excerpt: Field Assist lets Codex and a human expert turn a live phone camera into verified, object-tracked guidance—pointing users to the correct physical control. Like Comment Story Updates Connect a phone to the live support workspace with a one-time QR link. Phone-visible guidance points the operator toward the verified control. Codex asks the operator to confirm the identified physical device. The object-relative arrow remains associated with the target as the camera moves. Inspiration Earlier this week, before I discovered The WebMCP Challenge, I published experimental WebMCP support for GoFastr. When I saw the hackathon, my honest reaction was basically: “heck yeah—this is exactly what that package is for.” I wanted to test the browser-agent bridge against something much harder than a catalog or form demo. Remote support repeatedly fails at the last few inches: the operator is holding a phone, the expert says “press the button underneath,” and everyone is forced to translate vague language into physical action. Field Assist asks what happens when Codex, a human support representative, and the person holding the camera can share one live, structured workspace. Field Assist itself was built for this hackathon on top of that newly published GoFastr capability. What it does Field Assist creates a two-device support session. A support representative opens the desktop console and shares a one-time QR code. The operator scans it, grants rear-camera access, and selects a starter scenario or describes any problem in free form. The camera travels directly to the support browser over peer-to-peer WebRTC; the application server never records or relays the video. Codex joins through the authenticated support page’s WebMCP tools. It loads the application’s operating contract, reads the operator’s request, inspects the visible scene, and combines vision with product knowledge to form a hypothesis. When identity is uncertain, Codex asks the operator a bounded question on the phone. Once the device and its actionable control are separately verified, Codex can send a large phone-visible instruction and place an arrow at the control. The support representative can inspect, correct, compose, or remove the same shared guidance. OpenCV, Depth Anything V2, Canvas tracking, and short-lived phone orientation data help keep the arrow associated with the physical target as the camera moves. When geometry becomes unsafe, Field Assist suppresses the marker and asks for reacquisition instead of pretending it still knows. Why WebMCP Why is this a strong fit for WebMCP? Field Assist depends on live, authenticated browser state: a private camera session, changing scene geometry, operator answers, tracking confidence, and delivery receipts. WebMCP lets Codex use those application concepts directly instead of guessing at UI controls or receiving a giant screenshot-and-prompt dump. How does it create a better user experience? The operator keeps one hand on the phone and receives large, timely instructions plus spatial guidance where they are already looking. Codex and human support share the same backend-authoritative scene, conversation, question, and banner state, so the operator does not repeat context or translate ambiguous chat into physical action. What can people and agents do together that was difficult before? The person supplies intent, judgment, and physical confirmation. Codex contributes vision, product knowledge, structured questions, and rapid guidance. Together they can identify an unfamiliar device, confirm the correct object, locate a small control, guide the operator toward it, and withdraw the annotation if tracking becomes unsafe—all inside one live support session. How did I implement WebMCP? The authenticated support page exposes twenty-five tools generated by GoFastr through the standard document.modelContext.registerTool API. Read tools return versioned session and scene state. Mutating tools call the same authenticated Go handlers as the human controls and must include the current contextVersion. Landing and operator pages expose no support capabilities. How we built it Field Assist is one Go 1.27 service built on the released GoFastr v0.75.0 module. GoFastr provides the server-rendered application host, typed handlers, security middleware, WebSocket hub, lifecycle endpoints, structured logs, static plugin assets, and experimental WebMCP bridge. The authenticated support page declares twenty-five semantic tools for application context, scene inspection, object registration, room context, conversation, operator questions, banners, snapshots, and reversible spatial guidance. The mandatory get_app_info tool copies a versioned operating contract and the user’s current request into Codex context. Every state-changing tool must return that context version, which prevents an agent from acting against stale instructions. Browser-native WebRTC sends video directly from the phone to the support computer. GoFastr WebSockets carry only signaling and compact shared state. The support computer runs OpenCV ORB/RANSAC homography and PnP tracking alongside Depth Anything V2 Small through ONNX Runtime Web. A lightweight phone tracker and bounded DeviceOrientation samples bridge short visual gaps over a peer-to-peer data channel. Camera pixels, descriptors, depth maps, orientation samples, SDP, and ICE candidates are never stored by the application server. The interfaces are responsive and deliberately asymmetric: the phone prioritizes the live camera, large instructions, questions, answer acknowledgment, and chat; the desktop prioritizes the shared scene, support conversation, guidance controls, delivery state, and progressive diagnostics. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was not drawing an arrow—it was deciding when an arrow was trustworthy. Early versions anchored annotations to screen coordinates, confused a broad device with a tiny physical control, or kept displaying stale guidance after tracking loss. Reflective televisions and dark hardware exposed every weakness in monocular depth and feature matching. Another challenge was keeping three participants synchronized: the operator, human support, and Codex. Local optimistic UI caused banners and answers to disagree between screens, so the backend became authoritative for conversation, questions, banners, scene versions, and delivery receipts. Testing a two-device, hands-busy experience was also physically awkward. I repeatedly had to hold the phone in front of real hardware while Codex operated the support console. Those sessions forced the application contract to become explicit: inspect first, confirm uncertain identity, register the containing device before its control, send movement instructions to the phone banner, verify rendered delivery, and fail closed when tracking confidence drops. Finally, WebMCP is experimental. The application needed to make its own operating expectations discoverable without asking judges to install a separate skill. get_app_info became the handshake that teaches any compatible Codex session how to use Field Assist safely. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real iPhone-to-desktop, video-only WebRTC support session with no account required. Twenty-five authenticated WebMCP tools available only on the support page. Codex as the only runtime agent; Field Assist embeds no separate model API. Shared two-way conversation, phone-visible questions, answer acknowledgment, and backend-authoritative banners. Separate semantic objects for a device and its actionable physical control. Reversible object-relative arrows with explicit tracking-loss behavior. Support-side OpenCV and Depth Anything inference without uploading camera frames. Ten-minute, single-use QR links exchanged for role-scoped HTTP-only cookies. Deterministic Codex evaluations, Go tests, and two-browser Playwright coverage. A public live deployment, public MIT-licensed repository, and a complete narrated demo under three minutes. What we learned A useful agent integration needs more than tool schemas. The agent needs the application’s safety model, ordering constraints, versioned context, and definitions of success. Separating identity, localization, tracking, delivery, and physical confirmation prevented plausible-looking UI from being mistaken for proof. Depth estimation does not magically create a persistent 3D world model. It becomes useful when combined with visual features, stable object identity, bounded camera-pose estimation, and honest loss behavior. Reflective or texture-poor objects remain difficult, and the product should say so. Realtime UX also needs one source of truth. Once questions, messages, banners, observations, and guidance receipts came from backend state, the operator, support representative, and Codex stopped telling different stories. Most importantly, WebMCP works best when it exposes application meaning rather than mirroring buttons. Codex should ask for “the current scene” or

Before acting on the physical world, the operator confirms the detected object. That human checkpoint prevents the assistant from confidently guiding someone toward the wrong device. Once confirmed, the support console starts visual tracking and spatial perception. OpenCV follows image features, depth, and anything estimate scene structure, and phone orientation data helps compensate as the camera moves. Codex uses its product knowledge and the live visual context to locate the likely power control. It then sends one clear instruction to the phone where it is impossible to miss while the operator is holding the camera. The arrow is not merely pinned to screen coordinates. Field Assist continually corrects it against the tracked object and scene geometry as the operator changes position. The support agent can verify the placement, recalibrate when confidence drops, and keep the instruction synchronized across both screens. >> The same interaction applies far beyond consumer electronics, equipment repair, device setup, field service, accessibility, independent living, remote care, warehouse picking, inspections, and safety training. Anywhere pointing is clearer than describing, remote expertise can become actionable. The stack combines codecs and web MCP with go faster, web RTC, open CV, depth anything, ONNX runtime web, and phone orientation, all in one web app. Field Assist turns remote expertise into guidance anchored to the real world.

title: The Wringer
pitch: Put agent work on trial before you trust it.
about_excerpt: Put agent work on trial before you trust it. Like Comment Story Updates The agent operates the public TheWringer.ai application through WebMCP. ChatGPT begins with a rough task that must be made verifiable. The free read-only review inspects the active case without starting a paid action. The same visible form a human uses updates from the agent tool call. The Wringer identifies missing machine checks and unfalsifiable expected signals. The agent replaces the weak criterion in the same shared application state. A structured WebMCP call writes intent into the product rather than scraping controls. The agent prepares the real $1 audit workflow but does not start checkout. The page requires visible confirmation and reports that checkout and charging have not started. The final handoff remains visible to both the agent and the human. An existing MECHA result demonstrates the product beyond the free WebMCP judge flow. The report ties each acceptance criterion to an explicit outcome. The reviewer compares Claude, Codex, and Grok candidates and records failures honestly. The final report separates verified evidence, incomplete checks, and remaining human judgment. The evidence report explains the selected answer rather than returning an unsupported claim. Devpost submission Project name The Wringer Tagline Put agent work on trial before you trust it. Inspiration AI agents can complete increasingly consequential work, but the instruction they receive is often a vague sentence and the result is often accepted without evidence. That creates two failures: the agent does the wrong job because the request was underspecified, or it claims success without proving the result. The Wringer already helped humans turn rough requests into checkable work orders, stress-test those contracts, and execute them through a multi-agent MECHA run. WebMCP revealed the missing half of the product: the agent itself should be able to understand and operate that verification workflow without guessing at buttons, scraping the page, or creating a second agent-only interface. I built the challenge extension around one question: what if a website could help an agent challenge its own instructions before either the agent or the human trusted the outcome? What it does The Wringer turns vague agent work into a structured case file containing a finished-state goal, acceptance criteria, boundaries, an iteration budget, and explicit authorization for risky actions. Through six native WebMCP tools, a compatible browser agent can: create_case_file to write a structured request into the same visible form a human uses. review_case_file to expose missing machine checks and unfalsifiable expected signals. run_quick_attack to stage a $1 adversarial contract audit. apply_audit_repairs to put a repaired contract back into the shared case file. start_full_case to stage a real sandboxed MECHA execution. get_full_case_status to read bounded progress, evidence, verdict, and cost information. The Agent Docket makes each tool call, finding, repair, and approval handoff visible on the page. Read operations remain read-only. Paid operations can be prepared by the agent, but they stop at a visible human confirmation card. The tool response explicitly reports confirmation_required: true , checkout_started: false , and charged: false . The normal interface remains fully functional in browsers without WebMCP. How we built it The Wringer is a Next.js 14 and React 18 application deployed on Vercel. I added a dedicated WebMCP adapter using the current document.modelContext.registerTool() API, strict JSON Schema inputs, registration AbortSignal cleanup, execution cancellation, accurate readOnlyHint metadata, and untrustedContentHint for provider-derived output. WebMCP is not a duplicate implementation. The human interface and browser tools operate the same React state, contract compiler, route adapters, application services, payment boundary, and MECHA runtime. Server routes remain thin adapters over reusable services. The production system uses Stripe Checkout for paid entitlements, Upstash Redis for atomic payment redemption and bounded replay recovery, OpenRouter for Quick Attack and scoped MECHA model access, xAI for the Grok coach, Daytona for isolated per-run sandboxes, Resend for optional deliverables, and PostHog for product analytics. Challenge work also hardened the boundaries required to expose real product actions safely. It added XML-safe contract compilation, bounded input validation, a browser-bound Stripe callback, signed HttpOnly payment cookies, atomic claim consumption, per-run five-hour OpenRouter keys capped to the purchased budget, sanitized links, run ownership checks, security headers, replay recovery, and deterministic smoke tests. The Wringer existed before the challenge. The canonical pre-challenge baseline is commit a193707 , dated August 12, 2026. Supporting product work between 298162d and 642fd77 improved examples and deliverables but did not implement WebMCP. The challenge branch starts from 642fd77 ; the WebMCP tools, shared-service extraction, Agent Docket, security hardening, tests, browser verification, and documentation were added during the submission period. The complete boundary is documented in docs/hackathon-changes.md . Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was making WebMCP operate a real paid product rather than a disconnected demonstration. Once an agent can stage audits and multi-agent runs, schema validation alone is not enough. Authorization, payment redemption, replay behavior, ownership, provider credentials, cancellation, and human approval all become part of the tool contract. The security review found several boundaries that were acceptable for a human-only prototype but unsafe for an agent-accessible workflow. Payment consumption needed to become atomic. Checkout callbacks needed to stop trusting request origins. Stripe session IDs needed protection as bearer capabilities. Sandbox credentials needed narrower transport. Provider output and links needed to be treated as untrusted. I fixed those issues with Devin before exposing the workflows. WebMCP is also evolving. Chrome's testing implementation and current examples did not always present input schemas and execution arguments identically. Keeping all direct browser API usage in a small adapter, maintaining a capability smoke test, and verifying against Chrome 150 and ChatGPT's in-app browser prevented specification details from leaking throughout the application. The final challenge was demonstration clarity. A successful tool call is invisible unless the human can see what changed. That led to the Agent Docket and the explicit confirmation card, which make the collaboration legible without turning the product into another chat window. Accomplishments that we're proud of Six focused native WebMCP tools operate the production product rather than a mock catalog or challenge-only page. ChatGPT's in-app browser can create, review, repair, and stage a case against shared visible application state. The free judge flow reveals two concrete verification gaps, repairs them, and reaches the approval boundary without purchasing a Wringer run or invoking a paid backend provider. Paid and outward actions remain under human control. The agent cannot silently open checkout or spend money. The UI and WebMCP paths share business logic instead of drifting into separate implementations. Production health confirms the payment ledger, signed-cookie boundary, Stripe, Quick Attack, and Full Case provider boundaries are configured. The repository is public, MIT licensed, documented, reproducible, and explicit about what existed before the challenge. Chrome 150 discovered all six tools and executed the deployed create, review, repair, and confirmation sequence through document.modelContext . What we learned Agent-native does not mean adding a chatbot. It means publishing precise intentions, keeping state shared and visible, and enforcing trust boundaries on the server. A strict JSON Schema improves reliability, but it is not authorization. A valid tool call can still target the wrong resource, replay a paid entitlement, cross a user's ownership boundary, or trigger an irreversible action. The same authorization and audit expectations must apply whether the caller is a person, ChatGPT, or Devin. I also learned that human-agent collaboration needs a visual grammar. The Agent Docket tells the human what the agent called and what changed. The confirmation card makes the moment of responsibility unmistakable. Those interface elements did more for trust than exposing additional tools would have. Finally, fewer complete tools beat a broad unfinished surface. Each submitted tool has a precise purpose, strict schema, structured result, lifecycle behavior, error path, metadata, test coverage, and documentation. What's next for The Wringer The first post-hackathon target is to strengthen the WebMCP adapter into a version

video_transcript_excerpt: Agent work usually starts with a vague prompt and ends with an answer nobody can verify. The Ringer changes that. This is the live production site and ChatGPT's in-app browser has discovered six native web MCP tools. First, the agent creates a case file. The same form a human uses updates instantly. Next, it reviews the case. The Ringer catches two real gaps. There is no machine check and no falsifiable expected signal. The agent repairs both in the same shared state. Now it stages a $1 quick attack. Watch the boundary. Confirmation required. Checkout not started. Charged false. The agent can understand the product, improve the work, and prepare execution, but it cannot spend for me. The normal interface still works without web MCP and both humans and agents use the same application services. This is not remote-controlled clicking. The website publishes precise capabilities. The agent invokes them directly and the Ringer keeps the human in control.

title: Corealm
pitch: Corealm is a browser based medieval RPG built for an AI agent to sit beside you using WebMCP, whether that means guiding you with suggestions and overlays or playing the game itself.
about_excerpt: Corealm is a browser based medieval RPG built for an AI agent to sit beside you using WebMCP, whether that means guiding you with suggestions and overlays or playing the game itself. Like Comment Story Updates Corealm Inspiration This game is inspired by Runescape, Runelite, and Knight Online. There both games fight against bots while offering pay to win mechanics. Corealm takes a different stance and builds "botting" as part of the game. You can also choose to only use the agent as a guide in a similar way Runelite works, which uses overlays. What it does Its a browser based RPG where your ai agent can play alongside you. The agent can help you plan what's next, show you the steps for a quest, or grind away at tasks you might just not have the time for. How we built it Vite + TypeScript + Three.js, with Rapier for physics and Recast for navmeshes. The agent API is a thin WebMCP tool layer using the same functions the UI calls. The docs are generated from the same data the game runs on and is exposed two ways: the Astro site for humans, and corealm_search_docs that agents query directly. Challenges we ran into Honestly the WebMCP was the easy part, making a game in less than a week was the hard part. I wanted to make sure the game had enough content to feel worthwhile while not packing too much in and lowering the overall quality. Accomplishments that we're proud of The fact this went form an idea to a working prove of concept within a week. I've never built a full 3D RPG before, this was a huge undertaking for me. What we learned I learned a lot about how WebMCP works and came up with ideas how we can use this in fintech where I work. I also learned a lot about how 3D games are built and all the nuances to having a compelling game with proper animations sequences, sounds, good lighting, textures, ect its a lot. This makes me appreciate all the work that goes in to these types of games. What's next for Corealm Honestly might push this through and polish the content much more! Currently the game only has content for level 1-20, it'd be nice to continue to grow the game and refine the overall look and feel. title: AgentSignal
pitch: Share with site owners what AI agents had trouble finding so that they can update their website for future visits.
about_excerpt:
Share with site owners what AI agents had trouble finding so that they can update their website for future visits. 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 As someone who manages websites, I realized that I really have no way of knowing whether the website contained what a user was looking for. Sure, you can measure a new lead, but there are lots of situations outside of that where you simply don’t know. 

 What it does 

 AgentSignal provides a simple way for agents to let site owners know when they could not find information on a website they went to. Let’s say a user wants to know whether an event is wheelchair accessible. Their agent visits the event website, but it does not contain information about wheelchair accessibility. The agent can then use AgentSignal to provide a small amount of information on what they were looking for but could not find. The site owner can then see this and choose to update their website with that info to help future site visitors. 

 How we built it 

 This was made with Codex. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Privacy was a concern for this, so being specific about what type of information the agent should/should not share was important. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 This is a pretty simple project, but something I would find genuinely useful. 

 What we learned 

 I learned about WebMCP and I look forward to using it more in the future. 

 What's next for AgentSignal 

 I would like to integrate this into my own website. I will consider things like this in a professional setting also.
